triggerList.title: IRAN's Deportation Plan
triggerList.description: Iran has announced the deportation plan for 2 million refugees by March 2025. If the large number of Afghans has to return from Iran, that will create a huge burden for Afghanistan to accommodate. Considering the situation in Afghanistan, humanitarian assistance required for the existing population is high, these returnees from Pakistan and Iran on a sudden will create an extreme scenario, Afghanistan will not be able to adjust.

rationale:
Pakistan is hosting around 1.5 million Afghan refugees as of October 2024. In 2023, Pakistan government initiated a massive repatriation of approximately 4 million Afghans who were mainly undocumented and termed as illegal foreign nation. Alone in 2024, around 1.2 million Afghans has returned to Afghanistan from Pakistan and Iran, which has created a burning humanitarian need upon their arrival. The return is continuing in 2025 with an increase of 44% in February 2025 than the previous month. Afghanistan's dire economic condition and funding gap has impacted in people's food security, shelter and livelihood need which has intensified with US Funding Freeze declaration as an aggravating factor.  
According to IPC Afghanistan is facing severe food insecurity with projection of 14.8 million people classified in level 3 or above will need urgent humanitarian food assistance between November 2024 to March 2025. The scenario has high provability to worsen with the fund cut declared by US Government. Afghanistan is struggling to meet basic services need for the residents with an estimated 6.3 million people in protracted displacement. 
Pakistan has declared a deportation plan for Afghan Nationals living in Pakistan setting a deadline for 31st March 2025, while Iran also declared the plan to deport 2 million Afghans by March 2025. Approximately 1.2 million Afghan refugees in Pakistan are affected by the funding freeze, leading to the closure of over 60 health facilities that provided essential services, left many without access to essential medical services, exacerbating health risks. This situation has caused panic among Afghan refugees, who fear returning to Afghanistan due to potential persecution and economic hardships under Taliban rule.
Since the Taliban's takeover in 2021, over 500,000 Afghans have been living without proper documentation in Pakistan, awaiting resettlement. Afghan refugees in Pakistan, particularly those who collaborated with U.S. organizations, are confronting heightened risks due to the recent suspension of U.S. funding and the halt of resettlement programs. These individuals now face potential deportation from Pakistan, where authorities have intensified pressure on undocumented Afghans to return to Afghanistan. They fear persecution, and thus not willing to return to Afghanistan. 
Continuing with the current detention, arrest, harassment scenario by government agency in Pakistan and Iran, Afghan refugees will be forced to return to Afghanistan in any unsafe way, and they will face protection needs along with basic humanitarian assistance for survival. This will further create an emerging need of humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan, while the country is already having a dire situation specially after US Fund cut.

triggerList.title: Below-average precipitation continuation
triggerList.description: The onset of a precipitation deficit serves as a key early-warning trigger in Afghanistan’s drought cycle, as sustained below-average rainfall reduces soil moisture, delays snow accumulation, and weakens river and groundwater recharge. According to the World Meteorological Organization and FEWS NET, such early deficits rapidly translate into water shortages that undermine winter crop growth and pasture regeneration, threatening food and income sources for farming and herding households. As water scarcity deepens, communities face heightened competition for limited resources, while reduced snowmelt later constrains drinking-water access. This chain reaction beginning with rainfall failure marks the start of humanitarian stress, often leading to displacement, rising food insecurity, and increased reliance on aid in the most drought-prone provinces

triggerList.title: Above-average temperatures
triggerList.description: Extreme temperatures are expected to persist through December 2025, worsening vegetation stress and water shortages in rangeland and agricultural areas.

triggerList.title: Reduced snow water equivalent
triggerList.description: Snow water equivalent levels below average in most river basins limit spring meltwater availability for irrigation during critical agricultural periods.

rationale:
In Afghanistan, La Niña conditions started in October 2025 and are likely to persist until the February–March 2026 period. La Niña typically brings below-normal snowfall and rainfall combined with above-average temperatures in the country, driving drought-like conditions that significantly degrade agricultural productivity and water availability. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions face a heightened risk of both agricultural and hydrological drought, directly threatening food security and rural livelihoods for farming and pastoralist communities. The current agricultural deficit reflects cumulative climate stress. In the 2024–2025 period, Afghanistan faced its fourth consecutive season of below-average production, with documented crop failures across eastern and northern areas. Dry conditions are likely to affect 2025 second-season crops (rice, cotton, and maize), most of which are harvested at the end of October, while forecasted below-average winter precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 is likely to affect winter wheat production in 2026. Dry conditions also heighten concerns about fodder availability, likely affecting households dependent on pastoral income.
Below-average winter rainfall and snowfall are expected to curtail water availability in spring/summer, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and snowmelt-fed rivers vital for agriculture and drinking water. Agricultural stress and water scarcity will compound the impact of recent seismic events. A series of earthquakes in 2025 destroyed homes and water/sanitation infrastructure while displacing tens of thousands, simultaneously triggering emergency shelter and WASH needs. Earthquake impacts, layered atop drought and flood shocks, have dramatically increased pressure on already-stretched community resources and humanitarian response. Population movements further intensify pressure on resources; over 2.6 million Afghans have returned from Iran and Pakistan since January 2025. These overlapping movements place severe strain on basic services, employment opportunities, and social cohesion in hosting communities, particularly in water-stressed border provinces. ([FEWS NET et al. 07/02/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/07401c1b-0f71-46d4-810c-5e4e3a6064d1/2025_01_Afghanistan.pdf), [Mercy Corps 08/10/2025](https://www.mercycorps.org/press-room/releases/Crisis-Compounded-Afghanistan), [Alcis 01/07/2025](https://www.alcis.org/post/crop-estimates-for-six-provinces-in-afghanistan), [FEWS NET 06/10/2025](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/key-message-update/september-2025), [FSC 02/2025](https://fscluster.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Afghanistan%20EWIWG%20-%20Key%20messages%20Feb%202025.pdf))

triggerList.title: Lethal militant attack in a major Pakistani urban centre.
triggerList.description: A confirmed TTP attack targeting Pakistani security forces or government installations in cities such as Karachi, Peshawar, or Islamabad is likely to trigger further Pakistani airstrikes or ground operations in Afghan border provinces. Historically, such events have served as the primary political trigger for Pakistani retaliatory airstrikes and ground operations in Afghan border provinces like Paktia and Paktika. The 28 June attack was carried out by Pakistan, according to Pakistani authorities, in retaliation for an alleged TTP attack on security personnel in Karachi days earlier.

triggerList.title: Cross-border hostilities
triggerList.description: Clashes between army forces in bordering areas and the closure of borders will limit movement, constrain access of humanitarian aid, interrupt livelihoods and trade between communities. In past border closures food security and livelihoods have been significantly impacted.

rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps. ([CFR 18/03/2026](https://www.cfr.org/articles/why-are-the-afghan-taliban-and-pakistan-in-an-open-war), [The Guardian 29/06/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/29/pakistan-deadly-airstrikes-afghanistan-border), [HRW 15/07/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/07/15/pakistani-strikes-in-afghanistan-raise-civilian-casualty-concerns), [UNAMA 11/05/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/English%20-%20UNAMA%20HRS%20paper%20on%20cross-border%20civilian%20casualties%20-%20Jan-Mar%202026_Updated_11.05.26.pdf), [WFP 26/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/food-security-under-pressure-impacts-middle-east-crisis-and-pakistan-conflict-afghanistan-june-2026), [OCHA 28/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-situation-update-4-humanitarian-impact-afghanistan-pakistan-military-escalation-28-april-2026), [NPR 03/04/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/03/g-s1-116299/pakistan-says-a-new-round-of-peace-talks-with-afghanistan-is-underway-in-china), [Reuters 02/04/2026](https://www.aol.com/articles/pakistan-says-talks-afghanistan-end-071917568.html), [UNAMA 29/06/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/en/news/unama-statement-on-civilian-casualties))

rationale:
Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook. ([ACLED 20/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/taliban-losing-control-northern-afghanistan), [Hasht-e Subh 26/08/2026](https://8am.media/eng/badakhshan-health-centers-mothers-children/), [Amu TV 20/05/2026](https://amu.tv/240020/#google_vignette), [ACLED 13/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/five-years-seizing-power-afghanistan-internal-tensions-test-talibans-vulnerabilities), [Afghanistan International 17/08/2026](https://www.afintl.com/en/202608171939), [ACLED accessed 27/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/platform/trends), [FEWS NET 25/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-el-nino-conditions-expected-be-key-driver-202627-agricultural-season-june-25-2026), [TCA 25/08/2026](https://timesca.com/badakhshan-fighting-raises-risks-for-tajikistan-and-uzbekistan/), [SWJ 07/08/2026](https://smallwarsjournal.com/2026/08/07/badakhshan-and-the-first-signs-of-a-localized-anti-taliban-insurgency-in-afghanistan/))

triggerList.description: Perceived changes in Algeria's position on Western Sahara negotiations trigger protests, unrest, or increased tensions among Sahrawi refugees and Polisario supporters.

triggerList.title: Potential polisario leadership fragmentation
triggerList.description: The death of senior Polisario commander Lahbib Mohamed Abdelaziz leads to succession disputes, competing factions, or disagreements over leadership and decision-making within Polisario.

rationale:
The risk of increased instability and localised clashes in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, may rise over the coming months as humanitarian pressures, political uncertainty, and governance challenges compound a protracted displacement crisis.  

Several incidents between April–June 2026 suggest growing tensions within the camps. On 20 April, armed confrontations involving Polisario-linked elements and the Algerian National Army over humanitarian aid distribution highlighted tensions related to influence, compounded by the lack of resources. On 28 April, clashes between members of the Fakra and Oulad Moussa tribes in Smara camp escalated from a dispute over access to a water tap into armed confrontations involving live ammunition. The violence resulted in injuries and damage to tents, houses, and vehicles, raising concerns about the capacity of camp authorities to manage local disputes and prevent escalation. 

In this context, tensions are most likely to unfold through repeated, low-level disputes between tribes, families, or Polisario-affiliated actors in camps such as Smara, Laayoune, Awserd, and Dakhla, particularly around water points, aid distribution systems, and local administrative structures. These disputes are likely to remain contained but may escalate into short-lived violent incidents when mediation fails or when armed actors become involved. 

Political developments have further increased uncertainty and may be contributing to growing confusion and frustration among refugee populations regarding future governance arrangements. On 22 April, reports indicated increased US pressure on Algeria regarding the future of the Tindouf camps and the Western Sahara conflict. On 29 May, concerns emerged among Polisario supporters over a perceived shift in Algeria's position on negotiations. On 9 June, the death of senior Polisario commander Lahbib Mohamed Abdelaziz in a reported drone strike fuelled speculation regarding future leadership dynamics within the movement. 

Although these developments have not triggered widespread unrest, they indicate increasing pressure on camp governance, resource management, and political cohesion. Further reductions in humanitarian assistance, deterioration in living conditions, or renewed political tensions surrounding Western Sahara could increase the likelihood of additional intercommunal violence, protests, or localised instability within the camps over the next 6–12 months. ([ACLED accessed 18/06/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool\), [UNHCR 27/11/2025](https://algeria.un.org/fr/306201-plan-de-r%C3%A9ponse-pour-les-r%C3%A9fugi%C3%A9s-sahraouis-2026%E2%80%932027\), [Africanews 23/04/2026](https://www.africanews.com/2026/04/23/in-algerian-desert-sahrawi-refugees-still-dream-of-independent-homeland/), [Atalayar 22/04/2026](https://www.atalayar.com/en/articulo/politics/the-united-states-is-putting-pressure-on-algeria-and-urging-it-to-dismantle-the-tindouf-camps/20260422210000225067.html), [Algeria Times 20/04/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75054\), [Yabiladi 29/04/2026](https://en.yabiladi.com/articles/details/193455/violent-clashes-tindouf-s-smara-camp.html\), [Barlaman Today 30/04/2026](https://barlamantoday.com/2026/04/30/deadly-armed-clashes-reportedly-erupt-in-tindouf-camps/), [Assahifa 29/05/2026](https://www.assahifa.com/%D8%B9%D9%82%D8%A8-%D8%BA%D8%B6%D8%A8-%D9%85%D8%AE%D9%8A%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B1-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%B7%D9%85%D8%A3/), [Algeria Times 11/06/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75662\), [Belpresse 09/06/2026](https://www.belpresse.com/politique/%d9%85%d9%82%d8%aa%d9%84-%d9%86%d8%ac%d9%84-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b2%d8%b9%d9%8a%d9%85-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%a8%d9%82-%d9%84%d9%84%d8%a8%d9%88%d9%84%d9%8a%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%b1%d9%8a%d9%88-%d9%8a%d8%b6/)).

triggerList.title: Nationwide hartal calls or election boycott by major political parties
triggerList.description: If major political parties, particularly the BNP or allied opposition groups formally announce nationwide hartals or an election boycott, the likelihood of widespread political violence would increase sharply. Such announcements would likely prompt mass mobilization, transport blockades, and confrontations between party supporters, security forces, and rival groups. Based on patterns from previous election cycles, hartal calls are often followed by pre-emptive security deployments, arrests of opposition activists, and the use of force to keep transport routes and economic hubs open. These dynamics raise the risk of lethal clashes, retaliatory attacks, and attacks on infrastructure. A boycott would also undermine the perceived legitimacy of the electoral process, increasing incentives for disruptive or violent actions both before and during polling, particularly in urban centres.

triggerList.title: Post-election disputes over results or allegations of electoral fraud
triggerList.description: A public rejection of election results by major political actors, accompanied by allegations of widespread fraud or manipulation, would significantly heighten the risk of political violence. If opposition parties refuse to recognize the outcome, protests and counter-mobilization by ruling-party supporters are likely, increasing the probability of violent confrontations. Historical precedent in Bangladesh indicates that post-election disputes are often followed by targeted attacks against opposition figures, intensified police crackdowns, and mass arrests. In the current context, marked by unresolved political assassinations, online incitement, and the availability of unrecovered small arms, post-election disputes could rapidly escalate from demonstrations into sustained lethal violence, particularly if security forces are perceived as partisan or excessively forceful.

rationale:
Since the election announcement in December 2025, at least 16 political assassinations have been reported, predominantly targeting opposition figures. This reflects historical patterns in which contested electoral processes trigger targeted killings, intimidation, and cycles of retaliation. Primary perpetrators include supporters and affiliates of major political parties, including the Awami League, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, Jamaat-e-Islami, and associated groups, as well as security forces enforcing restrictions on opposition activity. Weakening institutional control has also allowed opportunistic criminal groups to exploit the unrest and further contribute to lethal incidents. The continued circulation of weapons looted during the July 2024 uprising – numbering over 3,600, with many still unrecovered – compounds the security situation.
Repeated hartals and transport blockades, largely organised by opposition groups and met with security crackdowns, are deepening economic stress, particularly for urban poor populations reliant on daily wage labour and public transport. These disruptions are reducing household income, fuelling grievances, and heightening the risk of violent mobilisation in major urban centres such as Chattogram, Dhaka, and Rajshahi.
Within this volatile environment, religious minorities, particularly the Hindu community, face targeted attacks, including assaults on Hindu temples and cultural organisations, such as Bangladesh Udichi Shilpigoshthi, often following online hate campaigns. Taken together, these dynamics create conditions for a rapid escalation of political violence, with serious implications for civilian safety, livelihoods, and access to essential services. riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis

triggerList.title: Continuation of the Strait of Hormuz disruptions
triggerList.description: Any intensification of the conflict or prolonged insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz would further constrain fuel shipments and delay imports.

triggerList.title: Deterioration in import capacity
triggerList.description: Further declines in foreign exchange reserves, high inflation, or additional increases in import costs may reduce the government’s ability to import the needed amounts of fuel.

triggerList.title: Increased seasonal demand during the Boro irrigation period
triggerList.description: Any increase in diesel and electricity demand during the Boro season (December–May) can intensify shortages, as existing supply constraints are insufficient to meet irrigation needs, particularly in northern districts.

rationale:
Geopolitical shocks, import dependency, and market distortions risk a prolonged or widespread fuel shortage across Bangladesh, worsening the humanitarian situation. The country imports about 95% of its petroleum – 63% from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates via the Strait of Hormuz. The 2026 war between Israel–US and Iran has disrupted this corridor, constraining imports; continued disruptions would further limit fuel supply. Despite diversifying imports towards the US after a February 2026 trade deal, alternative routes are unable to replace Middle Eastern volumes at scale, leaving near-term shortfall risks.
Bangladesh's capacity to absorb disruptions is eroding as economic conditions worsen. Inflation reached 9.13% in February 2026, and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation import costs rose by 29% year-on-year. Pressure on foreign exchange reserves, including reduced remittance inflows from the Gulf countries affected by the war, may constrain fuel imports. Distribution practices – hoarding, panic-buying, and first-come-first-served allocation – further limit access.
These supply constraints are converging with peak seasonal demand during Boro season – the December–May dry-season rice cultivation period that accounts for around 55% of annual production. Should fuel shortages persist through this period, the consequences for food security are likely to be severe. Limited diesel availability and government policies such as a two-litre-per-visit rationing cap are constraining irrigation, especially in northern districts, where demand exceeds supply. Farmers report shortages of both diesel and electricity. If constraints persist, rice output will likely fall and, with higher fuel-driven transport costs, raise staple food prices, disproportionately affecting low-income households already spending most of their earnings on food.
Given continued Hormuz disruptions, Bangladesh's import dependency, and deteriorating economic conditions, fuel shortages are likely to persist or worsen over the next three to six months, with cascading consequences for food security and essential services. ([ORF 16/04/2026](https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/beyond-diversification-bangladesh-s-fuel-crisis-and-role-of-neighbourhood-ties), [AJ 09/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/9/bangladesh-shuts-universities-limits-fuel-sale-as-iran-war-causes-shortage), [DT 29/03/2026](https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/406405/diesel-crisis-disrupts-irrigation-in-northern), [TDS 10/03/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/diesel-crunch-hits-farm-heartlands-4125026), [TDS 31/03/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/opinion/news/how-bangladesh-can-manage-fuel-shocks-economic-stability-4139506), [Prothom Alo 21/04/2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/amp/story/bangladesh/local-news/ai8kcp4avr), [TDS 07/04/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/opinion/news/how-hoarding-and-panic-buying-are-deepening-the-fuel-crisis-4145366), [TBS 13/04/2026](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/fuel-imports-14-costs-jump-29-so-why-shortage-1410106))

triggerList.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
triggerList.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian territory.
triggerList.objective: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if armed groups, militias, or proxy actors operating across the Chad–Sudan border become actively involved in cross-border hostilities, resulting in sustained violence, retaliatory attacks, or territorial insecurity in eastern Chad.

rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces. ([Africa Center for Strategic Studies 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/), [ISS Africa 03/04/2025](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire), [UNHCR 18/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-17-may-2026), [UNFPA 15/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026))

rationale:
Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.
The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.
Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin. ([ICG 09/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/oth/chad-cuba-horn-africa-pakistan/horizon-july-december-2026), [OCHA 07/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-2026-29-june-2026), [OCHA 29/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-29-april-2026), [RFI 23/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260623-aux-confins-nord-du-cameroun-une-commune-enclav%C3%A9e-sous-une-pression-jihadiste-constante), [AJ 18/05/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/18/how-iswap-and-boko-haram-are-reshaping-the-lake-chad-basin), [UNHCR 02/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/lake-chad-basin-regional-protection-and-displacement-crisis-humanitarian-priorities-and-funding-needs-across-cameroon-chad-niger-and-nigeria-june-december-2026), [UNHCR 03/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/unhcr-warns-lake-chad-basin-tipping-point-violence-and-displacement-surge), [ACLED 19/05/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/violence-involving-boko-haram-and-islamic-state-west-africa-province-rising), [ACSS 06/04/2026](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026a-mig-widening-militant-islamist-threat/))

triggerList.title: Breackdown of peace talks
triggerList.description:
Concerns are growing over the potential breakdown of peace negotiations between the Colombian Government and the Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (EGC), the largest and most influential non-state armed group in the country. According to official estimates, the EGC increased its membership by 95% between 2018 and 2024, reaching around 7,000 members—including 2,499 combatants and 4,563 support network members—by mid-2024. The group has expanded its territorial control in several departments, particularly Chocó, Magdalena Medio, southern Bolívar, and the Caribbean coast, where it has consolidated strategic corridors linked to illicit economies. Between 2023 and 2024, its armed capacity in southern Bolívar alone grew by 23%, highlighting a clear strengthening trend amid ongoing peace talks.
This continued military expansion and territorial consolidation raise doubts about the EGC’s genuine willingness to engage in disarmament or comply with potential peace accords. A collapse of the peace process could intensify clashes with other armed actors, notably the ELN and FARC-EP dissident factions, leading to further mass displacement, confinement, targeted killings, and restrictions on humanitarian access. The persistence of hostilities in areas such as southern Bolívar and the Magdalena Medio would likely deepen existing humanitarian crises, strain local institutional capacities, and expose civilian population, particularly rural communities, women, and children, to heightened protection risks.
triggerList.objective: No

triggerList.title: Increase in Electoral Violence
triggerList.description:
The 2026 electoral cycle in Colombia is taking place amid significant regional and national challenges. The assassination of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay during a campaign rally in June 2025 marked the first killing of a presidential candidate in more than three decades, adding urgency to concerns about political violence. At the same time, the territorial presence and influence of NSAGs, restrict free political participation and undermine the integrity of electoral processes, particularly in conflict-affected regions like southern Bolívar.
The Early Electoral Warning (ATEL 2025–2026), issued by the Ombudsman’s Office, highlights the risks arising from the dominance, consolidation, coexistence, or territorial disputes of these armed groups. These dynamics may affect fundamental rights such as life, liberty, integrity, and security, as well as political and civil freedoms during the electoral period. In regions like southern Bolívar, where NSAGs exert de facto control, armed intimidation and fear limit the safe participation of both candidates and voters.
Among the risks identified by the  Ombudsman’s Office for areas such as southern Bolívar are manifestations of illegal armed governance, the capture of political representation, and mechanisms of population control by armed groups. These dynamics are compounded by the growing use of disinformation and manipulation through social media and artificial intelligence, which threaten the quality of public debate and weaken trust in institutions. As a result, social tension and localized electoral violence are likely to increase, particularly in territories where political competition intersects with criminal influence and coercion.
triggerList.objective: No

triggerList.title: Increase in Military Operations
triggerList.description:
In response to escalating violence and territorial disputes among NSAGs, the Colombian Ministry of Defense has announced the continuation of offensive and territorial control operations in southern Bolívar. A new military unit of more than 2,500 soldiers has been deployed, with its command base established in Santa Rosa del Sur, to lead operations aimed at dismantling criminal structures operating across the region. These actions seek to restore security and state presence in areas affected by persistent clashes between the ELN, the EGC, and FARC-EP dissidents.
However, the intensification of military operations also poses heightened humanitarian risks for the civilian population. Armed confrontations between state forces and NSAGs may result in collateral damage, including civilian casualties, new displacements, and confinement, particularly in rural areas near combat zones. The deployment of troops and ongoing hostilities can further limit humanitarian access, disrupt livelihoods, and exacerbate protection risks for communities already exposed to armed violence. Reports of injured soldiers highlight the volatility of the security environment, suggesting that the conflict could further escalate.
triggerList.objective: No

rationale:
Territorial disputes between non-state armed groups (NSAGs) over the control of strategic corridors and illegal mining activities in southern Bolívar have intensified dramatically since 2023, escalating humanitarian needs. Historically, the National Liberation Army (ELN) maintained territorial control and governance throughout southern Bolívar. The arrival, however, of competing NSAGs – including the Gaitanist Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (AGC), Comandos de la Frontera, dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and others – has fractured this control. This violent competition has triggered frequent armed confrontations, targeted attacks against civilians, population displacement, and confinement, creating acute protection risks.
Conflict dynamics have steadily intensified over the past years. In Bolívar, mass displacements have become increasingly frequent. The number quadrupled from three incidents in 2023 to 16 in 2024, with 12 additional conflict-related emergencies recorded by mid-2025. All these events were in municipalities surrounding the Serranía de San Lucas, a strategic corridor at the centre of territorial disputes. By 8 August 2025, around 13,000 people were displaced, confined, or facing mobility restrictions; this figure had surged to 21,000 by 22 August.
Since July 2024, the Colombian Government has been engaging in peace negotiations with the AGC. The group's sustained violent operations in southern Bolívar demonstrate either the fragility of these talks or the group's unwillingness to commit to agreed terms, risking negotiation collapse and prolonged conflict. The 2026 electoral cycle is also likely to heighten political violence across the country. NSAGs may intensify intimidation campaigns, restrict political expression, and coerce voters, creating an environment where electoral competition deteriorates into armed coercion. Civic leaders and community representatives are particularly exposed to the risks of co-option, threats, or silencing.
The escalation of armed confrontations and associated violence increases displacement, confinement, and the recruitment and exploitation of children by NSAGs.
Rural communities face compounding protection threats, including widespread landmine and improvised explosive device (IED) contamination impedes safe returns and perpetuates mobility restrictions, while small-scale miners and subsistence farmers – economically dependent on accessing disputed territories – face direct violence including threats, homicides, and forced displacement. This convergence of armed violence and environmental hazards creates a negative cycle where people are unable to work safely and communities cannot rebuild livelihoods, deepening both economic vulnerability. rationale:
An above-average rainy season is forecast for northern and northwestern Colombia through the remainder of 2025 and early 2026 (November–January), as La Niña conditions are expected to persist across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean until the February–March 2026 period. This will likely lead to abundant rains, increasing the flood risk across Atlántico, northern Bolívar, Córdoba, La Guajira, Magdalena, Sucre, and the islands of San Andrés and Providencia department.
The second half of 2025 has already seen above-average rainfall, widespread flooding, and local and national response systems operating at full capacity, leaving the country more vulnerable to La Niña’s impacts. Heavy rainfall has affected almost 25,000 in just Bolívar, Córdoba, and Magdalena. Between November–January, rainfall is forecasted to increase by up to 30% in the regions expected to be affected, aggravating floods and landslides, damaging infrastructure, and destroying public buildings and main roads.
Flooding may affect crops and reduce agricultural production, particularly harming communities that rely on subsistence farming or that are already facing malnutrition. In 2025, 25% of households in Colombia faced consistent food access constraints, especially in rural communities, such as in Bolívar and La Guajira, which rely on their own crops for sustenance. Any disruption to the rice- and corn-growing cycles, which occur in November and December, would increase the limitations on these households' access to food.
The rains also limit the ability of affected communities to move freely in and out of their territories, effectively isolating them. Confinement decreases people’s ability to access essential services, such as health, education, and protection, meaning continued flooding would affect the livelihoods of these communities. This would worsen if the rains damage roads. Flooding will also worsen the humanitarian condition of the nearly 1.5 million people affected by violence-related incidents in Colombia from January–June 2025, marking the highest number in recent national history, particularly those displaced to the northern departments.
([CPC 13/11/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc_Sp.shtml), [CCO 26/09/2025](https://cco.gov.co/seguimiento-de-los-fenomenos-el-nino-la-nina-comunicado-no-09-de-2025/), [IDEAM 19/11/2025](https://bart.ideam.gov.co/wrfideam/new_modelo/CPT/informe/Informe.pdf), [IRI accessed 05/11/2025](https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/seasonal-climate-forecasts/), [FEWS NET 27/11/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/globalweatherhazard/Current.pdf), [El País 23/05/2025](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/2025-05-23/la-inseguridad-alimentaria-en-colombia-prevalece-en-las-areas-rurales-y-cae-en-las-zonas-urbanas.html), [OCHA accessed 24/11/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia))

triggerList.description: The significant strengthening of NSAGs since 2022, including a reported increase in membership, territorial expansion, adoption of new tactics, and increased reliance on illicit economies such as coca cultivation and illegal mining, increases the likelihood that armed groups will seek to consolidate control over contested territories and demonstrate operational capacity ahead of and during the anticipated offensive.

triggerList.description: A decision by the incoming government to end the outgoing administration’s “Total Peace” talks with NSAGs would remove an important mechanism for dialogue and de-escalation. The breakdown of ELN talks preceding the escalation of fighting in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) in January 2025 illustrates how quickly violence and displacement can increase following the collapse of negotiations.

triggerList.title: Bureaucratic cuts and public sector purges
triggerList.description: Implementation of the pledged 40% reduction in the state apparatus and removal of officials linked to the outgoing administration could trigger sustained protest mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the security risk through potential clashes with security forces and increased protection concerns.

rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity. 
([El País 21/06/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/elecciones-presidenciales/2026-06-21/las-propuestas-de-abelardo-de-la-espriella-seguridad-de-mano-dura-reduccion-del-estado-y-libertades-tributarias.html), [FIP 30/01/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-01/27-000-combatientes-y-record-en-disputas-el-deterioro-de-la-seguridad-marca-el-inicio-de-2026), [Valora Analitik 17/12/2025](https://www.valoraanalitik.com/grupos-armados-en-colombia-aumentaron-casi-70-desde-2022-crecen-homicidios-y-secuestros/), [Defensores de la Patria accessed 06/07/2026](https://defensoresdelapatria.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PROPUESTAS-DEL-TIGRE.pdf), [AJ 22/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/far-right-de-la-espriella-elected-colombia-president-whats-next), [NPR 21/06/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/21/nx-s1-5865676/delaespriella-colombia-election), [Atlantic Council 22/06/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/experts-react-what-a-president-abelardo-de-la-espriella-means-for-colombia-and-beyond/), [The City Paper 21/05/2026](https://thecitypaperbogota.com/news/colombia-on-guard-as-super-el-nino-threatens-record-heat-drought-and-food-security/))

title: Worsening energy shortages and U.S. pressure lead to essential service disruptions and rising humanitarian needs in Cuba
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis

Sources:

https://www.american.edu/centers/latin-american-latino-studies/cuba-s-economic

triggerList.title: Prolonged inability to secure fuel imports at market rates
triggerList.description: If Cuba cannot obtain licenses or afford commercial fuel purchases under new U.S. licensing policies within the next 4–8 weeks, the energy deficit will persist through summer 2026. This would maintain or intensify current service disruptions, worsening the humanitarian situation.

triggerList.title: Depletion of strategic fuel reserves
triggerList.description: If Cuba has been drawing on stockpiles since January, these reserves may be exhausted within 2–4 months. Reserve depletion would trigger more severe rationing and could force complete shutdown of non-essential services.

triggerList.title: Extreme weather events (hurricane season June–November 2026)
triggerList.description: Hurricanes or tropical storms affecting fuel supply lines, damaging electrical infrastructure, or disrupting already fragile food production systems. Cuba is particularly vulnerable given deteriorated infrastructure and reduced maintenance capacity.

rationale:
The reduction in Cuba’s oil imports – following the suspension of Venezuela’s daily supply of approximately 30,000 barrels and the continued pressure to prevent alternative sourcing from Mexico – has created an energy deficit equivalent to at least 30% of the country’s daily needs. Given Cuba’s reliance on imported fuel to operate even at reduced capacity, this shortfall is already contributing to prolonged power outages and fuel scarcity.
Over the next six months, unless alternative fuel supply arrangements materialise rapidly, the convergence of acute fuel supply disruption and structural economic fragility is likely to drive rapid and compounding humanitarian deterioration across Cuba. Power outages of 12–20 hours daily are already cascading across health, water, food, and social protection sectors in mutually reinforcing ways: hospitals losing electrical backup, ambulances unable to refuel, and refrigeration failures disrupting food imports collectively represent systemic stress – not isolated shocks – across interconnected service delivery chains. This trajectory is expected to further disrupt essential services, including water supply, healthcare, transportation, and food storage and distribution, while increasing economic pressure on households through rising prices and reduced availability of basic goods. At the same time, sustained energy and economic deterioration may intensify internal social strain and political instability, particularly amid active US efforts to incentivise political change, with potential consequences for civilian protection and humanitarian access. The geographic scope of disruption is countrywide, with disproportionate impacts in eastern provinces – including Santiago de Cuba and Holguin – and rural areas, where electricity availability has declined by up to 50% since January 2026.
Long-lasting power disruptions will compound the impact of extreme weather events, especially during the hurricane season (June–November). Cuba's aging grid and chronic blackouts make the country highly susceptible to hurricane damage, worsening fuel supply disruptions and extended outages. Fragile food production, reliant on cold chains and vulnerable crops, is routinely hit, with power failures spoiling perishables and storms destroying harvests, as exemplified by the impact of Hurricane Melissa in 2025.
As public services become increasingly unreliable, vulnerable populations – particularly older people, people with chronic illnesses, and low-income households – will likely face compounding protection and health risks. The progressive erosion of essential service delivery may in turn drive higher levels of internal displacement towards less-affected areas, as well as increased cross-border movement to countries with more stable economic conditions, further compounding regional humanitarian challenges.
([El Tiempo 20/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/mundo/venezuela/sin-el-petroleo-de-venezuela-que-tan-cerca-esta-cuba-del-colapso-economico-total-analisis-de-mauricio-vargas-3525770); [EFE 18/01/2026](https://efe.com/economia/2026-01-18/cuba-bloqueo-petroleo-venezuela-efectos-crisis-energetica/); [EMOL 30/01/2026](https://www.emol.com/noticias/Internacional/2026/01/30/1190117/cuba-petroleo-energia-venezuela-mexico.html); [AJ 22/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/22/trump-seeking-regime-change-in-cuba-by-end-of-the-year-us-media-report))

rationale:
Since June 2022, a customary land tax dispute between two communities in Kwamouth territory, Mai-Ndombe province, has gradually escalated to intercommunal violence between the so-called “native” and "non-native" communities. At least 300 people have been killed and more than 161,000 displaced since. In early 2023, the emergence of a communal militia called Mobondo, mainly composed of people from the Yaka and allied communities, marked a change in the conflict dynamics until then marked by sporadic clashes between communities. The Mobondo militia have repeatedly attacked people from rival communities, mainly Teke. Regular clashes between the Mobondo militia and the Forces armées de la république démocratique du Congo (FARDC) have also caused population displacements. Although their number is unknown, the Mobondo militia maintains an active presence in several areas in the west of the country, presumably to gain access to land and natural resources.
Violence by the Mobondo militia, is likely to intensify in the coming months despite FARDC military operations launched since May 2023. The increase of attacks in Mai-Ndombe, Kwilu, Kwango, Kongo-central provinces and Kinshasa periphery in recent months, illustrate the propensity of the militia to strengthen its presence. The periphery of DRC’s capital city Kinshasa is particularly exposed to this surge in violence namely because of the Mobondo militia being already active in the surrounding provinces.

title: DRC general elections trigger heightened levels of violence, leading to increasing protection threats, population displacement, and food insecurity
rationale:
The DRC’s Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) has officially set the general elections’ ballot date to 20 December 2023, which will include polls for the presidency, national legislature, provincial assemblies, and local councils. The electoral process started in December 2022 with voter identification and registration procedures that lasted until June 2023. The electoral campaign for the presidency started on 19 November and finish on 18 December, two days before voting day. The electoral process will then continue throughout 2024 with the swearing-in of the new president scheduled for 20 January and indirect elections for the senate, provincial governorates, and other official positions scheduled to take place through September 2024. The presidency, elected through a simple majority for a five-year term, will have President Félix Tshisekedi seeking re-election amid a list of 26 opponents, including prominent figures such as Martin Fayulu, a politician claiming to have won the 2018 elections; Moïse Katumbi, a wealthy businessman and politician; and Denis Mukwege, an activist and 2018 Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Logistical challenges, criticism towards the electoral commission for its alleged biases, and a defective electoral roll generate a climate of mistrust and heightened tensions, compounded by the failure of the Government and the CENI to engage with civil society observer missions. This tense situation engenders an environment that is ripe for discontent, hostility, and protests, increasing the probability of violence during the electoral cycle. The opposition’s reluctance to engage in the electoral process may lead to intentional election disruptions, also potentially instigating violence. At the polling stations, any denial of voter rights, perceived impartiality of officials, or restrictions imposed on observers could lead to confrontations involving officials, supporters of different political parties or rival groups, and security forces.

The tense political environment is heightening social and political divisions. Unresolved grievances from the 2018 contested general elections, which included some of the candidates for the current ballot, have fostered divisions and mistrust among political factions and communities. The opposition is still unsuccessfully discussing the potential for a joint coalition candidate. The fractured opposition landscape, marked by diverse political ideologies and ambitions, has been a source of tension during the electoral process. The fragmentation and lack of meaningful electoral odds for some opposition candidates can lead to frustration among supporters who may feel disenfranchised, increasing tensions and the potential for confrontation 
between rival political factions. Confrontations could also arise if results are contested. A re-elected incumbent and disputed results could trigger existing contentions between communities and ethnic groups to escalate into political violence. A losing party’s refusal to accept the results could incite confrontations and protests involving groups in dispute for prominence and power, potentially escalating into greater clashes between rival communities and larger scale political conflicts. In certain territories, communities are deeply politically attached to particular candidates, such as the Kasaï, who support the incumbent president, and the Katanga, who support Moïse Katumbi, one of the main opposition candidates. These divides could lead to strong reactions. The constant inflammatory language of the Government and opposition figures, including contentious debates around the definition 
of the Congolese identity, amplifies ethnopolitical and intercommunal tensions and divisions and heightens the threat of confrontations.

Continued repression and abuses by state security forces could trigger increased resistance and dissatisfaction, sparking demonstrations, civil unrest, or violent clashes. Reports of military abuse and limits on political freedoms provoke resentment and erode trust in both state institutions and the electoral process. At the same time, heavy-handed security responses and peaceful protest suppression are expected to result in further demonstrations 
and civil unrest.

title: The expansion of the areas under the control of the March 23 Movement (M23) in Nord-Kivu causes increased violence targeting Rwandophone communities, resulting in displacement and protection needs.
country: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda
rationale:
Since the resurgence of the M23 in November 2021, tensions have intensified between the DRC and Rwanda, which accuse each other of supporting rival armed groups in North Kivu province. Demonstrations by civil society organisations have taken place in several provinces of the country since May 2022 to support the Congolese army, demand a more offensive attitude from the East Africa regional force towards the M23, or even express their hostility towards Rwanda. These demonstrations often turn into attacks against people and their property because of their presumed Rwandan origins or proximity to the M23. 
Since January 2022, riots or attacks by armed groups targeting people of Rwandan origin have killed at least 12 people. These attacks have intensified since June 2022 in Maniema, North Kivu, and South Kivu provinces, shortly after the M23 took over the border town of Bunagana. In February 2022, demonstrations against the regional force’s lack of action escalated into the destruction and looting of shops believed to be Tutsi-owned. Churches were also ransacked on the grounds that they were mainly frequented by the Banyamulenge community (descendants of Rwandans). Because of the inability of the regional force, MONUSCO, and the Congolese army to curb the advances of the M23, violence against Rwandophone communities is likely to increase. 
In addition, these communities are increasingly being accused of sympathy for the M23. Some of them claim to have been threatened and beaten by Congolese troops or armed groups and militias fighting the M23 in Kitshanga (Masisi territory), forcing them to flee to other localities and hide. A ceasefire expected to start on 7 March 2023 and supposed to be implemented by the M23 was announced by the President of Angola, which is currently mediating peace efforts between the DRC, Rwanda, and the M23. That said, the ceasefire seems unlikely to lead to the M23 withdrawing from the controlled areas or to a decrease in the intensity of the anti-Rwandan sentiments in the DRC. While the ceasefire is supposed to have taken effect, clashes between the Congolese army and the M23 still continue, and both sides accuse each other of launching attacks on their positions.

The expansion of the area under M23 control is likely to cause an increase in retaliatory attacks against Rwandophone communities across the country. The property of many people from these communities will likely be destroyed or looted in the demonstrations that follow M23 advances. With the context of the tension between the Governments of the DRC and Rwanda being conducive to the expression of hostile feelings against the latter, some civil society members will continue to maintain a discourse of hatred against Rwandophone communities. Incidents involving armed groups and militias fighting the M23 and conflating ethnicity and ideological support are also likely to increase. 
Although not the whole country subscribes to such stigmatisation, and certain civil society organisations continue to defend Rwan dophones, such as Association jeunes Tutsi au Nord-Kivu and the Archidiocese of Kinshasa, the security of the latter will likely be increasingly threatened, particularly in areas where armed groups fighting the M23 are active. Many protesters will consider members of Rwandophone communities as foreigners and threaten them into returning to Rwanda. The announcement of the Rwandan President to no longer host Congolese refugees, without giving more details, risks further reducing the options of those who wish to find refuge in Rwanda. As a result, new IDPs (both Rwandophone and not) within the DRC will be added to the thousands already displaced by the resurgence of the M23, with critical needs for protection, health, livelihoods, and shelter.

Update 22/06/2023
Hostilities against Tutsi communities have persisted since the DRC government accused Rwanda of supporting M23. In April 2023, in Goma, Bukavu, Nyagenzi and Uvira, in eastern Congo, groups of young people threatened and beat Banyamulenge – Congolese Tutsi from South Kivu province – and temporarily refused them access to enrolment centres because of their ethnicity. Recent sources report an escalation of misinformation, xenophobia, hate speech and incitement to discrimination and violence, targeting in particular Tutsi/Banyarwanda and other people of Rwandan origin or presumed to be Rwandan.

triggerList.description: Since 7 October 2023, the likelihood of a prolonged Israeli military operation in Gaza, one that ends up pushing parts of the population into the Sinai Desert, has been low, at least until the Israeli Government’s announcement on 7 February 2024 of its intent to start a ground invasion of Rafah city. An estimated 1.2 million people, the majority of whom are IDPs, are staying in Rafah, which the Israeli army has previously designated as a safe zone. Rafah is the city immediately adjacent to the Egyptian border. Many families will likely be unable to flee to anywhere other than Egypt, as other cities in the Gaza Strip have already been heavily bombarded and seen Israeli military tanks on their streets.
triggerList.objective: The trigger is considered materialised once an Israeli ground invasion of Rafah starts.

triggerList.title: Movement of Gazan refugees towards Egypt
triggerList.description: In the case of escalation of clashes or an Israeli ground invasion of Rafah, displaced people in those areas will seek safety, likely trying to cross the border to Egypt's Sinai governorate.  An estimated 1.2 million people, the majority of whom are IDPs, are staying in Rafah.
triggerList.objective: The trigger can be considered materialised if people from Gaza displace into camp settlements in northern Sinai.

triggerList.title: Total blockade of the Red Sea
triggerList.description: The partial blockade of the Red Sea led to an over 40% decrease in the number of ships going through the Suez Canal from December 2023 to January 2024. More extreme tensions’ escalations in the Red Sea could result in a complete halt of traffic, reducing Egypt’s foreign currency revenues and increasing the prices of imported goods, such as fuel and some food items.
triggerList.objective: The trigger can be considered materialised if traffic on the Red Sea is 100% halted.

triggerList.title: Increased food inflation rates
triggerList.description: The impact of the Red Sea tensions and the consequences of the conflict in Gaza are driving shortfalls in foreign currency revenues. This, coupled with food supply shortages and increasing poverty rates, will likely further reduce consumers’ purchasing power and limit food access, particularly for those living below the poverty line. Food inflation rates, including for staple foods such as rice and wheat, are projected to steadily increase throughout 2024
triggerList.objective: This trigger can be considered materialised if food inflation reaches 70% (the same as the highest levels recorded in the last 10 years). Food inflation by May 2024 reached only 30%, and has been decreasing since September 2023.

rationale:
Egypt’s economy is suffering from currency floating and record-high inflation rates, which reached 38% in September 2023. The continuing war in the Gaza Strip will likely lead to its further deterioration despite a slight improvement in inflation rates since October.

Tourism revenues have dropped since October because of insecurity at the border area between Gaza and Egypt. Between October–December, ticket purchases for Egypt fell by 26% compared to the same period in 2022. Some rockets from either Israel or Yemen have been misfired and dropped over touristy cities in Egypt, such as Dahab.

The Red Sea blockade also reduces the number of ships passing through the Suez Canal, reducing Egypt’s revenues from transit fees. The canal contributes one-fourth of the country’s currency earnings. Traffic through Bab Al Mandib Strait was estimated to have dropped by 35% as at mid-December. Despite the Houthis claiming to block only ships headed to Israel, some major shipping companies have suspended all of their travel through the Red Sea for security reasons. In case of clashes between the Houthis and the US Navy, a total blockade of the Red Sea will likely take place, largely affecting Egypt’s economy. Generally, shipping and insurance costs have increased, leading to an increase in the commodities also meant to reach Egypt.

triggerList.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia's key Meher-producing areas
triggerList.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing by 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with precipitation deficits likely in the northeastern and central areas, where there is at least a 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more. This combination of reduced rainfall and above average temperatures during the critical Kiremt season is expected to suppress Meher crop yields, reduce agricultural labour demand, and accelerate pasture and water scarcity in pastoral areas.

triggerList.title: Strengthening El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December season in lowland and riverine areas of Ethiopia
triggerList.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during the October–December season across eastern East Africa. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, there is an increased likelihood of flooding across flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia, especially the Somali Region. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa.

rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre's May 2026 forecast indicates a high likelihood of below-normal June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with above-normal temperatures. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more.
Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray. Below-average rainfall would cut yields and household food production. In Tigray and Amhara, poor rains may also reduce agricultural labour income during the June–August lean season.
In past El Niño episodes, Meher maize and sorghum production fell across Ethiopia, most sharply in eastern Amhara,  northeastern Oromia, and Tigray; national yields dropped by around 2% below normal, with localised deficits of 10–15%. High fertiliser and fuel prices will likely limit farmers' input use during planting, lowering yield potential even with adequate rainfall, while raising transport costs for inputs and produce.
Staple food prices are already exceptionally high; annual food inflation reached 13.5% in April, up from 11% in March but down from 15.6% in April 2025 – a renewed monthly acceleration after disinflation, not a sustained year-on-year worsening. Drivers include increased fuel costs from Middle East conflict-linked energy disruptions, seasonal lean season food supply tightening, and trade disruptions, which are severely straining poor rural households.
El Niño typically also boosts the October–December rainfall across lowland/riverine eastern East Africa. Forecasts show a very high chance of above-average rainfall across central and eastern Ethiopia, likely driving flooding in flood-prone lowlands. ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/), [FEWS NET 03/06/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/ethiopia/key-message-update/may-2026), [FEWS NET 10/03/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/ethiopia/food-security-outlook/february-2026), [FEWS NET 18/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/may-2026), [GEOGLAM Crop Monitor 02/06/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-amis), [WMO accessed 08/07/2026](wmolc.org/seasonPmmeUI/view?winName=PlotView1781162850270))

triggerList.title: La Niña persistence and intensification
triggerList.description: Climate forecasts predict La Niña conditions through November 2025 to January 2026, increasing rainfall across Haiti, which will bring flooding and landslides.

rationale:
La Niña started in October 2025 and is expected to persist through February 2026. Historically, La Niña is associated with above-normal precipitation and increased tropical cyclone activity in Haiti, driving severe flooding, landslides, and water-borne disease outbreaks.
Seasonal forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 and above-average temperatures until March 2026, across the whole country. While these anomalies will mostly occur outside the rainy season, which ends in November, flooding has become more common in recent years. La Nina-driven above-normal activity of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, which is expected to last until the end of November, may trigger additional flooding, landslides and damage—repeating destructive patterns seen from Tropical Storm Melissa in late October 2025. Crops' waterlogging in lower-lying agricultural zones may damage crops and reduce yields, to be harvested between December and March, compounding food supply shortages and driving food inflation. Rural populations already displaced by gang violence are particularly vulnerable to flooding, as damage to water and sanitation infrastructure may stretch already limited water, sanitation and hygiene conditions. In October 2025, there was a surge in cholera cases, especially in the West department. The combination of flooding and above-average temperatures may create favourable conditions for waterborne pathogens, increasing the risk of further spread of cholera and other waterborne diseases.
Additionally, flooding and landslides may damage or destroy homes, health infrastructure, and roads, forcing affected communities to relocate to other regions to seek refuge and humanitarian aid, increasing the number of people internally displaced. ([Fews Net 16/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Haiti/Current.pdf); [Copernicus Accessed 05/11/2025](https://climate.copernicus.eu/charts/packages/c3s_seasonal/products/c3s_seasonal_spatial_mm_rain_3m?area=area06&base_time=202510010000&type=tsum&valid_time=202512010000); [CPC 09/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml); [IPC 10/10/2025](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159760/?iso3=HTI); [DTM Accessed 05/11/2025](https://dtm.iom.int/haiti))

rationale: El Niño is very likely to emerge by July 2026 and persist until December 2026 to February 2027. Between June–August 2026, seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation associated with El Niño across the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid region that spans from eastern Guatemala, northern El Salvador, and southern and southwestern Honduras. The region is highly vulnerable to climate shocks, with 21 million people living in rural areas – over 20% of them employed in agriculture, and more than one-third living below the poverty line. While dry and warm conditions in Central America are typical of El Niño events, current forecasts indicate a stronger-than-average El Niño in 2026, with higher temperatures and significantly reduced or irregular rainfall compared to past years. The effects of El Niño in 2026 may be particularly severe as they could affect both the primary and secondary crop seasons, leading to reduced maize, beans, and cash crop yields. Drought may also reduce the availability of water for domestic use, increasing the risk of unsafe water consumption. Above-average temperatures also raise the risk of heatwave events, posing significant public health concerns for at-risk populations, including children, elderly, pregnant women, and people with pre-existing medical conditions. triggerList.description: A continued rise in hotspots and burned area across West and Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra, Riau, and Jambi, particularly where fires spread into deep peat, would indicate that suppression operations are not containing the fire season.
