triggerList.title: Prolonged dry conditions and peak El Nino
triggerList.description: Below-average rainfall, extreme heat, declining water availability ahead of El Nino peak towards the end of 2026 could dry vegetation and peat further. This would allow fires to spread more rapidly and simultaneously across several provinces, stretching firefighting capacity.

rationale:
Indonesia's annual forest and peatland fire season has intensified sharply during the 2026 dry season. Nearly 95,000 hectares burnt in July alone, almost doubling the area burnt during the first six months of the year and bringing the January–July total to more than 202,000 hectares. By late August, around 285,000 hectares had burnt, and thousands of hotspots were being detected across Kalimantan and Sumatra. West Kalimantan, including Ketapang and Pontianak, is among the areas most affected, while fires are also concentrated in Central Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra, particularly Jambi, Riau, and South Sumatra.
The risk could deteriorate over the next one to three months as El Niño conditions intensify and prolong hotter, drier weather. Fire risk normally peaks during the late dry season, while peatland fires can burn underground, spread beyond visible fire lines, and remain difficult to extinguish. Agricultural land clearing and fires within company concessions are also contributing to the ignition and spread. More than 9,000 hotspots were recorded in August, exceeding the number recorded in the same month during the severe 2015 fire season.
Haze is already affecting populated areas across Kalimantan and Sumatra, particularly Jambi city, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, Pekanbaru in Riau, and Pontianak and Singkawang in West Kalimantan, where poor air quality and reduced visibility have disrupted education and transport.
Indonesia has substantial national response capacity. The National Agency for Disaster Countermeasure, provincial authorities, the military, police, and forestry services are conducting ground suppression, water bombing, cloud seeding, hotspot surveillance, and law enforcement operations. By the end of August, authorities had mobilised around 48,000 officers, more than 1,400 volunteers, and 34 firefighting aircraft, while permits had been issued for foreign aircraft. Even so, persistent peat fires, limited water, poor visibility, and simultaneous fires across remote areas could exceed local response capacity and prolong exposure to hazardous smoke. Humanitarian organisations may be required to provide targeted health, education, and livelihood support if the haze persists or national capacity becomes overstretched. ([Reuters 31/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/how-severe-are-indonesias-wildfires-2026-08-31/), [Reuters 31/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/indonesia-inspects-19-companies-linked-wildfires-official-says-2026-08-31/), [Reuters 01/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/reducing-indonesia-wildfires-will-be-challenging-el-nino-peaks-this-month-2026-09-01/), [AP 21/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-forest-land-fires-toxic-haze-7d103393659ecc93a4a7d8dee147491a), [AP 23/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-malaysia-forest-peatland-fires-haze-28e8ce3543e18336db989a67e45c5e6e), [BNPB 04/07/2026](https://www.bnpb.go.id/berita/perkembangan-situasi-dan-penanganan-bencana-di-tanah-air-4-juli-2026), [BNPB 16/04/2026](https://www.bnpb.go.id/berita/perkuat-sinergi-nasional-hadapi-musim-kemarau-bnpb-gelar-apel-kesiapsiagaan-karhutla-di-kalimantan-barat)).

triggerList.title: Prolonged Drought and Heatwaves
triggerList.description:
Iran’s worsening water crisis is being driven by prolonged drought and intensifying heatwaves, which have sharply reduced rainfall, surface water, and groundwater reserves. Between October 2024 and March 2025, precipitation declined by 41% below long-term averages and 21% compared to the previous year, severely limiting inflows into dams and reservoirs.
The deficit now affects 30 of 31 provinces, with the harshest shortfalls recorded in Hormozgan (–75.9%), Sistan-Baluchestan (–75.4%), and East Azerbaijan (–60%). Record-breaking heat has accelerated evaporation, compounding the depletion of already scarce supplies. In Tehran, key reservoirs, Latian, Lar, Mamloo, and Amir Kabir, have dropped to just 5–12% capacity, with the Lar dam nearly empty, threatening water security and essential urban services.
The combined effects of persistent drought, extreme heat, and excessive groundwater extraction have disrupted Iran’s hydrological balance, leading to land subsidence, reduced agricultural output, and growing food insecurity. These climatic pressures are central triggers of Iran’s water crisis, exacerbating structural weaknesses in governance, infrastructure, and livelihoods.

triggerList.title: Climate Change Amplification
triggerList.description:
Climate change is a major amplifier of Iran’s water crisis, intensifying droughts, heatwaves, and rainfall variability across much of the country. Rising temperatures have accelerated evaporation and reduced snowpack in key mountain ranges, diminishing surface runoff that feeds rivers and reservoirs. Over the past two decades, Iran’s average temperature has increased by more than 1.5°C, with extreme heat events becoming longer and more frequent.
This climatic shift has disrupted traditional rainfall cycles, concentrating precipitation into shorter, more intense bursts that fail to replenish groundwater or sustain agriculture. As a result, 30 of 31 provinces now face chronic water stress, with southern and central regions, such as Khuzestan, Yazd, and Sistan-Baluchestan, experiencing the most severe shortages.
Higher temperatures also drive surging demand for irrigation and domestic consumption, compounding existing overuse of groundwater and depletion of reservoirs. The resulting imbalance has caused widespread subsidence, declining crop yields, and rural displacement.

rationale:
Iran’s current water crisis is expected to worsen, with warnings that Tehran could face severe water shortages affecting large parts of the city by October 2025 if water consumption is not drastically reduced. The country has endured a five-year drought, and reservoirs supplying major cities have fallen to their lowest levels in a century. In Tehran, key reservoirs dropped to roughly 14% capacity during peak heat periods, causing widespread water service cuts and outages lasting 12–18 hours in some districts.
Critically low reservoir levels have also hampered hydroelectric power generation, aggravating electricity shortages already driven by fuel constraints and extreme heat. Between June–August, temperatures exceeding 50° C in provinces including Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Yazd led to power and water outages disrupting cooling systems, medical facilities, and water pumping networks. Hospitals report difficulties in maintaining refrigeration for medicines and stable operations during rolling blackouts. At the same time, heat-related mortality has spiked among vulnerable populations, particularly older and displaced people, highlighting severe strain on public health infrastructure. Waterborne disease outbreaks are becoming increasingly likely as water quality deteriorates and sanitation systems falter.
As water scarcity and livelihood pressures intensify, affected populations are likely to seek opportunities in neighbouring countries, including Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, and Türkiye. Political tensions and security concerns may increase irregular migration flows, further aggravating humanitarian needs for displaced people.
Recurrent protests across Fars, Isfahan, and Khuzestan over water and electricity shortages also signal eroding public patience and raise the risk of broader civil unrest amid mounting climate pressures and governance challenges.
([Stimpson 26/03/2025](https://www.stimson.org/2025/no-easy-solutions-for-irans-water-shortages-and-power-outages/), [DW 19/06/2024](https://www.dw.com/en/irans-water-crisis-leads-to-alarming-ground-collapse/a-69405927), [Middle East 18/04/2025](https://middleeast.observer/iran/article/4073/ ), [NCRI 13/08/2025](https://www.ncr-iran.org/en/news/economy/why-iran-is-running-out-of-water-power-and-patience/), [KUNC 17/08/2025](https://www.kunc.org/2025-08-17/iranian-officials-warn-tehran-could-run-out-of-water-in-weeks-amidst-massive-drought),  [Thomson Reuters 17/08/2025](https://www.context.news/climate-risks/opinion/irans-water-crisis-is-driven-by-bad-policies-but-tech-can-help))

triggerList.description: If US conducts "limited" strikes to pressure Iran into deal, Iranian doctrine and Khamenei's threats suggest retaliation targeting US assets, regional partners, or maritime chokepoints (Strait of Hormuz), triggering escalatory spiral.

rationale:
Since January 2026, US–Iran tensions have intensified significantly, with the US assembling the largest military force in the region since the 2003 Iraq invasion. Iranian officials’ rhetoric and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz for military drills on 17 February 2026 demonstrate Iran's willingness to escalate if attacked.
The most probable escalation pathway begins with limited US air strikes targeting strategic Iranian sites, prompting Iranian retaliation through ballistic missile attacks against US military bases in the region, proxy attacks on regional responders, or the closure or militarisation of the Strait of Hormuz. This would trigger US counter-retaliation against Iranian military assets and command structures, potentially expanding the conflict through an escalatory spiral involving Iranian proxies in Yemen, Gulf states facing missile and drone threats, and Israel conducting strikes on Iranian targets, ultimately transforming bilateral US–Iran confrontation into a protracted regional war with multi-front humanitarian consequences.
Direct US military strikes against Iranian strategic targets will likely trigger immediate humanitarian deterioration through mass civilian casualties, critical infrastructure damage, acute protection crises, displacement, and the collapse of already-strained essential services, affecting millions of Iranians and Afghan refugees. ([Reuters 23/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-pulling-non-essential-staff-embassy-beirut-amid-iran-tensions-2026-02-23/), [AJ 24/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/24/trump-hits-out-at-reports-that-top-general-flagged-risks-of-attacking-iran), [TWP 23/02/2026](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/02/23/dan-caine-iran-risk-trump/), [AJ 24/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/2/24/iran-cannot-defeat-us-military-might-but-it-can-still-win))

The leader of Kata'ib Hezbollah has explicitly warned of "total war" in this scenario, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard has reportedly discussed activating alternative support arenas in Iraq in the event of a direct confrontation. triggerList.objective: No

rationale:
A US–Iran confrontation triggered by a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement (placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March 2026) could increase humanitarian needs in Iraq through two compounding mechanisms: direct Iranian proxy escalation via the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and broader regional economic disruption, including potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in Syria and Israel's weakening of Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, Iraq has become a significant regional asset for Iran. The PMF, an official Iraqi security institution composed largely of Iran-backed militias, represents Iran's likely vector for retaliation against US interests in Iraq. Kata'ib Hezbollah, the largest militia within the PMF, has publicly warned of military response if Iran is attacked.
Iraq's political trajectory compounds this risk. Government formation remains contested between the US administration and Iraq's Coordination Framework over the composition of leadership, with the Trump administration threatening to cut Iraq off from its oil revenues if a candidate closely aligned with Iran and the PMF assumes the premiership. Sitting Prime Minister Al Sudani actively restrained the PMF during the June 2025 Iran–Israel conflict, but a pro-Iran administration would significantly increase militia escalation risk. Political instability, combined with PMF escalation, would likely worsen conditions for Iraq's approximately one million IDPs and deepen sectarian tensions.
Beyond direct proxy conflict, a US–Iran confrontation could trigger humanitarian needs through economic disruption. Prior to the escalation, over 90% of Iraq's oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz, with the remaining oil exported through the currently closed Ceyhan pipeline connected to Türkiye via Iraq's autonomous Kurdish region. A potential closure of the strait would eliminate Iraq's primary export route, driving oil price shocks that cascade through Iraq's oil-dependent economy and creating pressure on government services and humanitarian response capacity at a moment when political instability already constrains governance. ([AJ 26/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/26/iraqs-kataib-hezbollah-warns-of-total-war-if-iran-is-attacked), [The Irish Times 28/01/2026](https://www.irishtimes.com/world/middle-east/2026/01/28/trump-issues-warning-as-maliki-is-nominated-as-iraqi-prime-minister/), [The Arab Weekly 11/02/2026](https://thearabweekly.com/trumps-veto-over-maliki-could-give-iraqs-sudani-new-political-lease-life), [AJ 03/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/2/3/will-hezbollah-continue-to-avoid-responding-to-israels-attacks-on-lebanon)]

triggerList.description: Misleading narratives regarding candidates’ eligibility, foreign interference, or electoral fraud could fuel anti-government sentiment and trigger unrest, especially among disenfranchised voters.

rationale:
Côte d’Ivoire is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for 25 October 2025. Although recent elections have been relatively peaceful, the political environment is becoming increasingly tense. The Independent Electoral Commission (CEI) released the final electoral roll on 4 June, confirming the exclusion of four prominent opposition leaders: Laurent Gbagbo, Tidjane Thiam, Charles Blé Goudé, and Guillaume Soro. While Thiam was excluded based on nationality concerns, the others were barred because of past judicial convictions. All four are also prohibited from voting.
The exclusion of these high-profile figures has triggered strong criticism from their parties, which have withdrawn from the CEI and denounced a lack of institutional independence. Some, such as Thiam and his party, have appealed to international bodies such as the UNHRC. Others, including former first lady Simone Gbagbo, have warned that the conditions are not in place for peaceful elections. Some parties have announced protests, and public calls for boycotts or civil disobedience could escalate in the coming months.
The memory of the 2010–2011 post-electoral crisis, which caused over 3,000 civilian deaths, still shapes public perception. While today’s situation differs—institutions are more stable, and international scrutiny is higher—the exclusionary political landscape and growing polarisation echo the warning signs of past unrest. The delayed announcement of President Ouattara’s candidacy adds further uncertainty. If he decides to run for a fourth term, in potential breach of constitutional limits, it could become a flashpoint. ([RFI 24/04/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/en/africa/20250424-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-judge-rules-main-opponent-out-of-presidential-election), [TV5 Monde 26/07/2025](https://information.tv5monde.com/afrique/video/presidentielle-en-cote-divoire-ouverture-du-depot-des-candidatures-2786984), [GSDI accessed 07/07/2025](https://www.idea.int/democracytracker/country/cote-divoire))

rationale:
This risk is materialising at a slow pace. A progressive deterioration of the security situation in the northern regions of West African coastal countries is observed. Between October 2022 and January 2023, more than 73 violent incidents involving mostly non-state armed groups have been reported in the northern regions of Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo. On the same period in 2022, around 30 incidents were reported. These incidents included attacks on civilians and security forces, kidnappings, the destruction of property, and the use of improvised explosive devices. Benin is the country recording the highest number of attacks by armed groups, followed by Togo. In Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the attacks are on a smaller scale given a still-low presence of armed groups, but these are becoming more regular. 
The violence has started to trigger internal displacement in Benin and Togo. In Benin, at least 1,200 IDPs have been reported in the department of Atakora, while in Togo, more than 2,200 IDPs are registered in the region of Savanes.  Armed group activity in the northern regions of Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo has not seemed to affect food insecurity levels, as the number of food-insecure people remained stable between October–December 2022 compared to the same period in 2021.

title: Electoral violence and increased intercommunal conflict throughout Kenya result in displacement, the disruption of livelihoods, and protection concerns.
rationale:
Kenya has experienced electoral violence during past elections. There is a likelihood of electoral violence before/during the August 2022 election period. There is currently high political tension, worsened by hate speech by some politicians. The tone of the media is also quite divisive and disinformation campaigns on social media are becoming more frequent. Politicians could also weaponise ongoing resource-based conflicts for their own political gains. 
There is a possibility of displacement of 150,000 people due to localised violence and intercommunal conflicts. Access constraints are also likely to increase in drought affected areas due to intercommunal conflicts.
In 2022, more than 1,060 political disorder events were reported as at 5 August-the highest since 1997. Many of these events happened during party primaries from March to April.
General elections held on 9 August had relatively low voter turnout(65.4%), allegations of voter bribery and technology failures. Even though a petition challenging the presidential election results was rejected by the Supreme Court, there was peace countrywide until William Ruto was inaugurated as President on 13 September.

triggerList.description: A spike in cross-border displacement particularly from Somalia’s Gedo region or Sudan’s Darfur could overwhelm current camp capacity. Without adequate contingency plans, the humanitarian system would be unable to absorb the new caseload, increasing protection risks, tension with host communities, and possible spillover of insecurity.

rationale:
Kenya’s refugee camps, particularly Dadaab and Kakuma, are facing an increasingly fragile situation owing to severe underfunding, overstretched infrastructure, and surging new arrivals. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. Without urgent interventions, the situation risks spiralling into a protracted crisis marked by localised violence, cross-border insecurity, or forced returns, particularly in light of Kenya's shifting asylum policies and security stance in border regions.
Gaps in healthcare access are increasing the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly as overcrowded living conditions and limited water supplies worsen. Economic hardship and congested settlements are also heightening protection concerns, including gender-based violence. As services and water availability decline, households are expected to relocate within or between camps in search of support, further straining space and social cohesion.
Kenya’s Shirika Plan also continues to face implementation hurdles and growing scepticism among host communities related to resource competition and security. There are concerns that the plan will only benefit those already with resources (business owners and skilled people) rather than the most vulnerable. Given that, the situation may evolve into a sustained protection and humanitarian crisis marked by deteriorating health conditions, rising insecurity, and the potential for forced or premature returns. Refugees may increasingly move outside formal camps in search of livelihoods or better services, often without documentation or assistance. This trend could heighten risks of exploitation, detention, or deportation and further complicate humanitarian coordination and protection efforts. ([TNH 23/05/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/05/23/dadaab-voices-what-aid-cuts-mean-kenyas-refugees), [AJ 20/07/2025](https://liberties.aljazeera.com/en/refugees-in-kenya-face-deepening-hunger-as-aid-cuts-bite/)

triggerList.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September rainfall across western and northern Kenya
triggerList.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing during May–July 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal JJAS rainfall across western and northern Kenya — where the unimodal long rains season in fact extends into August/September and has already tracked below average in April and early May — alongside above-normal temperatures. This combination is expected to reduce soil moisture during the critical grain-filling and maturation stages of long rains crops in the North Rift and western Kenya, directly threatening the October–November harvest. Pastoral areas across the ASALs are likely to experience accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability, compounding already fragile livestock recovery.

triggerList.title: El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December short rains season in eastern and coastal Kenya
triggerList.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during Kenya's October–December short rains season, particularly across eastern and coastal areas. During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comparable pattern of enhanced short rains is likely. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Should this materialise, flooding would damage infrastructure and cropland in areas already weakened by successive climate shocks, further compounding humanitarian needs heading into early 2027.

rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.
The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.
In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.
The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households. ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/), [GEOGLAM Crop Monitor 02/04/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [FEWS NET 04/06/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/key-message-update/may-2026-0), [FEWS NET 07/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/april-2026), [NDMA 14/04/2026](https://ndma.go.ke/drought-situation-brief/), [IPC 21/03/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159540/), [FEWS NET accessed 08/07/2026](https://fews.net/sites/default/files/2024-07/KE-Seasonal-Calendar-202406.pdf))

triggerList.title: Worsening economic condition for refugees in Lebanon

rationale:
Inflation, rising prices, and the depreciation of the Lebanese lira threaten the livelihoods of Syrian refugees, who struggle to survive on cash assistance (delivered in Lebanese liras) or receive low to no salary from their employers in the informal sector. Because of these factors, as well as Lebanese governmental policies on return, an increasing number of refugees might opt for an unsafe return to Syria.

While the severity of people’s needs has worsened, during 2020, the number of voluntary refugees returning to Syria was only 9,351 – half of the figure registered in 2019. The refugees' decisions to return to Syria were influenced mainly by the security and safety situation, economic growth, public service availability, and personal relationships in their place of origin, while refugees’ poor living conditions in Lebanon were less likely to be an influence. Unless the situation significantly improves in Syria, refugees are unlikely to return.

rationale: Since 8 October, the exchange of airstrikes between Hezbollah and Israel following the start of the conflict in Gaza has been mainly near the Blue Line area (southern Lebanon) and mostly targeting military locations. Recent attacks since mid-February 2024 have been expanding into more areas in Lebanon and affecting more civilians. Israel carried out at least two airstrikes in Ghaziyeh town, five kilometres outside a key Lebanese city (Saida), on 19 February. This attack was considered the largest airstrikes carried out near a major population centre since 8 October. A factory producing electrical generators was targeted. On 26 February, an Israeli air strike targeted the outskirts of Buday village near Baalbek city, eastern Lebanon for the first time since 8 October 2023. The attacks targeted a convoy of trucks carrying food, killing at least two people. Hezbollah has also been responding with expanding the geographical area targeted in Israel, increasing the likelihood of further clashes and impacting more areas in Lebanon.

triggerList.title: Military setbacks weakening Hezbollah
triggerList.description: The assassination of Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024 and the pager attack on 17 September 2024 significantly undermined Hezbollah’s operational capabilities. Additionally, the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024 disrupted the supply routes for arms and funds from Iran, further weakening the group. These events have collectively contributed to the perception that Hezbollah’s military strength is in decline.

triggerList.title: Foreign pressure and ceasefire conditions
triggerList.description: Foreign governments, notably the United States and Israel, are pressuring the Lebanese government to marginalize Hezbollah by excluding it from power. The ceasefire agreement signed on 27 November 2024 includes conditions such as the enforcement of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which mandates the withdrawal of Hezbollah fighters from south of the Litani River and prevents further arms transfers.

triggerList.title: Ongoing Israeli military activity
triggerList.description: Despite the ceasefire, Israeli forces continue to conduct air strikes and infiltrations into Lebanese territory, creating a persistent security threat. Israel is actively working to blockade Hezbollah via land, air, and sea to cut off the flow of arms and funds from Iran.

triggerList.title: Growing frustration among the Shia population
triggerList.description: The Shia community, which makes up over 30% of Lebanon’s population, is increasingly frustrated by the government's failure to prevent Israeli attacks on their villages and to support the reconstruction of their homes. Protests and riots, such as those that occurred on 14–15 February 2025 over the ban on Iranian airplanes at Rafic Hariri International Airport, reflect their frustration. This growing discontent risks further mobilising the community against government policies that are seen as marginalising their interests.

triggerList.title: Economic hardship and reconstruction challenges
triggerList.description: The escalation of clashes with Israel has left many areas of southern Lebanon, predominantly inhabited by Shia Lebanese, in ruins, creating an urgent need for reconstruction services. If the needs of the people affected continued to be delayed, it is likely to contribute to their growing frustration with the Government and trigger social tensions and protests. About 99,000 housing units were damaged and destroyed as of 13 February.

rationale:
Since the escalation of conflict with Israel on 8 October 2023, Hezbollah has experienced military setbacks, resulting in its political and military marginalisation. A new Lebanese Government was formed on 9 January 2025, with a prime minister appointed on 8 February. While the leadership tries to balance power, it faces pressure from Israel and the US to exclude Hezbollah, which they label a ‘terrorist’ organisation.
The 27 November 2024 ceasefire agreement included implementing UNSC Resolution 1701, requiring Hezbollah’s withdrawal from south of the Litani River and blocking arms transfers to the group. The resolution also strengthens the role of the Lebanese Armed Forces and UNIFIL in southern Lebanon, which Hezbollah sees as an effort to weaken its military role.
The deadline for Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon was on 18 February 2025, but their troops continue to occupy five border areas. Despite the ceasefire, Israeli air space violations and air strikes continue, resulting in casualties. The Lebanese army has not responded, leaving civilians in southern Lebanon (mostly the Shia community) without protection. Hezbollah is not retaliating, likely because of its commitment to the ceasefire and challenges in smuggling arms from Iran, signalling a possible weakening of the group.
Lebanon’s Shia community, which makes up around 30% of the population, is growing increasingly frustrated with the Government and the Lebanese Armed Forces for failing to prevent Israeli attacks. Many believe that the Government is deliberately weakening Hezbollah, preventing it from protecting the Shia community. Frustration is likely to lead to more protests, such as those on 14–15 February 2025, after the Government blocked Iranian planes from landing in Beirut in response to Israeli threats. These flights are believed to play a key role in receiving Iranian funds to rebuild homes destroyed by Israeli air strikes. It has been reported that the people affected by the conflict feel that their sacrifices in defending Lebanon’s southern border are unappreciated and that their needs are being neglected. At the same time, Hezbollah is struggling to secure funds for rebuilding homes and key infrastructure damaged in the conflict, particularly in Shia-majority southern Lebanon. The destruction includes over 99,000 housing units, 26 health facilities, 46 water facilities, and 2,192 hectares of agricultural land.
Rising tensions are likely to lead to more riots and protests from the Shia community against the Government. This could result in clashes with security forces, further intensifying tensions between the Government and Hezbollah. A civil war remains unlikely, but social tensions leading to localised clashes and displacement may happen as the needs of affected people remain unmet and Hezbollah continues to be sidelined.

rationale:
Rising intercommunal tensions between host communities and IDPs in Lebanon have intensified by late March 2026 amid large-scale displacement and mounting socioeconomic pressure. The re-escalation of hostilities between Hezbollah and Israel since 1 March has displaced an estimated 1.2 million people, mostly from southern Lebanon.
Reports indicate growing host community fatigue, with increasing complaints over overcrowding, pressure on basic services, and the repurposing of schools and public buildings into collective shelters, disrupting education and raising concerns over some IDP sites becoming permanent sites rather than temporary ones.
Besides the high number of IDPs, many other factors drive the tensions, including economic deterioration, rising fuel and commodity prices, and a highly polarised information environment that is fuelling sectarian tensions between Shia and Christian/Sunni populations. Misinformation, especially on social media, including security-related rumours and anti-IDP rhetoric are fuelling tensions. Host communities also express security concerns, fearing that the presence of IDPs may expose their areas to Israeli air strikes. Already, OCHA has reported instances of intercommunal tensions within host communities, although their nature is unclear.
Further escalation may emerge from additional waves of displacement, the expansion of Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon, and Israeli air strikes on areas considered ‘safe’ for IDPs. For example, between 12–13 March 2026, Israeli air strikes expanded into residential areas hosting IDPs in Beirut and Mount Lebanon, killing at least eight people and injuring several others. Such attacks on what is perceived as ‘safe areas’ are heightening tensions between host communities and IDPs.
These dynamics are likely to translate into localised clashes over the next three to six months as displacement continues, particularly in high-density urban areas where resources are scarce and governance is weak. Clashes are most likely between host community residents and IDPs (the majority of whom are Shia) but may also involve civic authorities or security forces enforcing restrictive measures. Such clashes are likely to increase insecurity and fatalities and drive further displacement, particularly for already displaced populations. The risk is assessed as Medium, as key triggers, including large-scale displacement, host community pressure, and rising anti-IDP rhetoric are already present, and recent incidents indicate increasing tensions; however, while widespread intercommunal violence is unlikely, the probability of localised incidents remains significant. ([UNDP 30/03/2026](https://admin.tms-lebanon.com/StaticFiles/Files/TMS_Tensions_Pulse_-_30_March_2026.pdf), [UNHCR 30/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/middle-east-situation-lebanon-flash-update-4-23-29-march-2026), [Megaphone 30/03/2026](https://megaphone.news/oped/%D9%87%D9%84-%D9%85%D8%A7-%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%AF-%D9%85%D9%85%D9%83%D9%86%D8%A7), [OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [IM Lebanon 13/03/2026](https://www.imlebanon.org/2026/03/13/lebanon-1389/))

triggerList.description: An increased Russian presence could strengthen Khalifa Haftar’s position. Already on 31 December, reports indicated that Haftar's forces had taken control of a camp affiliated with the Presidential Council, though it did not trigger further clashes as of 8 January 2025

rationale:
On 18 December 2024, Russia transferred approximately 1,000 military personnel, including former Syrian soldiers, from Hmeimim airbase in Lattakia governorate in Syria to Benghazi airport in Libya, which is under the control of the Haftar Affiliated Forces. The personnel included officers from Syria’s 5th Corps and 25th Special Tasks Division, along with dismantled S-400 air defence systems. The move appears to be Russia’s strategic aim to strengthen its military presence in Libya, a key asset for its operations in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also likely an opportunity to compensate for the loss that Russia experienced in Syria following the fall of Bashar Al Assad regime on 8 December.
Since 2008, Russia has sought to expand its influence in Libya, using bases near Benghazi and Al Jufra districts to support operations across the Sahel region (Mali, Burkina Faso) and Sudan. Libya's location near NATO's southern border and its shorter access to the Sahel region make it key for Russia's strategic goals.
An increased Russian presence will likely empower Khalifa Haftar to dominate Libyan politics, potentially undermining UN negotiations and creating threats to Europe, including trade and energy disruptions, as an escalation of clashes can halt the export of Libyan oil to Europe. This is especially important as Russia seeks to maintain Mediterranean power projection, leveraging facilities such as the Al Khadim airbase and Tobruk port. That said, Turkish military presence in Libya is another critical factor shaping this dynamic. Since 2019, Türkiye has maintained a military foothold in western Libya to counterbalance the Russian-backed Haftar forces and protect the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity.
The empowering of Haftar's forces may intensify military confrontations with Turkish-backed forces aligned with the Government of National Unity and other militias and armed groups in western and southern Libya. Islamist groups still active in Libya, such as the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant and Al Qaeda, will also likely exploit the instability for their own agendas, potentially clashing with Haftar's forces.
If the risk materialises, it could escalate into a proxy battle between Russia and Türkiye. On that note, both states are also likely to avoid direct confrontation for several reasons, most of which are economic, related to interests in energy, trade, and arms deals. Türkiye’s continued presence could contribute to maintaining the status quo, as it deters Haftar from initiating major offensives while limiting the extent of Russian influence.

rationale:
On 12 May 2025, Tripoli security forces announced the killing of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli (also known as Ghnewa), commander of the Stability Support Apparatus (SSA). His assassination immediately triggered armed clashes in southern Tripoli. Militia units loyal to the SSA fought the 444th Combat Brigade forces (aligned with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah), resulting in intense gun battles and killing eight civilians. By 14 May, a ceasefire was declared. As part of the political impacts, Tripoli saw large protests with demonstrators demanding Dbeibah’s resignation. By mid-May, at least three ministers announced their resignations in solidarity with the protesters.
In eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA) remains under the control of General Khalifa Haftar, with his son, Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar, taking on an increasingly central operational role. In April 2025, Saddam held meetings in Ankara and Washington, signalling growing diplomatic outreach. Domestically, he has overseen new military deployments and Russian arms deliveries since December 2024. On 20 May 2025, LNA patrols under his command were reported deploying towards southwest Libya, likely indicating a strategic shift of eastern forces to the southern region. With Dbeibah's recent consolidation of power in Tripoli and Ghnewa’s defeat, Saddam may likely be preparing for a countermove. Drawing on past events, such as in 2019 when Khalifa Haftar led a military campaign to control Tripoli but failed, Saddam could escalate militarily through deployments from Sebha or Sirte districts or by mobilising southern tribal militias. His actions indicate readiness to exploit any perceived weakness in the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity.
Any prolonged fighting in Tripoli is likely to draw in external factions and lead to militia skirmishes extending beyond Tripoli into Zawiya and Misrata cities or some cities in Fezzan region, or provoke direct LNA intervention from the east or south. For instance, units from Zawiya and Warshefana were seen moving towards Tripoli during the recent clashes in May. The clashes could shift from being between militias to involving more formal forces, such as the LNA’s southern brigades, resulting in fighting erupting in civilian neighbourhoods and leading to displacement. ([Atlantic Council 16/05/2025](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/the-killing-of-abdul-ghani-al-kikli-may-be-a-turning-point-for-libya/#:~:text=On%20May%2012%2C%202025%2C%20Abdulghani,%E2%80%9Dhttps://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/20/libya-civilians-caught-militia-clashes#:~:text=Heavy%20fighting%20broke%20out%20between,government), [Reuters 16/05/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/middle-east/two-ministers-internationally-recognized-libyan-government-resign-2025-05-16/), [AJ 17/05/2025](https://aje.io/3tcjm6))

triggerList.title: Escalating security incidents and political assassinations
triggerList.description: The killing of Saif Al Islam Gaddafi on 3 February 2026 and the subsequent prosecutor-led investigation on 5 February have heightened political tensions, reinforced perceptions of militia impunity, and increased the risk of retaliatory violence and destabilisation.

rationale:
Amid a stalled UN-backed political process and deep institutional fragmentation, political tensions in Libya will likely increase over the next three to six months around the April 2026 presidential and parliamentary elections and ensuing impacts.
The immediate political context is marked by institutional paralysis. Disputes between the east-based House of Representatives (HoR) and the Tripoli-based High Council of State (HCS) over the reconstitution of the High National Election Commission (HNEC) board have stalled the electoral timeline. On 29 December 2025, the HoR voted to fill vacant HNEC board seats, prompting the HCS head to accuse the HoR speaker of violating the UN-backed political agreement. On 5 January 2026, the HCS elected a new HNEC president, triggering objections from eastern authorities. UNSMIL publicly warned on 6 January that these escalatory steps risk undermining the political process. By mid-February, UNSMIL reported “no meaningful progress” on agreeing to election rules or forming a unified Government.
Several triggers could spark election-related violence. First, unilateral actions by either side on electoral institutions or rules risk provoking armed responses from rival authorities and affiliated militias. Second, the proposed UNSMIL structured dialogue risks reinforcing existing power imbalances, particularly if perceived as bypassing key stakeholders or legitimising contested authorities. Third, rising economic pressure – including fuel shortages, declining living standards, and the devaluation of the Libyan dinar by nearly 15% on 18 January – is deepening public frustration. Fourth, escalating security incidents and assassinations are heightening tensions. Most notably, the killing of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi on 3 February, followed by a prosecutor-led investigation announced on 5 February without visible accountability measures, may reinforce perceptions that armed groups can carry out political violence with impunity, contributing to heightened tensions and fears of politically motivated targeting.
If violence erupts, it will most likely take the form of localised armed clashes between rival armed groups aligned with eastern and western authorities instead of conflict on nationwide front lines. High-risk areas include Tripoli and its surroundings, where competing militias operate; Benghazi city and eastern Libya, where tensions between political authorities and security forces persist; and southern border areas, where armed groups and criminal networks are active. Violence could include targeted killings, attacks on electoral institutions, the intimidation of political figures, and clashes over strategic infrastructure. Given Libya’s history, even limited clashes could trigger localised displacement, disrupt basic services, and restrict humanitarian access, particularly in urban centres and contested southern regions.
Regional involvement, including Tunisia’s February proposal with Algeria and Egypt in coordination with UNSMIL, may help reduce tensions by supporting a Libyan-led dialogue. Without agreement among Libyan authorities and armed groups, however, it is unlikely to prevent election-related violence. ([TNA 03/11/2025](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/libyas-18-month-gamble-uns-political-roadmap-nowhere), [TNA 05/02/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/libya-probes-killing-late-ruler-gaddafis-son), [AJ 27/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/1/27/%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%86%D8%B3-%D8%AA%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B1%D8%AD-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%B8%D9%8A%D9%85-%D9%85%D8%A4%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B1-%D8%AC%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%A9), [ICG accessed 24/02/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/crisiswatch/january-trends-and-february-alerts-2026), [Peace News 16/02/2026](https://peacenews.com/fragmentation-governance-and-the-limits-of-political-settlement-and-peacebuilding-in-libya/), [UNSC 18/02/2026](https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16298.doc.htm))

triggerList.title: Rainfall deficits and above average precipitation affecting agricultural production
triggerList.description: Dry conditions are likely to lead to reduced soil moisture, crop failure, and declining pasture availability, which in turn limit household food production and income from agriculture. This reduces food availability at the household level and increases reliance on markets at a time of constrained purchasing power.

rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity. title: Deterioration of humanitarian situation in Mali
rationale: On 18 August, troops in Bamako conducted a mutiny and arrested the country's president, Ibrahim Boubacar Keita, and vice-president. Late in the night between 18-19 August, IBK resigned dissolving the parliament and the government. Men claiming to be the spokespeople of the "National Committe for the Salvation of the People" gave an address on the country's public TV station where they announced that the country's borders were now closed and a curfew was in place. They also promised that the Malian armed forces would honour all of their current commitments (G5 Sahel and Barkhane, 2015 peace deal), and that elections would be organized in a "reasonable" amount of time. People have been protesting since a controversial ruling by the country's Constitutional Court flipped 31 legislative seats, including 10 that went to IBK's party. The protests were organized by the M5-RFP coalition under the guidance of Immam Dicko. So far, there is no evidence of coordination between the coup plotters and M5-RFP. The main difference between this coup and the one in 2012, which makes predicting outcomes difficult, is that this time high-ranking officers are involved (The leader is Colonel Assimi Goita). The TV statement also makes it seem like the coup plotters are politically savvy. The coup has drawn international condemnation, including ECOWAS, AU, France, USA and the UN. Consequences so far: ECOWAS has called on their members to close their borders with Mali and stop financial flows. A prolonged dispute between ECOWAS and Mali could mean economic problems for the local population, and access issues for the humanitarian sector. If the coup leads to even lower state and coalition presence in conflict-affected areas, we could see a dramatic rise in violence. As of writing all senarios are plausible. Rainy season is underway, with shifted priorities, humanitarian response could be affected.

title: An increase in security incidents lead to displacement in Niono circle.
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since July, clashes have resumed in the Niono circle (Ségou region) between the Katiba Macina armed group linked to Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (Aqmi) and the traditional dozo hunters militia in the area, who tried to face them. The ceasefire agreement that was reached in March 2021 has been broken.  The situation has deteriorated particularly since the end of September with daily attacks targeting civilians but also clashes between armed groups and militia. Dozens of deaths are reported even though there is no reliable figures yet. The Dozo militiamen are also accused of extortion, forced recruitment and cattle theft. These incidents occur during the harvest period, preventing farmers from going to the fields. Many people have started to flee to safer places, especially in Ségou. With the violence continuing, the risk of increased attacks on civilians and displacement seems very likely in the weeks to come. The needs for essential goods and food security are likely to increase.

title: Economic sanctions lead to the loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity.
rationale: On 9 January 2022 the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) decided to apply several economic sanctions against Mali, including the closure of land and air borders with member countries, the suspension of all commercial and financial transactions between ECOWAS countries and Mali, and the freezing of Malian assets in the Central Banks of ECOWAS. These sanctions were applied in reaction to the decision of the Transition authorities to postpone the presidential election, initially scheduled for February 2022, and following the submission of a timetable for a transition period of five years at the end of the Assises Nationales de la Refondation −consultations with the population with the objective to fix the date of the next elections and to guarantee the return of civilians to power. The five-year period was judged too long by ECOWAS.

rationale:
Since September 2025, Jama'a Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an Al Qaeda–affiliated group, has expanded its blockade strategy from the traditional conflict zones in northern and central Mali (Gao, Mopti, Tombouctou) to southern and southwestern regions, including Kayes, Koulikoro, and Ségou. This expansion signals a shift towards a strategy of coercive governance, with JNIM using economic strangulation – via targeted attacks on fuel convoys and the imposition of checkpoints along critical trade routes – to undermine state legitimacy and force power-sharing negotiations. The blockade marks the first large-scale attempt to encircle Bamako, Mali’s capital, and demonstrates the group’s increasing operational reach.
The blockades have resulted in acute shortages of fuel, electricity, and essential goods across the country. Fuel prices in Bamako surged by over 400% in October, with queues lasting hours and some car owners abandoning vehicles at petrol stations. Major public services, including health and education, have been severely disrupted. The Government closed schools and universities nationwide from 27 October to 9 November, citing the inability of staff and students to reach facilities amid the fuel crisis. Power cuts have intensified, and hospitals in peripheral cities, such as Sikasso and Koutiala, have reported severely limited operations. JNIM has enforced the blockade by destroying an estimated 200 fuel tankers since September, as well as killing at least 15 drivers and abducting others. The group has openly threatened transporters and companies attempting to defy the blockade. Humanitarian responders report that key corridors – particularly those linking Mali to Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire – are patrolled through armed checkpoints, and the Government is unable to maintain secure access despite military escorts. Several areas, such as Loulouni in the south and towns in Mopti and Gao, remain fully or partially isolated.
The humanitarian situation is likely to deteriorate further as a result of the blockade. Food insecurity, protection risks – particularly for women and girls – and displacement are expected to worsen amid prolonged service collapse. The blockades are likely to further destabilise Mali by directly undermining state authority and creating conditions for civil unrest. The fuel crisis caused by the blockade has led to the disruption of essential services, such as electricity, healthcare, water, and transportation, which are crucial for state legitimacy. When citizens cannot access hospitals, schools close, electricity fails for weeks, and food prices rise, they are likely to have a negative perception of the junta. The junta’s initial legitimacy came from promises of security and order; the blockades have destroyed both, leaving only the appearance of powerlessness. ([AJ 06/11/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/6/is-mali-about-to-fall-to-al-qaeda-affiliate-jnim), [The Conversation 31/10/2025](https://theconversation.com/bamako-under-siege-why-malis-army-is-struggling-to-break-the-jihadist-blockade-of-the-capital-268521), [RFI 27/10/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251027-mali-les-cours-suspendus-dans-les-%C3%A9coles-en-raison-de-la-p%C3%A9nurie-de-carburant), [DW 14/11/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/mopti-crise-carburant-electricite/a-74754156), [Protection Cluster 01/10/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/resume-note-de-protection-du-deuxieme-trimestre-2025), [CARE 21/10/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/hunger-extreme-weather-and-funding-shortfalls-drive-humanitarian-needs-mali), [IRC 21/10/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/irc-together-local-authority-respond-huge-needs-after-blockade-lifted-lere-northern-mali), [FEWS NET 30/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-key-message-update-elevated-assistance-needs-persist-insecure-areas-northern-and-central-mali-september-2025))

triggerList.title: Expansion of coordinated JNIM–FLA operations
triggerList.description: Coordinated attacks by JNIM and the FLA against military bases, urban centres, and strategic infrastructure may continue or expand into additional regions, increasing territorial contestation and exposing civilians to heightened insecurity. Although likely tactical and temporary, continued operational coordination between both actors could allow simultaneous attacks across multiple regions and increase pressure on Malian forces. Sustained cooperation may also increase pressure on transport corridors and urban areas, particularly around central and northern Mali, while complicating military operations and humanitarian access. Further attacks on strategic towns or military positions could increase insecurity in areas previously considered comparatively more stable.
triggerList.objective: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if coordinated JNIM–FLA operations expand beyond current areas of activity and result in sustained attacks against additional strategic urban centres, transport corridors, or military installations across northern and central Mali.

triggerList.title: Intensification of military operations and retaliatory violence
triggerList.description: In response to the coordinated attacks, Malian forces and allied armed actors may increase military operations, aerial strikes, and security measures in contested areas. Expanded military deployments around strategic towns, transport corridors, and urban centres may increase movement restrictions and insecurity for civilians. Escalating confrontations and the militarisation of strategic urban centres and transport routes may increase protection risks for civilians, including displacement, restrictions on movement, and disruptions to humanitarian operations and access to essential services. Communities perceived as supporting rival armed actors may also face heightened risks of reprisals, arbitrary restrictions, or violence by conflict parties.
triggerList.objective: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if expanded military operations and retaliatory violence result in sustained movement restrictions, significant civilian displacement, widespread protection incidents, or major disruptions to humanitarian access and essential services in conflict-affected areas.

rationale:
Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation.

JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly signalling southward expansion following the capture of Kidal region, citing Gao and Tombouctou as its next targets, and JNIM threatening a full blockade of Bamako region along the Senegalese and Ivorian corridors, populations in major urban centres face mounting risks of acute fuel and food shortages. Critically low stocks in the capital mean any sustained suspension of truck traffic could rapidly disrupt electricity, healthcare, and water access for millions already living under severe humanitarian stress. Towns such as Bandiagara and Douentza are already becoming more isolated because of road insecurity and flight suspensions, significantly constraining humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

Escalating resource scarcity and growing disillusionment within the military following the Kidal withdrawal increase the likelihood of intra-junta fracture or countercoup in the coming weeks. Political instability at the centre would further constrain the junta's capacity to manage insurgent pressure, negotiate humanitarian access, and sustain basic service delivery, deepening civilian vulnerability across northern, central, and western Mali. ([RFI 12/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260512-mali-%C3%A0-bamako-sous-blocus-jihadiste-les-aliments-ne-manquent-pas-les-difficult%C3%A9s-non-plus), [RFI 23/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260523-mali-le-jnim-attaque-cinq-villages-pr%C3%A8s-de-bandiagara-faisant-une-vingtaine-de-morts), [FEWS NET 21/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-food-security-outlook-update-reduced-food-access-worsening-acute-food-insecurity-north-and-center-april-september-2026), [WFP 19/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-may-2026), [RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [ACLED 30/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/heni-nsaibia-fall-kidal-turning-point-malis-conflict), [OCHA 08/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-bulletin-humanitaire-fevrier-mars-2026), [FEWS NET 14/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-key-message-update-persistent-insecurity-hindering-food-security-center-and-north-march-september-2026), [WeWorld 30/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/4aae42fc-2e51-487b-bff2-f923a8d1f7ca/Mali%20Flash%20Update%20%231%20-%20April%202026_WeWorld.pdf), [BBC 29/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy818zdv831o), [Credendo 11/05/2026](https://credendo.com/en/knowledge-hub/mali-coordinated-tuareg-rebel-and-jihadist-assaults-push-regime-brink-collapse))

triggerList.description: As food stocks deplete and pasture scarcity peaks during the lean season (June–September), competition over land, water, and grazing areas intensifies, increasing the risk of localised clashes between refugee, host, and returnee communities.

rationale:
As of July 2025, pressure over limited resources continues to increase, especially in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya, where the number of Malian refugees continues to increase, while drought and seasonal dry conditions continue in depletion of water and grazing resources, which may trigger tensions and localized clashes. 
The southeastern Hodh Chargui wilaya, which borders Mali, now hosts over 160,000 Malian refugees as of 30 June 2025, compromising over 25.5% of the total population of the wilaya, up from 19% in 2024. The refugee-to-host population ratio in some areas exceeds 1:4, straining access to local sources of water, fuel wood, and grazing land. Competition for scarce water, land, and grazing resources is intensifying between refugees, local communities, and Mauritanian returnees, who were previously displaced from Mali due to insecurity and violence. Localised tensions over access to farmland and grazing areas are often reported and is likely, as was the case in 2022 following a large influx of Malian refugees into Mauritania. Simultaneously, recurring climate shocks such as prolonged droughts, which have affected the country for several decades, and floods in 2024, which displaced 1,125 people and caused damage to agriculture and grazing areas, have weakened rural livelihoods, especially in agropastoral areas where over 60% of the population depends on rain-fed agriculture and livestock.
If refugee flows from Mali continue or host resources become further depleted, social cohesion could be further disrupted, triggering localised clashes between communities over land, water, and grazing access. Departments such as Bassikounou, Fassala, and Amourj, that host the highest Malian refugees population and where land tenure is contested between returnees and local families, are likely to report localised clashes. ([UNICRI accessed 12/09/2025](https://unicri.org/Publication-Climate-Security-Violent-Extremism-Guide-Mauritania-2025), [UNICEF 28/07/2025](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/117790), [WB accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.ncr-iran.org/en/news/economy/why-iran-is-running-out-of-water-power-and-patience/), [ECHO 16/10/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/mauritania-floods-ifrc-office-national-de-la-meteorologie-noaa-west-africa-echo-daily-flash-16-october-2024), [Soueilem, S. rationale:
The Migrant Protection Protocol (MPP) in the United States will be back in force from Monday 6 December. Through this programme, initially implemented by Trump's administration, the aim is for migrants to wait in Mexican border cities while asylum applications to the United States are processed. This policy works alongside Title 42, which means that, in addition to preventing asylum seekers from passing through, the US government will be able to return asylum seekers already in the US to Mexico's borders. 
This represents a risk for the migrant population, due to the high levels of xenophobia at the borders. In addition, the Protocol would increase the number of migrants at Mexico's borders, where most shelters are almost at capacity (as is the case in Tamaulipas and Reynosa). There is also a risk to the sectoral needs of the migrant population, as many of the border cities are heavily controlled by drug cartels. To date, 1,544 assaults against MPP asylum seekers have been recorded. Legal representation for MPP asylum seekers is limited (only 10% have access).

rationale:
The “dzud” is a multiple natural disaster comprising summer drought resulting in inadequate pasture and production of hay, followed by severe winter conditions consisting heavy snow cover, winds, and lower-than-normal temperatures. The phenomenon prevents livestock from accessing pasture or from receiving adequate hay and fodder, resulting in high mortality levels, especially in steppe (dry and grassy plain), vast grassland, devoid of trees and with little diversity in vegetation.

The frequency of severe winters has doubled in the past 20 years, making only 1% of the steppe suitable for growing crops. These conditions are commonly preceded by a dry summer with equally scant grazing.  Livestock struggle to build up the stores of fat they need for winter, and farming families risk losing their main source of income. A quarter to a third of the national herd population were lost in the past two dzud events.

According to the National Agency for Meteorology and Environmental Monitoring, around 15% of the Mongolian territory is at the highest level of risk (extreme risk) and around 45% is at high level of dzud risk in 2023.

The usual peak period for livestock mortality is February to April. December through February are the coldest months of the year, when livestock lose most of their fat and become malnourished. Assessments identified the period January to April 2023 to be the critical period to act early and protect herder livelihoods.

rationale:
On 9 October 2024, Mozambique held general elections featuring three main presidential candidates: the Frelimo party’s Daniel Chapo, successor to outgoing President Filipe Nyusi; Venâncio Mondlane of the new Podemos party; and Ossufo Momade of the Renamo party.  Allegations of vote tampering, restricted access for opposition representatives and observers, 
and the misuse of state resources marred the election process  Though Chapo led early results, Mondlane alleged victory on 
10 October based on parallel vote counts.
On 21 October, protests erupted after Mondlane called for demonstrations and a nationwide general strike. The police’s heavy-handed response – including firing live ammunition at demonstrators; the targeted killing of two senior opposition figures, including  Mondlane’s lawyer, who was preparing a case claiming electoral fraud; and the declaration by the National Election Commission on 24 October of Chapo as the winner with 71% of the votes– intensified the protests across the country, including in Beira, Maputo, Nacala,  Pemba, Nampula, Zambezia, and Chimoio. Mondlane subsequently went into hiding, 
although he has continued to incite protesters, through social media, promising to continue until the Frelimo party concedes the election. 
Between 21 October and 13 December, 275 protests and riots were reported, with at least 130 people killed, more than 2,000 injured (including by bullets), and almost 4,000 arrested and detained, including children. Protests have grown violent in urban centres, such as Maputo, Nampula, and Zambezia, 
evidenced by the increasing number of casualties, arrests from the riots, and violent clashes with the police, who have used live ammunition and tear gas. After Cyclone Chido hit northern Mozambique on 15 December, Mondlane called for a temporary halt in the protests to mourn the victims.  According to Mondlane, protests, which will be “life or death”, should restart on 23 December.
Since the protests began, economic disruption has been extensive and continues to worsen as general strikes shut down businesses and block key infrastructure. Protests that cause road closures frequently paralyse urban centres, including Maputo, Nampula, and Zambezia. Between 7–9 December, the state-owned Electricidade de Moçambique announced electricity provision restrictions in the south of the country, including 
Maputo, because of the protests. Until 11 December, operations in Maputo port remained suspended since 6 November, affecting the flow of goods. The border with South Africa has also been temporarily closed on different occasions, most recently between 9–12 December, affecting crucial imports such as food supplies.
Since the start of the protests, government crackdowns on free speech – including mobile network and internet shutdowns, press restrictions, and intimidation – have further fuelled tensions. While foreign governments and human rights organisations condemn the excessive use of force, more opposition parties and figures, including the Renamo party, have joined the call to overturn the elections. Protests have evolved from rejecting alleged election fraud to include broader demands for systemic reform, citing corruption, poverty, a lack of opportunities, and restricted freedoms under the Frelimo party’s decades-long rule.
Over the next one to three months, there is a very high probability of escalating civil unrest across the country, as neither Mondlane nor the Government appears willing to compromise. The unrest could worsen with the expected 23 December annoucement by the Constitutional Council of the verified election results, continued internet shutdowns and press restrictions,  direct incitement to violence or extremism from either side, and increasing violent crackdowns and police brutality. An escalation could damage the economy and lead to a widespread breakdown in law and order, intensifying poverty, aggravating humanitarian needs (such as protection and food security), and further limiting humanitarian access, including for the humanitarian response to Cyclone Chido.
____________________________
Update 28/02/2025
From 21 October 2024 to 25 February 2025, over 300 deaths related to post-election protests have been reported nationwide. A Mozambican civil society monitoring group indicated that at least seven additional people died in clashes with security forces on 15 January 2025. Maputo province appears to be the most affected area, with more than 100 fatalities documented. There have also been reports of unlawful arrests, detentions, forced disappearances, and injuries.
Despite the absence of substantial post-election demonstrations in February, tensions remain elevated. The initial catalyst for these protests was the controversial outcome of the previous national elections in October 2024, which many deemed fraudulent. That said, the current unrest has evolved, with the cost of living becoming a primary concern. This was evidenced in Inhambane province on 25 February, where protesters violently vandalised and torched the headquarters of Mozambique’s governing Frelimo party. The economy of Mozambique contracted by 4.87% in the fourth quarter of 2024 compared to the same period the previous year as a result of post-election protests.
____________________________
Update 27/03/2025
As of March 2025, more than 350 people have been killed from the disputed October 2024 elections as the country continues to experience civil unrest and economic challenges.​
On 05 March, Mozambican police fired upon supporters of opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane during a protest march in Maputo, injuring more than 15 people. The demonstrators were protesting ahead of President Daniel Chapo's signing of an agreement with certain political parties aimed at ending months of post-election protests. Mondlane, who was excluded from these negotiations, pledged to continue his protests against the government. However, on 23 March opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane and President Daniel Chapo had a meeting in Maputo and agreed to put an end to the unrest and was part of “the ongoing effort to promote national stability and strengthen the commitment to reconciliation and the unity of Mozambicans.’’
Both parties have agreed to end all forms of violence, including state violence and attacks on members of Frelimo and other groups. Those injured during the post-election protests, including police officers and Frelimo members, will receive free medical care and medication. Families of those killed in the protests will be provided with social assistance and compensation, while psychological support will be available for those affected by the violence. Additionally, detainees arrested in connection with the protests will be granted pardons. To formalize these commitments, teams are being established to draft an official agreement reflecting the consensus reached.
The situation remains volatile, with uncertainty if protests will continue, a heavy-handed security response, and significant economic downturns. Efforts to mediate the crisis have yet to yield substantial results, and the potential for further unrest persists.
