triggerList.title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
triggerList.description:
Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: 
During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers.

triggerList.title: Above-average rainfall in northern provinces
triggerList.description: El Niño conditions can enhance moisture inflow in parts of northern Mozambique, leading to above-average and more intense rainfall events. This increases the likelihood of river overflow, flash floods, and waterlogging, especially in low-lying and flood-prone districts. Saturated soils reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff, amplifying flood severity even during short periods of heavy rainfall. Flooding can damage homes, crops, and transport infrastructure, disrupt market access, and increase the risk of population displacement and waterborne diseases, further compounding humanitarian needs.

triggerList.title: Delayed onset and irregular distribution of rains
triggerList.description: El Niño is often associated with a late or erratic start to the rainy season, followed by uneven rainfall patterns throughout the season. In Mozambique, this disrupts the agricultural calendar, delaying planting and reducing the effective growing period for key crops such as maize. Intermittent dry spells during critical crop growth stages can further reduce yields. At the same time, unpredictable rainfall undermines farmers’ decision-making and increases the likelihood of replanting, leading to higher input costs and reduced resilience among households dependent on farming.

rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health. ([WMO 02/06/2026](https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/wmo-prepare-el-nino), [FEWS NET accessed 11/06/2026]( https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique), [CoM 18/05/2026](https://clubofmozambique.com/news/mozambique-inam-warns-el-nino-may-affect-key-sectors/), [WMO 24/04/2026] (https://wmo.int/media/news/wmo-likelihood-increases-of-el-nino), [Noticias 16/05/2026](https://www.noticiasaominuto.com/economia/2990923/mocambique-em-alerta-face-a-nova-previsao-de-um-evento-el-nino-forte), [Afroline 17/05/2026](https://afroline.co.mz/2026/05/mocambique-alerta-el-nino-2026-2027-ameaca-agravamento-de-secas-e-inundacoes/), [FEWS NET 21/05/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Mozambique/Current.pdf))

The 3 September ISM attack on a hunting camp in Marrupa occurred during the current hunting season, indicating that this seasonal activity can create opportunities for NSAG operations in Niassa.

triggerList.description: A significant reduction, redeployment or change in operational coverage by Rwandan or other external security forces in Cabo Delgado could create additional space for ISM activity and facilitate movement into southern Cabo Delgado and neighbouring provinces. Rwanda was still rotating personnel into Cabo Delgado in July 2026, while Mozambique has continued to describe the Rwandan deployment as an important component of counter-insurgency operations.

rationale:
Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.
Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations. ([ACLED 05/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-august-2026), [IOM 24/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/mozambique-movement-alert-report-163-24-june-2026), [ACLED 08/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-september-2026), [OCHA 08/09/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-2026-humanitarian-response-conflict-overview-july-2026-enpt), [Gov.UK accessed 22/09/2026](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/mozambique/regional-risks))

In 2024, the military junta forces experienced significant number of desertions and defections. They also saw their officers surrendering to armed resistance forces rather than fight. Many of the military junta forces have been demoralised due to them being isolated in rural encampments and surrounded by armed resistance forces, with inadequate basic supplies. triggerList.description:
Generally, Myanmar military junta has been receiving economic, political, and/or military support from ally countries, particularly China, Russia, and India. UPDATE (05/01/2025)
China has continued its economic, political, and military support for the Myanmar military junta. The support includes investments in infrastructure projects; and sale of defence equipment, such as ammunition, tanks, and fighter jets, and raw materials such as copper, aluminium, and steel. China has also proposed joint security venture with the Myanmar military junta.

rationale:
On 10 February 2024, Myanmar’s military junta announced the activation of the conscription law enforcing mandatory military service for young people. Evading conscription could result in a prison sentence.
Around 14 million civilians are eligible for conscription. The annual recruitment target is estimated to be around 50,000 to 70,000 people. The activation of the law is considered a response to the loss of military junta troops through deaths, injuries, desertions, and defections in the armed conflict against armed resistance groups, comprising anti-coup resistance forces and ethnic armed organisations (EAOs). 
Similar conscription has also been observed among some of the EAOs, both against and allied with the military, in northern Shan state, indicating a possible expansion of the warscape in the state. 
It has been widely reported that young people are reluctant to serve in the military under the military junta and some may even join the armed resistance groups instead of the military as, in general, they oppose the military junta. Many other are reported to be reluctant to join any groups that are implementing conscription laws.
There have been reports of people being kidnapped, arrested, or compelled into joining the military and used as human shields in 2023 and 2024. Rohingyas living in the IDP camps of Rakhine state are reportedly a target of the military junta for forced recruitment. There have been reports of people trying to leave the country, especially to Thailand, which has increased the risk of increased refugee influx in Thailand.
Conscription laws implemented by the military junta and some EAOs will likely geographically expand and intensify armed conflict in the country in 2024.
______________________________________________
UPDATE (05/01/2025)
Tens of thousands of working-age young people were forcibly recruited in 2024, both by the military junta and anti-military resistance forces. This conscription drive has led to several consequences. It caused a wave of emigration, which adversely affected various industries, particularly agriculture, due to a decrease in employment. Additionally, it prompted numerous domestic companies to leave the country. In Rakhine, conscription of the Rohingya fuelled intercommunal tensions between the Rohingya and the ethnic Rakhine residents. It also contributed to increased early marriages, especially in rural communities. The conscription law is depleting the youth population, which is a driving force of humanitarian action, and has further restricted humanitarian access in the country.

Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.
Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. Continued resistance activities by the KNLA, National Unity Government-affiliated People’s Defence Forces, and other local resistance groups operating in and around the Dawei SEZ could trigger further military sweeps, preventing safe returns and causing new and repeated displacement. Prolonged separation from homes, farms, and plantations will reduce food production and household income, increasing dependence on markets and host communities and worsening food, shelter, and health needs. triggerList.title: Increased frequency of direct clashes between JNIM and ISSP in western Niger
triggerList.description: Reports of repeated armed confrontations between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and Tahoua indicate a shift towards sustained inter-group rivalry and territorial contestation. An increase in the frequency, scale, or geographic spread of these clashes would signal a deterioration in the security environment and a higher likelihood of violence against civilians and displacement in affected areas.
triggerList.objective: Yes: At least 3–5 reported clashes per month between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and/or Tahoua, or evidence of sustained clashes over a period of 2–3 consecutive weeks.

triggerList.title: Increased targeting of civilians in contested areas
triggerList.description: Reports of killings, abductions, or threats against civilians in areas where JNIM and ISSP are competing for influence, particularly in Tillabéri and Tahoua. Increased violence against civilians may reflect retaliatory dynamics and efforts by both groups to assert territorial control, increasing protection risks and displacement.
triggerList.objective: Yes: civilian casualties per month linked to armed group activity in Tillabéri/Tahoua, or a clear increasing trend over 2–3 consecutive months.

triggerList.title: Expansion of inter-group violence into new areas
triggerList.description: Attacks or presence of JNIM or ISSP reported in areas previously less affected, including new localities in Tahoua or neighbouring regions. Geographic expansion would indicate a widening scope of inter-group rivalry and increasing insecurity beyond established hotspots.
triggerList.objective: Yes: Confirmed presence or attacks by JNIM and/or ISSP in at least 2–3 new administrative areas (departments or communes) beyond previously affected zones.

triggerList.title: Increase in displacement from western Niger
triggerList.description: Rising displacement flows from Tillabéri and Tahoua linked to insecurity and inter-group clashes. Increased displacement would indicate worsening protection conditions and reduced population resilience in affected areas.
triggerList.objective: Yes: An increase of newly displaced people within a short period (1–2 months) linked to insecurity in affected regions.

rationale:
In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military. 
The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access. 
Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone. ([Reuters 09/04/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/fighting-between-sahel-based-jihadist-rivals-spills-into-niger-2026-04-09/), [Crisis Group 20/02/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/rpt/africa/sahel-west-africa/321-le-jnim-et-le-dilemme-de-lexpansion-au-dela-du-sahel), [RFI 09/03/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260309-niger-des-groupes-terroristes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-pour-la-premi%C3%A8re-fois-l-importante-ville-de-tahoua))

triggerList.title: Security Vacuum and Porous Borders
triggerList.description: Capitalising on weak cross-border collaboration, the group/Lakurawa exploited challenging terrains to infiltrate remote areas in northwestern states and disseminate its ideology. Moreover, the already strained relations between Nigeria and Niger exacerbated by Niger’s July 2023 coup disrupted joint military operations, thereby enabling the Lakurawa group to broaden its influence further. The porous borders between northwest Nigeria and its neighbouring countries, along with limited border control, have significantly contributed to the prevailing insecurity in affected communities. This vulnerability is compounded by the lack of a strong security presence in many remote areas. Non-state armed groups like Lakurawa take advantage of these weaknesses; they do not recognise established borders or state authority but instead strive to carve out their own mini-states, where they govern, levy taxes, and impose their rules and ideology.

triggerList.title: Increased Militant Activity
triggerList.description: Escalation in the frequency and severity of attacks targeting local communities, security forces, or infrastructure.

triggerList.title: Local Community Grievances
triggerList.description: Lakurawa is exploiting local grievances by providing financial and material support to attract followers and gain local backing. They distribute money, farm tools, fertilizers, seeds, and water pumping machines to vulnerable communities. New recruits are offered up to 1 million naira ($645), while local informants receive about 10,000 naira ($6), further incentivizing cooperation. Villagers who refuse to support the group face threats and violent reprisals, with Lakurawa-related attacks already resulting in numerous deaths. This exploitation of local needs and coercion is contributing to the growing instability in the region.

rationale:
Lakurawa is a violent extremist group active in northern Nigeria, with suspected links to the Islamic State – Sahel Province. Originating from herders migrating from Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger in the 2010s, the group initially operated as a criminal gang before evolving into a self-proclaimed protector against banditry. Over time, it has imposed strict religious ideologies and sought territorial control.
In November 2024, Lakurawa launched a deadly attack in Kebbi state, Nigeria, killing at least 15 people. Since then, it has expanded operations into Niger, enforcing taxes, imposing their interpretation of Islamic law, and distributing resources to gain community support. Despite Nigerian military operations, the group remains largely free to operate in Niger, aggravating security gaps along the border.
Its growing alliances with armed groups in the Sahel provide it with external backing, increasing the likelihood of prolonged instability. Heightened tensions with regional bandits, particularly in Sokoto and Kebbi states, could escalate into cycles of retaliatory violence, deepening the crisis and destabilising the region.
Compounding these challenges, poor intelligence and a lack of coordination among security groups have led to conflicting assessments of Lakurawa. While police forces downplay the threat, the military categorises Lakurawa as an ‘emerging terrorist organisation’ – highlighting a critical coordination gap. Operating from inaccessible forests along the Nigerien border, the group is able to launch attacks on civilians with relative impunity, underscoring the persistent issue of ungoverned spaces in Nigeria.

triggerList.description: On 17 November 2025, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) adopted a resolution backing a US-proposed stabilisation plan for Gaza, including deployment of an “international stabilisation force” and transitional governance structures. triggerList.description: It is likely that Gaza will be indirectly impacted if a war between Israel and Iran starts, as either border crossing will be closed again or the Israeli airstrikes will intensify to prevent Hamas from backing up Iran.

rationale:
On 10 October 2025, Hamas and Israel agreed upon a new ceasefire following two previous ones. The first lasted between 24–30 November 2023 and the second from 19 January to 18 March 2024, and both proved to be fragile. Under the 2025 agreement, Israel and Hamas committed to a withdrawal and unimpeded humanitarian access; Israel began marking a ‘yellow line’ on 20 October 2025 as a withdrawal boundary.
This new ceasefire is also likely to collapse owing to several factors: repeated violations, Israeli control of at least 60% of the strip, continued restrictions on humanitarian access, a recent UNSC decision that ignores Palestinians’ right to self-govern, and escalations related to the US/Israel attacks on Iran.
According to the Gaza Government Media Office, between 10 October and 22 December 2025, Israel committed at least 875 separate violations of the ceasefire, killing 114 Palestinians and wounding 1,112 others. Repeated Israeli violations may eventually prompt a response from Hamas, contributing to a collapse of the ceasefire and a return to full-blown conflict.
Under the ceasefire, Israel was supposed to withdraw to the yellow line, but reports show that Israeli military positions remain established across Gaza, controlling roughly 58–60% of the territory, including key areas in Rafah, Khan Younis, and parts of Gaza city. Israeli forces have also repeatedly crossed beyond this yellow line, occupying more areas than the ceasefire intended for the long term. This de facto occupation undermines the possibility of a stable ceasefire, and Palestinians are likely to perceive it as annexation.
Israeli forces continue to control the flow of humanitarian aid, goods, fuel, building materials, and humanitarian shelters into Gaza. Despite the ceasefire, many aid convoys and shipments remain blocked, and key supplies, such as tents, medical equipment, generators, and construction materials, have been rejected or delayed. Humanitarian needs in Gaza continue to be very high, especially during winter (typically from November–March). For example, Storm Byron resulted in widespread flooding in Gaza on 11 December, affecting 55,000 families. Without unimpeded access to aid, basic survival needs cannot be met, increasing hardships among the population and raising the incentive for armed groups to resume fighting.
On 17 November 2025, the UNSC adopted a resolution backing a US-proposed stabilisation plan for Gaza, including the deployment of an “international stabilisation force” and transitional governance structures. Many Palestinians reject the resolution, arguing that it disregards their right to self-determination and places Gaza under de facto foreign control. They view it as undermining legitimate Palestinian governance, making the renewal of armed resistance more likely if the stabilisation force appears as foreign occupation rather than protection.
If a war erupts between Israel and Iran, it will likely prompt Israel to close all border crossings into Gaza and potentially intensify air strikes. This will highly contribute to a return to conflict in Gaza and a collapse of the ceasefire.
A renewed war will likely begin with intense Israeli aerial bombardment across all areas west of the yellow line, targeting what Israel identifies as Hamas positions but inevitably hitting densely populated neighbourhoods where civilians are sheltering in damaged buildings or makeshift tents. Ground incursions may follow, especially in the central and southern areas, where Israeli forces already maintain forward positions. Urban fighting would expand again into Deir Al Balah, Khan Younis, and the remaining parts of Gaza city. It is also likely that Palestinian militias backed by Israel will be deployed to launch attacks on Hamas and loot humanitarian convoys. Inside Gaza, armed groups, mainly Hamas, would resume rocket fire and improvised attacks from the remaining pockets where they operate. This would prompt further Israeli strikes and expand the combat zone. ([ISPI 30/10/2025](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/gazas-limbo-fragile-ceasefire-and-the-roadblocks-to-trump-plans-phase-two-221961), [The Guardian 19/10/2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/19/palestinians-in-gaza-fear-ceasefire-could-collapse-at-any-moment), [OHCHR 24/11/2025](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2025/11/un-experts-urge-states-act-israeli-violations-threaten-fragile-gaza), [NPR 09/11/2025](https://www.npr.org/2025/11/09/nx-s1-5603399/the-fragile-truce-in-gaza-edges-toward-its-next-phase), [IBA 29/10/2025](https://www.ibanet.org/Israel-Gaza-A-Fragile-Ceasefire-leaves-region-wary), [AJ 22/12/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/12/22/israel-kills-two-palestinians-in-gaza-city-as-ceasefire-violations-mount), [OCHA 18/12/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-349-gaza-strip))

triggerList.title: Increased Israeli restrictions and settlement expansion
triggerList.description: The sharp rise in demolitions, settlement approvals, and movement obstacles is likely to increase tensions and trigger more clashes, protests, and confrontations between Palestinians, Israeli forces, and settlers, particularly in highly restricted areas and around checkpoints.

triggerList.title: Implementation of the death penalty law
triggerList.description: Attempts to apply the new law against Palestinian prisoners are likely to trigger widespread protests, strikes, unrest, and retaliatory attacks, given the strong public reaction already observed across the West Bank following its approval.

triggerList.title: Escalatory political and armed rhetoric:
triggerList.description: Calls by armed groups, including Hamas’ Al Qassam Brigades, for intensified resistance and “lone wolf” attacks may encourage shootings, armed operations, and localised violence involving Palestinian armed groups, Israeli forces, and settlers, especially in Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, and East Jerusalem.

rationale:
In April 2026, pressure on Palestinians in the West Bank notably intensified, with the monthly average of people displaced by lack-of-permit demolitions reaching 160, the highest monthly average recorded since 2009. In the largest single approval on record, Israeli authorities authorised 34 new settlements, bringing the total number of approvals under the current Government to 103. This pressure is compounded by movement restrictions, which reached 925 obstacles, the highest level in 20 years. These increased Israeli restrictions may drive conflict escalations between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups affiliated with Hamas.

Other triggers for escalations include the death penalty and related escalatory political discourse. On 30 March 2026, the Israeli Knesset passed a law mandating death by hanging for Palestinians convicted in military courts of carrying out deadly attacks against Israelis; the law could affect more than 9,300 Palestinian prisoners, and it has already triggered widespread Palestinian protests and strikes across the West Bank.

Following Israel’s adoption of this law, a Qassam Brigades spokesperson warned that attempts to impose executions would ignite broader confrontation. The spokesperson also called for intensified resistance in the West Bank, including individual “lone wolf” attacks and armed operations against Israeli forces. By late May, no such attacks had been reported, but the implementation of the law will likely trigger escalations of confrontations with Israeli forces and settlers.

Increased Israeli restrictions, annexations, and attempts to implement the death penalty law over the next three to six months will likely drive further clashes, shootings, and individual attacks. Hamas-affiliated cells, Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighters, and emerging regional armed groups such as the Jenin Brigade and Lions’ Den – particularly in East Jerusalem and Jenin, Nablus, and Tulkarem cities – are all likely to be involved in these escalations, which may include intensified Israeli raids, arrests, settler attacks, and movement restrictions around refugee camps, checkpoints, and settlements. rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive. ([BIPP 06/03/2026](https://www.bakerinstitute.org/research/israeli-elections-cast-doubt-gaza-peace-plan), [NPR 23/07/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/23/nx-s1-5891506/israel-will-hold-elections-this-fall-gadi-eisenkott-could-be-the-next-prime-minister), [Chatham House 22/07/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/07/israels-general-election-will-be-no-other), [CNN 20/07/2026](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/07/20/middleeast/israel-far-right-settlements-gaza-intl), [The Conversation 24/07/2026](https://theconversation.com/as-israel-prepares-for-october-election-the-government-is-accelerating-its-land-grab-in-the-west-bank-and-gaza-288286), [DAWN 21/07/2026](https://dawnmena.org/israels-elections-will-not-end-its-genocidal-and-expansionist-policies/), [ACLED accessed 25/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [Haaretz 07/07/2026](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/israel-security/2026-07-07/ty-article/.premium/as-netanyahu-battles-for-votes-he-could-reignite-gaza-fighting/0000019f-390c-d62f-a39f-7d2c08a00000), [LWJ 19/10/2025](https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/10/profiles-of-anti-hamas-militias-in-the-gaza-strip.php), [AP accessed 01/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-gaza-yellow-line-barrier-ceasefire-941ed80f6d4398ce88916f6b08753dd8), [TOI 17/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-on-official-dispersal-of-parliament-wrapping-up-final-legislative-blitz/), [AJ 22/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/creeping-death-israel-weaponises-yellow-line-to-annex-gaza))

rationale:
The E1 settlement plan is a longstanding Israeli initiative that was revived in July 2025 after four years of suspension and approved for advancement by the Israeli Government on 20 August 2025. The plan aims to expand Ma’ale Adumim municipality and create a continuous built-up area between the Israeli settlements and Jerusalem city. Its implementation could further fragment the West Bank, particularly by disrupting geographic contiguity between central and southern areas, and increase the likelihood of severing East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank. Its advancement could accelerate the displacement of entire Bedouin communities in the area, generating additional humanitarian needs.
Implementation has accelerated in 2026. In August, Israel issued a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, followed on 17 September by a further 2,167 units, bringing the total to 3,401. Bidding on the 2,167-unit tender was scheduled to open on 25 October, two days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections.
Government efforts to advance the tenders before the election could accelerate implementation of the approved plan and trigger a faster-paced displacement. The awarding of tenders would allow the Israeli Government to move faster towards infrastructure works and construction, making the project more difficult for a future government to reverse. Implementation could accelerate if the tender process proceeds despite the postponement and the current Government retains power after the election. Court challenges or an election outcome that produces a government less supportive of E1 could, however, delay further implementation.([OCHA 21/08/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-316-west-bank), [OCHA 16/07/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-305-west-bank), [MAP 19/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/map-warns-palestinian-healthcare-workers-face-mounting-attacks-amid-escalating-west-bank-violence), [BBC 20/08/2026](https://www.bbc.com/arabic/articles/cvgx03d488yo), [OCHA 28/09/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026), [OCHA 25/05/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-may-2026), [Reuters 17/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-adds-tender-2167-housing-units-settlement-expansion-plan-rights-groups-2026-09-17/), [HRW 19/08/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/08/19/west-bank-illegal-e1-settlement-tender-opens-for-bids), [Al Arabiya 24/08/2026](https://www.alarabiya.net/arab-and-world/2026/08/24/%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A4%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A-%D9%8A%D8%AD%D8%B0%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%85-%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%81%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%B1), [WAFA 17/09/2026](https://english.wafa.ps/Pages/Details/174831), [Peace Now 19/08/2026](https://peacenow.org.il/en/e1-tender-published-and-open-for-bidding), [Times of Israel 27/09/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ag-postpones-tenders-for-e1-settlement-project-smotrich-accuses-her-of-election-meddling/), [The New Arab 27/09/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/israel-attorney-general-delays-e1-settlement-tender))

title: Continued protests across Panama, following the government's approval to exploit a mining area in a biodiverse jungle, result in access constraints and disruption of services and economic activities for some population groups
rationale:
---------BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE-------
The Panamanian government signed a concession contract (arrangement between a public authority and an economic operator) with the Canadian mining company First Quantum Minerals, which allowed the latter to continue operating an open-pit copper mine in a richly biodiverse jungle. Panama’s National Assembly, the country’s legislative body, and the country’s president fast-tracked the contract and approved it on 20 October 2023. 

Since the contract was approved, Panama has been facing protests across the country. Protestors claim the contract was fast-tracked with little public input and lacks transparency, making allegations of corruption of the lawmakers. The protests are being led by construction workers, educators, indigenous groups, and activists, mainly calling for the revocation of the mining contract. Tens of thousands of people have been reported to be participating in the protests across the country. According to the protesters, there are significant environmental risks of the contract, including for the vital water sources required for water consumption.

As at 10 November 2023, the protests have generally been peaceful; ACLED data shows that around 80% of the protests occurring since 20 October 2023 have been peaceful and 20% violent demonstrations which include incidents of clashes between protestors and security forces, use of tear gas to disperse protestors, arrests, vandalism, and robbery. Significant increase in the deployment of security forces has been observed since the protests began. As at 14 November 2023, two fatalities have been reported: an elderly man was apparently frustrated with the blockage and tried to force the protestors to remove a barrier blocking the Pan American highway and then he allegedly opened fire on the protestors, killing two of them.

On 3 November 2023, the National Assembly signed an indefinite moratorium on new mining concessions into law, which also prohibits renewing existing concessions. However, the new law still allows Minera Panama, the Panamanian subsidiary of First Quantum Minerals, to operate. Hence, the protests are still ongoing. The country’s Supreme Court stated that it will consider two lawsuits filed against the renewed contract with First Quantum.

The protests led to countrywide road blockades that have negatively impacted the economy, transportation, food security, education, healthcare, and WASH, and raised protection concerns.
Due to the insecurity caused by the protests, educational authorities closed all schools across the country. 

There have been reports of attack on healthcare, including assault on healthcare personnel, ambulances, and vehicles transporting patients by people among the protestors. On 27 October 2023, the Panamanian National Operations Center requested interinstitutional support to the Red Cross Society of Panama to provide assistance, especially through healthcare services, to the population affected by the protests and blockades. The IFRC has initiated an operation targeting 3,500 people. In several provinces, supplies required for water purification are running low, leading to the risk of clean water rationing. 

Several areas in the provinces of Bocas del Toro, Chiriqui, Darien, Herrera, and Los Santos have reported fuel shortages and rationing of food supplies by supermarkets and stores. An electricity generation company, whose production depends on fossil fuels, has issued warnings of potential controlled power outages to manage the electricity supply.

Rice is the staple food in Panama. Darien, Herrera, Los Santos, and Chiriqui provinces comprise the primary rice producers. Rice mills are unable to distribute their stored rice during the harvest period due to road closures, resulting in considerable losses. Significant loss in perishable goods, including fruits and vegetables, have also been reported due to the inability to sell and transport perishable products to markets and storage facilities.

In early October of 2023, Panama and Costa Rica announced a plan to provide a bus service to quickly move thousands of migrants crossing the Darien Gap through Panama to the Costa Rican border. On 24 October, it was reported that more than 30 buses from Darien to Costa Rica were stranded in the Chiriqui as they could not move forward towards Costa Rica. On 25 October, another 20 buses were not permitted to pass in San Felix, Chiriqui province; as a result, the migrants on the buses started their journey by foot from San Felix to Paso Canoas, Costa Rica.

-----AGGRAVATING FACTORS--------
Copper is the major export good for Panama. Analysts estimate that revoking the mining contract would cut Panama’s GDP growth from a forecast 6% in 2023 to just 1%. So, repealing the mining contract will have significant negative impact on the economy; however, not repealing it would also likely cause significant negative environmental (and consequently economic) impacts. This situation is aggravated by the current drought, exacerbated by a severe El Nino weather system, which has reduced water levels in the Panama Canal, prompting the Panama Canal Authority to implement additional vessel reductions in an effort to conserve water.

--------EXPECTED IMPACT--------
Continued protests will worsen the abovementioned situation, which could lead to a political and socioeconomic crisis in Panama, and possibly to humanitarian consequences for some more exposed population groups, These consequences could include lack of healthcare support, education, and clean water in some areas of the countries. There would also be raising food insecurity concerns, loss of livelihoods, especially among rice and vegetable farmers, and heightening of protection concerns for those participating in protests that become violent. 

--------UPDATE--------
The risk has only partially materialised. The expected impact was not realised. So far, it has not generated humanitarian needs other than those already mentioned in the background and rationale section. 

Panama's Supreme Court of Justice ruled that Panama’s new mining contract with the Canadian company First Quantum was unconstitutional. Following the ruling, the president of the country said that a process to close the Cobre Panama mine was set to begin. Protests have also began to subside after the ruling.

The protests have already had significant impact on the economy. Retail associations estimated a loss of around US$200 million in the first 30 days of protests. Logistics losses are estimated to be around US$4.6 billion. 

Panama’s economy is heavily based on the ability to facilitate the transit of global merchandise, which has been negatively affected by the protests. The logistics sector has been estimated to account for around 20% of the country’s GDP and employs around 10% of the Panamanian workforce.

The protests also have reportedly reduced Panama’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination. Large losses in the tourism and hospitality sectors have been reported, with many international tourists cancelling their trips to the country through January 2024. 

Shortages in food, fuel, and medicines have been reported in some cities and the government is importing such supplies from neighbouring Costa Rica to fill the gaps.

The company said that it has initiated international arbitration against Panama. Estimates suggest that Panama might have to pay at least US$20-50 billion (25-65% of the country’s GDP) if it loses the case. 

Livelihoods of the mine's employees and the people whose jobs are indirectly related to the mine are considered to be affected. The mine is reported to employ around 6,600 people (more than 5,500 are Panamanians). In total 40,000 jobs, directly and indirectly, are reportedly linked with the mine. 

It is to be noted that, if Panama loses the international arbitration case, which would be compounded by the negative impacts of the closure of the mine, there will likely be significant socio-economic distress in the country.

Papua New Guinea has been facing a persistent fragile social and economic state, especially high youth unemployment, reduced purchasing power, and limited water, sanitation, and electricity services. People living in the urban areas are constantly alert to the possibility of theft and assault. The situation is such that when an opportune moment arises, such as a strike called by security forces, a part of the population facing the socioeconomic issues tend to take advantage through rioting and looting. 

UPDATE (05/01/2025)
The fragile social and economic situation in Papua New Guinea has continued throughout 2024. However, no issues, such as government policies, triggered significant violent incidents, such as riots in urban areas.

triggerList.title: Past events of violent riots in the country
triggerList.description: Papua New Guinea's recent history, especially the past two years, has seen many violent riots. Such history indicates the tendency of violent riots occurring. A lot of incidents of social tensions such as disputes and security incidents such as death of civilians in the hands of security forces have been met with riots, involving looting in since 2021.
triggerList.objective: 100% as it is based on past incidents.

triggerList.title: Possible unpopular government policy or sustained ineffective government policy
triggerList.description:
Papua New Guinea is marked by high political instability, socioeconomic vulnerability, and administrative and governance inefficiencies. The government already is facing a challenge in terms of recovery from the January 2024 riots. The government thus far has only offered loans to rebuild businesses impacted by the riots, but the latter community wants grants as it would be impractical for them to replay the loans of such amount. This kind of sustained ineffective policy or any new unpopular policy could bring about dissatisfaction expressed in terms of riots and looting.

UPDATE (05/01/2025)
No government policies triggered significant violent incidents, such as riots, in urban areas.
triggerList.objective: 30% due to businesses being unsatisfied with government recovery policy for them.

rationale:
Papua New Guinea is marked by high youth unemployment and poverty, reduced purchasing power, lack of provision of basic services for its people, and poor governance. Only a quarter of the population who are engaged in work have formal, stable jobs. Many people reportedly flee from the violence-affected Highlands region to seek refuge and opportunities in urban centres, especially the capital of Papua New Guinea, Port Moresby. 
 
Nearly 60% of women and girls aged 15—49 have experienced some form of physical sexual violence, which is almost twice the global average. The overall state of the healthcare system is very poor, with lack of trained personnel, inadequate wages, a deteriorating infrastructure, and frequent lack of critical drugs and dressings.
 
Such underlying factors are considered to trigger social disruptions. In January 2024, the police went on strike over underpay, which was later revealed to be a technical glitch in the public servants’ payroll system. The initially peaceful protests turned into riots, comprising mass opportunistic looting, arson, and violence, mainly in Port Moresby. At least 15 people were killed in the riots, with some reports indicating a much higher number. Widespread sexual violence was also reported. 
 
Protests, riots, and incidents of violence against civilians in the non-Highlands areas rose significantly in 2023. The fragile social and economic situation may trigger more violence incidents, particularly riots, in non-Highlands urban centres in 2024. Lack of security forces’ capacity to deal violence also serves as an aggravating factor for riots.

UPDATE (05/01/2025)
The risk did not materialise. The fragile social and economic situation in Papua New Guinea has continued throughout 2024. However, no issues, such as government policies, triggered significant violent incidents, such as riots in urban areas. 

Riots stemming from tribal tensions and disputes have been common in the country and has continued in 2024. Riots and protests and fatalities related to such incidents in the entire country has fallen in 2024 compared to 2023.

rationale:
Electoral violence across the Philippines is a threat for the current three-month long election season that started on 8 February. Voters will choose the next president, vice president, and 18,000 other political positions on 9 May (The Diplomat 07/02/2022). Electoral violence by privately hired armed groups include voter intimidation, attacks on polls, and assassination of political rivals (Benar News 02/02/2022 ; New Mandala 08/07/2021 ; PNA 09/02/2022 ; University of Portsmouth 30/09/2021 and  08/10/2021 ; Rappler 14/02/2022; Inquirer 01/12/2021).    

The leading candidate is Ferdinand Marcos Jr., son of Ferdinand Marcos, who held the presidency from 1965 until he was ousted in a people’s revolution in 1986 (Aljazeera 14/12/2022 ; VOA 06/01/2022). In southern Mindanao, Marcos’ policies contributed to land grabs, human rights abuses, and conflict (Inquirer 28/12/2016; Asia Society 08/03/2022). The controversial Marcos Jr.’s candidacy will likely contribute to increased political tensions and violence in Mindanao.   

Mindanao is still affected by ongoing armed group attacks and their clashes with the military. Armed groups, including the New People’s Army (NPA), Maute, Abu Sayyaf, and Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters all refuse peace talks and negotiations with the government, and seek independence from the Philippines (Global Initiative 20/02/2020).  These armed groups may conduct more attacks than usual, taking advantage of the political tensions and authorities’ focus on the elections. Security forces are already being deployed to areas of security concerns across the country, most of which are in Mindanao (Business Mirror 14/02/2022).   

Intercommunal violence in the form of clan feuds including over land disputes also affects Mindanao and causes displacement. Conflict and violence in Mindanao are exacerbated by a shadow economy that provides economic and political means for the groups involved (Global Initiative 20/02/2020; International Alert 04/2014). Mindanao is therefore at a high risk of increased violence and armed groups attacks, including electoral violence by ‘private’ armed groups hired to attack polls and political candidates by rivaling politicians (Benar News 30/06/2021; PhilStar 15/02/2022; Philippine Army 13/01/2022). Polls situated in areas with armed groups presence, particularly the NPA, are most at risk (New Mandala 08/07/2021; Manila Bulletin 13/02/2022).

Barangay (which is a native Filipino term for a village) is the smallest administrative division in the Philippines. Sangguniang Kabataan is a regional council that represents youth in a barangay. Village and youth council elections are scheduled to be held on 30 October 2023 across the country. 

The village and youth council elections will significantly heighten electoral violence in Mindanao islands, especially in the BARMM region. For the BARMM, these elections are going to be the precursor for the first parliamentary elections to be held in 2025. Nearly 1,000 villages, out of the nearly 2,600 villages, in the region have been classified as potential violence hotspots by law enforcement agencies due to intense political rivalry among local election aspirants, clan politics and feuds, and the presence of non-state armed groups. 
 
Overall, electoral violence in the Philippines is a recurrent concern. 

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) have also been reported to be closely monitoring 300 villages in the Zamboanga Peninsula, the Caraga Region, the BARMM, the Bicol, Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), and Central Luzon regions due to presence of non-state armed actors.

Update:
The risk has not materialised. No significant humanitarian needs were reported. 

There were pockets of electoral violence during the electoral period of the village and youth elections in the Mindanao islands.  The Commission on Elections reported that 19 people killed and 14 others injured in election violence, mostly in the BARMM. 

Candidates for and winners of the village council elections were targeted during the electoral violence. Very few people have been displaced during the electoral period and post-election violence.  

In one incident, close to a hundred villagers were displaced by gunfight between rival two groups in Maguindanao del Norte. The displaced informed that the hostilities between the groups were related to the village and youth elections, where both groups had favoured candidates.

triggerList.title: Monsoon Intensification and Tropical Cyclone Surge
triggerList.description: During La Niña years, the southwest and northeast monsoons tend to be stronger and more persistent, which enhances rainfall intensity. Research shows La Niña is associated with increased extreme rainfall events in Southeast Asia via monsoon–ENSO interactions. Moreover, tropical cyclone activity in the western North Pacific- Philippine area also tends to increase in La Niña conditions—both in number and landfall likelihood. The combination of incessant monsoon rains, saturated soils, and successive storms or surge-events creates a compound scenario of flooding, landslides and coastal inundation.

rationale: La Niña arrived in the Philippines in October 2025 and is likely to persist until February–March 2026. La Niña events have typically been linked to a higher frequency of tropical cyclones late in the year, along with increased rainfall and flood risk across much of the country. Current seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average precipitation and above-average temperatures between November 2025 and March 2026. This indicates that between late 2025 and early 2026, the country could face compounding hazards, including storms and intense northeast monsoon rains, which may cause widespread flooding and landslides, especially across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Coastal and riverine communities in the Bicol region, Eastern Visayas, and Mindanao are particularly exposed, while informal urban settlements in Metro Manila and Cebu face a high risk of waterlogging and infrastructure collapse. Dam overflows and disrupted transport routes could isolate villages, delay aid delivery, and damage essential facilities, such as schools, health centres, and evacuation sites. The humanitarian consequences are expected to be severe: displacement, loss of livelihoods, and growing food insecurity among farming and fishing families. Waterborne and vector-borne diseases (such as leptospirosis, cholera, and dengue) may also surge because of stagnant floodwaters and poor sanitation. These risks will strain an already overburdened health system recovering from successive disasters. La Niña could push thousands of households into renewed crisis throughout the first half of 2026, amplifying humanitarian needs nationwide. ([PAGASA 26/08/2025](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/press-release/185), [NOAA 01/12/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/lanina/enso_evolution-status-fcsts-web.pdf), [PNA 26/08/2025](https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1257335))

triggerList.title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
triggerList.description: El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation.  Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.

rationale:
The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.
Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.
The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.
In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities. ([PAGASA accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring), [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/), [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en), [WB accessed 17/06/2026](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/philippines/enso), [GMA 26/04/2026](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/weather/content/985366/drought-philippines-2026/story/))

rationale:
In Somalia, the failure to hold general elections by February 2021 created disagreements and high levels of tension between the Government and the opposition, which culminated in conflict in Mogadishu in April 2021. Parliamentary elections were set for October–November 2021, but most states did not conclude elections within that period. Resentment among the opposition rose as the President continued to stay in office long past his mandated term.

In September 2021, a rift between the President and Prime Minister raised political tensions, polarised the country, and nearly resulted in conflict. While this rift ended in a truce in October 2021, another political stalemate began in December 2021, with both the President and Prime Minister blaming each other for stalled elections. The international community made significant mediation efforts to de-escalate tensions. Any political stalemate in Mogadishu risks affecting the functioning of security institutions. Coupled with a lack of cohesion within the army, this could result in increased insecurity across the country, with armed groups potentially intensifying fighting and gaining more territorial control.
Al-Shabaab has already increased its attacks countrywide as part of an attempt to derail the electoral process. These attacks may continue to escalate as elections are repeatedly delayed, and factions of the army could clash again in Mogadishu.

triggerList.title: Escalating disputes between Federal Government and Federal Member States
triggerList.description: Disagreements between Mogadishu and states such as Puntland and Jubbaland could escalate as electoral preparations advance, particularly if federal authorities attempt to impose electoral frameworks without consensus. Past disputes have already resulted in violent clashes in Jubbaland.

triggerList.title: Al-Shabaab exploiting political instability
triggerList.description: Al-Shabaab’s resurgence is being fuelled by political fragmentation, providing opportunity to disrupt voter registration sites and polling, intensifying insecurity.

rationale:
Somalia is transitioning from a clan-based indirect electoral system to universal suffrage for the 2026 elections, marking the first attempt in over 50 years to hold nationwide one-person-one-vote polls. In August 2025, the Federal Government and opposition leaders signed an agreement establishing the framework for parliament members to be directly elected. The agreement has also deepened rifts within the main opposition coalition, the Forum for National Salvation, with former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed insisting that the prevailing insecurity makes the implementation of such extensive electoral reforms unfeasible.
While representing democratic progress, this shift is occurring in a fragile political environment marked by unresolved disputes between the Federal Government and federal member states (FMSes). Puntland has rejected the constitutional reforms underpinning universal suffrage, warning of potential violence. Jubaland state has also experienced armed clashes over disputed electoral processes in recent years.
As voter registration rolls out and constituency boundaries are drawn, clan grievances and FMS–Federal Government tensions are likely to intensify. This political disunity, characterised by persistent rivalries and potential boycotts from opposition and states such as Puntland and Jubaland, will impede unified counterterrorism efforts, consequently increasing overall insecurity and humanitarian needs. Regions and dominant clans feeling marginalised may resist the reforms politically or militarily, sparking localised violence as they seek to assert control. If the elections are ultimately delayed, boycotted, or politically contested, the resulting legitimacy crisis could also escalate into violent clashes or a governance breakdown. Specifically, the collapse of the federal electoral process risks reigniting widespread clan conflicts and political violence.
Simultaneously, Al Shabaab is poised to exploit this instability. Leveraging an intensification of offensives and territorial gains expected in 2025, the group will target voter registration sites, polling centres, and civilians. This will not only undermine electoral credibility but also worsen the security environment ahead of elections and disrupt critical humanitarian access. These conflict dynamics will be severely multiplied by climate shocks and persistent food insecurity, further straining community resources and worsening the complex security and humanitarian landscape. ([Africanews 26/08/2025](https://www.africanews.com/2025/08/26/somalias-president-and-opposition-leaders-reach-historic-election-agreement/), [Reuters 08/08/2024](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/somalias-cabinet-approves-bill-universal-suffrage-2024-08-08/?), [The Guardian 05/04/2024](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2024/apr/05/fears-violence-somalia-constitution?), [RVI accessed 07/10/2025](https://riftvalley.net/publication/prospects-for-somalias-transition-from-clan-based-politics-to-multipartyism-in-the-2026-election/))

triggerList.title: La Niña and Negative Indian Ocean Dipole Likely to Suppress Deyr Rains
triggerList.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high likelihood of La Niña conditions developing through December 2025, coupled with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole persisting until November. This combination is expected to suppress rainfall across Somalia, particularly in southern and central regions. The reduced moisture inflow and weaker monsoon activity are likely to delay the onset and shorten the duration of the Deyr season, worsening soil moisture deficits and compounding drought conditions in already water-stressed areas.

triggerList.title: Delayed onset and reduced seasonal performance
triggerList.description: Seasonal forecasts point to a delayed start and poor performance of the 2025 Deyr rains, constraining crop cultivation and pasture regeneration. The shortened growing window is likely to reduce cereal production and limit fodder availability, leading to livestock body condition decline and rising food prices. Reduced river flows in the Shabelle and Juba basins are also expected to curtail irrigation access, undermining food and income sources for riverine farmers and heightening food insecurity during the 2026 lean season.

rationale:
A below-average Deyr season (October–December), the third consecutive poor rainy season in northern and central areas, is forecast, at the same time that the probability of La Niña conditions is projected to reach around 60%. This climatic development is expected to reduce rainfall across much of Somalia, prolonging dry conditions and intensifying the effects of several consecutive below-average rainfall seasons. River levels in the Shabelle and Juba River Basins are likely to drop further, increasing water scarcity in riverine and agropastoral zones. Reduced rainfall coupled with rising temperatures will accelerate crop and livestock losses, placing rural livelihoods under severe strain.
In key food-producing regions, such as Bakool, Bay, and Lower Shabelle, maize and groundnut yields have already declined by up to 40% during previous drought years. Many of these areas have shifted from being net exporters to net consumers of basic staples. Declining soil fertility and shrinking pasture resources are expected to raise livestock mortality rates significantly, particularly in Galgaduud, Gedo, and Togdheer. This will erode household incomes and undermine a critical source of national exports.
The deterioration of water infrastructure is a pressing concern. Extended dry periods have reduced groundwater recharge and increased salinity, especially in coastal and riverine areas, making many sources unsafe for consumption and raising health risks. Access to safe water and functional health services continues to diminish, with approximately 40 primary healthcare facilities and 16 mobile health teams closing across 21 districts. Water contamination and displacement have contributed to favourable conditions for disease outbreaks, with more than 6,550 cases of cholera and acute watery diarrhoea reported between January–July.
The compounded impacts of failed rains, collapsing rural livelihoods, and disruptions to basic services are expected to heighten food insecurity and trigger further displacement, particularly in Bakool, Bay, Galgaduud, Gedo, and parts of Mudug and Lower Shabelle. Resource scarcity will likely fuel localised tensions and competition over water and grazing areas, especially between pastoralist and farming communities as well as among ethnic clans. Armed group activity is also expected to intensify, with Al Shabaab likely exploiting the drought to strengthen territorial control. Tactics may include imposing informal taxes on herders and traders, restricting access to water points and interfering with humanitarian aid delivery to consolidate influence. ([OCHA 21/09/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-monthly-humanitarian-update-august-2025), [OCHA 05/08/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-drought-conditions-central-and-northern-regions-flash-update-no1-5-august-2025) [ICPAC 26/08/2025] (https://www.icpac.net/news/below-normal-rains-and-warmer-than-usual-conditions-are-expected-over-most-parts-of-the-greater-horn-of-africa/))

rationale:
Rising tensions between Southwest state authorities and the Federal Government of Somalia continue to significantly increase the probability of armed confrontation and large‑scale displacement in the coming weeks and months. The formal severing of ties with Mogadishu, federal declarations that the Southwest leadership’s mandate has expired, and mutual accusations over the diversion of weapons and security interference point to a deepening political rift. Around Baidoa, deployment orders for regional forces and reported movements of federal troops indicate an elevated risk of localised clashes escalating into a wider confrontation, particularly if no negotiated settlement is reached before key political milestones. Upcoming electoral processes in Southwest state and nationwide are likely to further heighten tensions, as competition over power and representation may trigger protests, the contestation of results, or targeted violence around Baidoa and other strategic locations.
At the same time, Southwest state faces severe and compounding humanitarian pressures that would heighten the impact of any political or security escalation. Prolonged drought has already driven mass internal displacement from districts such as Waajid and other parts of Bay and Bakool, eroding pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods and sharply increasing food insecurity. Many displaced families have moved towards Baidoa and other already-overstretched host areas, where services, water availability, and livelihood opportunities are extremely limited. Further conflict‑related displacement from urban centres or along key road corridors would add to existing caseloads, strain coping capacity, and heighten protection risks, including family separation, exploitation, and gender‑based violence. In a context of recurrent access constraints and insecurity, even a temporary disruption of humanitarian operations around Baidoa or in drought‑affected rural areas could quickly translate into sharp deteriorations in food security, health, and protection conditions for hundreds of thousands of people. Overall, the combination of unresolved federal–state tensions, upcoming electoral contests, and severe climatic stress maintains a high probability that political and armed escalation in Southwest state could trigger large‑scale displacement and a rapid deterioration of humanitarian conditions, even though a full‑scale armed confrontation has not yet occurred.

triggerList.title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
triggerList.description: Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis.

triggerList.title: Entanglement with the war in Sudan
triggerList.description: South Sudan's conflict risks becoming entangled with the war in Sudan. Though Juba has maintained official neutrality, its close links to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which control much of Sudan's border with South Sudan, are widely observed. The Sudanese army is suspected of reactivating ties with Nuer opposition forces in a bid to pressure Kiir and disrupt RSF supply lines — a dynamic that, if confirmed, would effectively transform Upper Nile into a proxy theatre of Sudan's war. Compounding this, Uganda's continued military backing of Kiir is not guaranteed; Kampala's willingness to underwrite his survival is uncertain given South Sudan's economic collapse and Uganda's competing regional commitments. A withdrawal of Ugandan support, combined with increasing Sudanese entanglement, could significantly alter the military balance, accelerating conflict escalation and further collapsing humanitarian access

rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. ([ICG 25/03/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war), [ISS 30/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/race-against-time-to-stabilise-south-sudan-as-elections-loom), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-january-2026), [OCHA 16/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-update-1-17-april-2026), [MSF 30/01/2026](https://www.msf.org/south-sudan-government-blocks-opposition-held-areas-humanitarian-access))
