rationale: After the ousting of President Omar Al Bashir in April 2019, a transitional military government – specifically, the Transitional Military Council (TMC) – was installed. Many TMC members, including the new Vice President, were aligned with the Bashir regime and guilty of committing human rights violations during the conflict in Darfur in the early 2000s, aggravating anger and frustration among the civilians protesting since December 2018. Dialogue between the TMC and the opposition alliance called Forces of Freedom and Change to ensure a transition to a civilian government has not progressed, and protests have met with increasingly violent dispersals. For example, on 3 June 2019, the Rapid Support Forces violently dispersed peaceful sit-ins, killing around 118 people and injuring at least 780. A military government will likely establish itself for the long term, with the backing of international and regional alliances, including China, Egypt, Russia, and Saudi Arabia. That said, the TMC appears fragile because of internal differences in opinion. This increases the likelihood of fragmentation within the security apparatus, with different factions vying for power, further destabilising the country. Following the recent escalation in Khartoum, increased violence and intercommunal fighting between civilians, armed groups, and security forces have been observed countrywide. A military government is unlikely to pursue peace talks with armed groups in either Darfur, South Kordofan, or Blue Nile states based on historical disagreements. With reduced government influence, armed groups in these regions are likely to take advantage of the volatile security situation and reassert their position through increased use of violence.

rationale:
Political instability in the country – a result of tensions between the military and civilian components of the transitional Government – hinders Sudan’s economic growth and increases inflation rates. Loss of livelihood opportunities, increasing poverty rates, and higher food insecurity levels are likely.

Timeline of related events:
By 25 February 2021, Sudan's central bank had sharply devalued its currency, the Sudanese pound, in an attempt to get debt relief, crack down on the black market, and attract money back to the country. The bank unified the price of the currency with the black market at SDG 370 per USD 1.

Sudan's annual inflation rate, one of the world’s highest, is more than 300%, and protests have broken out over the struggling economy. Unifying the Sudanese currency will stabilise the exchange rate and encourage grants, loans, and emergency subsidies. At the same time, it could increase poverty and inflation.

Inflation in Sudan is currently at 300%, and prices for food were very high in January and February, which has led to nationwide protests. Seven states have declared a state of emergency because of these protests. Curfews have been imposed, and schools have been forced to close. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network has said that food insecurity could reach Crisis (IPC Phase 3) levels in parts of Kordofan and Darfur in the coming months.

On 10 June, hundreds of Sudanese protested the Government’s decision to lift all subsidies on petrol and diesel fuel, which will cause prices to double. By April 2022, the number of food insecure people was expected to double and reach 18 million people. Crop and livestock production has been reduced by up to 50% in 14 states across Sudan compared to the last five-year average. Wheat prices have increased by 180% compared to the same period last year.

Political instability has been growing since mid-September, with protests blocking goods from entering Port Sudan and mass demonstrations in Khartoum following a military takeover of the country. On 2 Jan 2022, Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok of the civilian party resigned, leading to more instability and an increased likelihood of an economic crisis.
Food security levels have deteriorated in Sudan, and needs across all sectors have increased.

triggerList.title: Intercommunal clashes, increase in violent incidents, more fatalities

rationale: Peaceful sit-ins have sprung up in towns across Darfur and in other parts of Sudan, which are also protesting the presence of armed militias. On 13 July, Sudan declared a state of emergency in the region of Darfur after violence and unrest in two towns. The Sudanese police broke up a sit-in in the town of Kutum, North Darfur state, on 12 July, after firing live ammunition and tear gas to disperse the protesters, who objected to a government delegation, who was visiting a similar sit-in. The protesters in Fata Borno in Kutum locality demanded disarmament of the militiamen and a ban on motorcycles in the area, expulsion of the new settlers from the displaced peoples’ farms and villages, the restructuring of the police departments in Kutum, and rehabilitation of the civil service institutions and administrative units in the locality. Sudanese activists say armed groups have attacked a protest camp in the Darfur region, killing more than a dozen people. Monday’s attack came a day after security forces violently broke up another sit-in in Kutum. The African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur said it had sent a team to Kutum in North Darfur state following the reported burning of a police station and cars by unidentified protesters. Darfur is one of the poorest regions in Sudan, with around 50,000–150,000 people in need of humanitarian assistance and more than 1.6 million IDPs in the region. A peace agreement with armed groups in Darfur was postponed after attacks in North Darfur at an IDP settlement that left nine people dead and 16 wounded. Clashes between security forces and groups protesting the violence had earlier led to a declaration of a state of emergency in the region. If violence escalates further, it is expected that the number of IDPs and people in need will increase, which risks jeopardising Sudan's democratic transition.

rationale:

13.4 million people in Sudan (29% of the total population) are already in need. More than 9.7 million people face high levels of food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or worse). The number of people affected by social unrest and a lack of basic commodities is likely to be high. 

Sudanese authorities reported a coup attempt on 21 September 2021 by a group of soldiers tied to the previous regime from the armoured corps – including high-ranking officers – but said the attempt failed and that the soldiers responsible for the coup were arrested. The armed group tried to take over several government institutions, including the radio and television building. Following the coup attempt, tension between military and civilian components of the transitional government increased. On 26 September, the joint forces guarding the office building of the Empowerment Elimination Committee received orders to abandon their posts. The building was left without security forces, but police returned to guard the site again in the evening. On 13 October, the security service restricted travel for 11 civilians tied to the government, increasing tension between military and civilian components of Sudan’s transitional government. By 16 October, thousands of pro-military protesters had gathered in Khartoum city and accused the political party of the government of mismanagement, while pro-civilian political counter-protests were scheduled to take place on 21 October.

triggerList.title: Expanded RSF-SPLM-N operational coordination

rationale:
The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state. 
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.
External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. If sustained, such external support would significantly raise the possibility of a scaled-up offensive by insulating RSF operations from battlefield setbacks ([ACLED 26/01/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/blue-nile-peripheral-front-central-battleground-sudan-conflict ), [MEE 26/01/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-rsf-launches-offensive-blue-nile-state), [AJ 19/08/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longform/2025/8/19/inside-the-nuba-mountains-and-the-alliance-reshaping-sudans-civil-war ), [ACLED 15/04/2025](https://acleddata.com/report/two-years-war-sudan-how-saf-gaining-upper-hand), [ICG 07/04/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/sudan/two-years-sudans-war-spreading), [Reuters 10/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/ethiopia-builds-secret-camp-train-sudan-rsf-fighters-sources-say-2026-02-10/ ), [ST 25/01/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/309824))

rationale:
Since October 2025, RSF has mobilised troops near Al Obeid's borders, including deploying combat vehicles along the western side. The sustained mobilisation and positioning of these forces indicate preparation for a renewed offensive to reinstate a siege of the city. A previous siege of the city between May 2023 and February 2025 demonstrated RSF's operational ability to isolate Al Obeid for prolonged periods, resulting in a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions, including severe food insecurity.
RSF has a strong strategic incentive to restore the siege because of Al Obeid's role as a key logistic and commercial hub linking western and southern Sudan to Khartoum and central Sudan. Control of the city would provide RSF with greater leverage over supply routes, trade flows, and access to corridors into SAF-controlled areas, particularly central Sudan. Al Obeid's role as a major crop and livestock market and a gate for Kordofan exports further increases its strategic and economic importance to RSF.
Despite recent SAF advancements and repositioning in North Kordofan, fluid conflict dynamics and continued shifts in areas of control between SAF and RSF increase the likelihood of renewed attempts to siege the city over the next six months. This likelihood is further reinforced by increasing logistical and technical support provided to RSF by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which may improve the group's operational capacity to sustain offensive and siege tactics. ([UN 19/12/2025](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/12/1166633), [Darfur24 13/11/2025](https://www.darfur24.com/en/2025/11/13/military-document-reveals-rsf-preparations-for-major-attack-on-el-obeid/), [YSPH HRL 16/01/2026](https://files-profile.medicine.yale.edu/documents/8dce0cc5-35fb-4078-b2aa-748e51cc8e9d), [BBC 06/01/2026](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74w54783zeo), [Sudan War Monitor 24/02/2025](https://sudanwarmonitor.com/p/sudan-army-breaks-rsf-siege-of-el), [OHCHR 19/09/2025](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/country-reports/human-rights-situation-sudan-1-january-30-june-2025), [MEE 24/02/2025](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-army-breaks-rsf-siege-strategic-city-el-obeid), [The National 09/12/2025](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2025/12/09/al-obeid-gripped-by-fear-as-sudans-army-and-rsf-square-off-for-fierce-battle/), [AJ 14/11/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2025/11/14/will-sudans-rsf-turn-strategic-city-of-el-obeid-into-another-el-fasher), [TNH 29/04/2026](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/analysis/2026/04/29/how-sudan-el-obeid-survives-drone-strikes-siege-warfare), [AJ 06/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/6/sudanese-army-retakes-bara-secures-el-obeid-in-north-kordofan), [Le Monde 22/03/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/le-monde-africa/article/2026/03/22/the-uae-is-reorganizing-its-arms-supply-network-for-sudanese-paramilitaries_6751682_124.html), [DW 13/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-civil-war-ethiopias-uaes-role-under-scrutiny/a-75913225), [TRT World 21/02/2026](https://www.trtworld.com/article/e24ea66b0dc2))

rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state. rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan. title: Türkiye's military incursion into northern Syria triggered by the nearing general elections results in the displacement of people from areas of conflict.
rationale:
In May 2022, Türkiye announced that it plans to continue its 30km military incursion into northern Syria, along the border, as part of its regional conflict against Kurdish armed groups that considers part of PKK network. Türkiye also announced plans to move 1 million Syrians back to Syria. This is a renewed rhetoric from similar statements in October 2021.

On 1 June, President Erdogan confirmed some of the areas that will be targeted sometime in the future when the military operation takes place: Tal Rifat and Manbij cities. He added that once these cities are under control, the forces will move to other areas, which means Kobani and the areas north of M4 route are likely to be targeted in the military offensive. Türkiye would seek to link the two separated areas under its control in northeast Syria.

Displacement and protection concerns are likely for the civilians living in the area. The estimated population of Tal Rifaat, Manbij (450,000), and Kobani is over 500,000.

The probability of an offensive was still low in June, with no significant military deployment at the border. The Turkish military plan has been opposed by the US, Russia and Iran., the Syrian government, and the de facto Kurdish authorities in the north, and is only backed by the Syrian armed groups that Turkey supports. 

In August, Turkiye announced that it is in the last stage of preparations for the military incursion into northern Syria. In the same month, the Turkish president hinted at readiness to contact the Syrian government. By late September, it became known that the Turkish intelligence chief held multiple meetings with the Syrian counterpart in Damascus, likely because of Russian mediation. 

In November an explosion hit the center of Istanbul, killing six and wounded 81 people. Turkish authority blamed the PKK/YPG in Northwest Syria for the explosion and is said the commands for the attack came from Kobane city, a Kurdish stronghold in Northwest Syria.

In the event of an incursion, there is also a low yet existing possibility of ISIS taking advantage of the conflict escalation to increase attacks across northern Syria, with the SDF being focused on fighting against the Turkish military.

Inflation rate has reached over 80% in October 2022, the highest in 24 years. High inflation and the economic crisis is the main challenge for the ruling party in next year's election. In early October, Erdogan renewed his pledge to send one million Syrians back to Syria at the Parliament. As the economic crisis deteriorates and opposition parties in Turkiye regularly call for Syrians to return to Syria, the issue is increasingly likely to shape the upcoming election season.

triggerList.title: A sense of marginalisation among many former President Al Assad loyalists
triggerList.description: The dismantling of Al Assad’s security apparatus without offering former personnel reintegration or salary continuity has deepened feelings of marginalisation among Alawite loyalists. Attempts to incorporate them into the new army have been met with mistrust from both opposition groups and minority communities, who fear a return of past abuses.

triggerList.title: Return to the War Spoils Committee activity
triggerList.description: Alawite communities fear the revival of the War Spoils Committee, originally established to confiscate the properties of Al Assad loyalists and later rebranded under different names. Although officially dormant, reports suggest its activities may have resumed in Damascus, heightening concerns of economic marginalisation and rising tensions.

triggerList.title: Delays in the investigations into the coastal killings
triggerList.description: If investigations into the coastal killings are delayed or neglected, unresolved grievances among Alawite communities—especially demands for justice and protection—could fuel further violence. Many Alawites view the investigation’s extension as a tactic to delay accountability and conceal facts.

rationale:
There is a high risk of tensions escalating between groups still loyal to the former President and others affiliated with the transitional Government. Resulting clashes in the next months could affect communities along religious lines, particularly conflict between Alawite communities and Sunni groups. The formation of armed groups, such as the Military Council to Liberate Syria, localised in western Syria and led by former Al Assad army commanders, indicates the likelihood of organised resistance against the transitional Government. Conflict dynamics are likely to be localised but could evolve into sectarian clashes in mixed-population areas, such as Homs and parts of Rural Damascus. Road blockages, targeted assassinations, and raids on civilian populations are likely scenarios, considering what already transpired in March 2025: clashes began on 6 March after armed Al Assad loyalists ambushed a security force convoy near Lattakia, killing 13 officers and prompting a harsh military response from the transitional Government’s allied forces. Between 6–8 March, transitional Government security operations targeting Alawite neighbourhoods and villages in Hama, Lattakia, and Tartous killed at least 396 people, predominantly Alawite civilians. Unconfirmed estimates indicate up to 1,500 fatalities during these attacks.
The current sociopolitical dynamics in the country point towards a high probability of an escalation of social tensions along sectarian lines. The dismantling of Al Assad’s security apparatus without a clear reintegration plan, such as restoring former personnel to comparable roles or maintaining their salaries, has deepened a sense of marginalisation among many former President Al Assad loyalists, most of whom are Alawite. Attempts by the new authorities to absorb some of these forces into the new national army have largely been met with suspicion, both from opposition groups — those who previously opposed Al Assad’s regime — and other minority communities, such as Druze and Kurds. These minority communities are concerned about the potential return of oppressive practices, referring both to the military tactics that the Al Assad regime used and to fears that former regime loyalists could regain influence. The latter has the potential to drive imbalances in representation within the new forces, as Kurdish and Druze participation remains limited or symbolic in key command structures.
Minority groups, including the Alawite community, are also concerned that the War Spoils Committee, originally established in 2015 in Idleb to confiscate the properties of Al Assad loyalists, may resume its activities in Damascus and other parts of Syria under the new transitional Government, despite reports that its operations have been dormant and rebranded in 2022 under different names, such as the Properties Committee or Housing Institution. The confiscation of properties will further economically marginalise the Alawite and aggravate tensions. Some reports indicate that confiscations have resumed, though there has been no official announcement that the War Spoils Committee has been re-established. In January 2025, unidentified armed men claiming to be from the General Security Service of the transitional Government ordered an unknown number of Alawite families to evict their homes in Damascus.
Despite the factors contributing to the likelihood of further clashes between Al Assad loyalists and Sunni armed groups, there are efforts aimed at de-escalation. President Ahmed Al Sharaa has condemned the killings of Alawites and pledged to hold all involved accountable, including those within his own ranks. In March, he announced the formation of an independent national committee comprising judges to specifically investigate the events and violations in coastal areas. The committee has also engaged in controversial dialogue with figures from the Al Assad Government, including Fadi Saqr, a former commander of the National Defence Forces accused of abuses against Sunni civilians, as part of broader efforts to engage Alawite communities and prevent renewed violence.
If the investigations are delayed or neglected and the grievances among Alawite communities are not adequately addressed, particularly demands for justice, transparent accountability for the killings, and protection from further reprisal, besides addressing fears of exclusion and collective punishment, this will likely contribute to further violence. Already, the Alawite have found unwelcome a three-month extension beginning in April granted by President Al Sharaa on the deadline for the investigation of the coastal killings, stating concerns of buying time to hide facts. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

triggerList.title: Weak control over Sunni armed groups
triggerList.description: The transitional Government’s weak control over Sunni armed groups has been a key trigger for renewed clashes with the Druze, as some militias operate independently and target minority communities. This lack of oversight undermines state authority and fuels sectarian violence, particularly around Al Sweida and Damascus.

triggerList.title: Fractured security landscape
triggerList.description: The fractured security landscape, marked by divisions within the transitional Government’s forces and perceived bias toward Sunni factions, has eroded trust among Druze communities. Failed mediation efforts and the involvement of affiliated militias in the violence have further exposed the state's inability to ensure protection.

triggerList.title: Israel likely to deepen its involvement
triggerList.description: Israel is likely to escalate its involvement by moving from airstrikes to deploying troops or proxies near Druze-majority areas, citing protection as a pretext. This risks triggering clashes with the transitional Government and fueling wider sectarian conflict.

triggerList.title: Growing division among the Druze
triggerList.description: The Druze community is increasingly divided, with some leaders cooperating with the transitional Government and others rejecting its legitimacy and calling for international protection (especially from Israel) or self-governance. These internal fractures risk sparking local clashes and creating openings for external interference or renewed attacks by Sunni armed groups.

rationale:
A further escalation of clashes between Sunni armed groups and Druze communities is likely, following a sectarian flare-up in late April 2025 and the transitional Government’s failure to contain the security fallout. Escalations may spread across Al Sweida and southern Damascus districts, particularly if Israel’s involvement intensifies or Druze factions become fragmented further.
On 26 April, a fabricated audio recording attributed to a Druze individual insulting the Prophet Muhammad circulated online, prompting enraged Sunni non-state armed groups to attack Druze neighbourhoods near Damascus. Clashes broke out on 28 April in the predominantly Druze districts of Jaramana and Sahnaya in Damascus as local Druze fighters exchanged fire with Sunni gunmen. The fighting spread south to Al Sweida governorate in villages including Al Soura Al Kubra, Ira, and Rasas, killing around 100 people from both sides. The clashes displaced an unknown number of families from some affected areas, likely within the governorate and temporarily.
The transitional Government’s inability to maintain security, coupled with weak control over Sunni armed groups, has emerged as a major trigger for renewed Druze-Sunni clashes. Some of these militias have independently targeted minority communities, including the Druze. Sunni armed groups, whether affiliated with the transitional Government or operating independently, are likely to launch further attacks on Druze-populated areas in Al Sweida and around Damascus, especially along the Damascus–Al Sweida highway and the Al Sweida–Dar’a border.
Sunni armed groups in Syria may target Druze communities for a combination of sectarian and strategic reasons. Some Sunni factions, including former HTS members, have historically viewed the Druze as heretical, leading to attacks, forced conversions, and property seizures justified by extremist ideology. Al Sweida is also important for Sunni armed groups to control because of its strategic location and political symbolism. Geographically, it borders key Sunni-dominated regions such as Dar’a and provides access to smuggling routes into Jordan, making it a vital corridor for the movement of fighters, weapons, and supplies. Politically, asserting control over Al Sweida allows Sunni factions to disrupt any future attempts at Druze autonomy or external support from Druze populations in Lebanon and the Golan Heights.
In response, Druze fighters are expected to retaliate, particularly in the absence of swift and effective intervention by the authorities. Previous government efforts to contain the violence have failed, as affiliated militias have themselves been involved in the clashes, exposing deep operational fragmentation. In April, the Government deployed limited forces and attempted mediation, but divisions within the security apparatus and perceived bias towards Sunni factions weakened its response. This fractured security landscape has intensified mistrust among Druze communities, especially following the mass killings of Alawites by Sunni armed groups in March 2025, an outcome the Druze fear they may also face. As a result, Druze militias have refused to disarm, with no indication that the transitional Government can address its current issue of having weak state control.
Israel will likely deepen its involvement, shifting from air strikes to deploying troops or proxies near the Druze-majority areas under the pretext of protecting them, risking confrontation with the transitional Government. In such cases, fighting could erupt in Al Sweida and surrounding villages, the outskirts of Damascus (Jaramana and Sahnaya), and possibly Quneitra, where the Druze are mostly located. Displacement from Druze-majority and nearby Sunni areas will likely follow, increasing humanitarian needs.
Israel’s interference in the tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government is likely to drive wider confrontations between Druze and Sunni armed groups, especially in the case of further Israeli ground incursions or the direct arming of Druze factions. In the clashes that happened in late April, Israeli drones and jets targeted Sunni armed groups near Sahnaya and bombed sites close to the presidential palace in Damascus. While Israel claimed these were defensive actions in support of the Druze, most Druze leaders have rejected the gesture, fearing it serves Israeli interests in expansion and not theirs. It also portrays them as allies to Israel, an idea that most Druze reject. Syrian officials have condemned the strikes as violations of sovereignty, and activists have accused Israel of using the clashes between the Druze and Sunni armed groups to justify deeper interference and military expansion in southern Syria.
A compounding factor likely to aggravate this conflict and the subsequent humanitarian impact is growing division among the Druze. Some Druze groups, including leaders from the Men of Dignity movement, have engaged with the transitional Government, joined ceasefire talks between Druze and Sunni armed groups, and integrated into local security forces to protect their areas. Others, led by figures such as Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, have rejected cooperation, calling the Government ‘terrorists’ and demanding international protection. Some activists in Al Sweida have even called for Druze self-governance over Al Sweida, citing instances in the past when the Druze managed their own affairs independently. So far, no fighting has broken out internally between Druze factions, but tensions are rising. If one side accuses the other of compromising community safety, local clashes are likely to erupt, causing more insecurity in affected areas in southern Syria or some districts in Damascus. Fractures among the Druze community can also allow for foreign interference from Israel or create openings for Sunni armed groups to attack the Druze again, possibly leading to further tensions.
De-escalation between Druze and Sunni armed groups depends on the transitional Government’s ability to control Sunni militias and protect Druze areas. Local ceasefires show that dialogue with Druze leaders can lead to a de-escalation of fighting, avoiding further clashes. That said, these arrangements remain fragile given some opposing Druze factions rejecting deals, local resistance to disarmament, the absence of official investigations into the violence, and the role of external parties such as Israel, whose interventions can contribute to deepening sectarian divisions. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

triggerList.description: The transitional Government’s ongoing inability to maintain security in southern Syria has created a power vacuum that Israel is increasingly filling. As armed groups remain active and state control weakens, Israel has issued ultimatums and taken military action to prevent perceived threats near its border.

triggerList.title: Israeli actions in Southern Syria cause a legitimacy crisis for Al-Sharaa
triggerList.description: Currently Al-Sharaa's takeover of SDF territories allows him to project a strong image at home to deal with insecurity, aloowing for diplomatic efforts to supercede military responses to Israel. However, Israeli forces in Al-Quneitra are increasing their activity, with arrests of farmers, spraying of crops and shootings at civilians. If local protest grows to this, as well as increased action by the Druze, Al-Sharaa may politically be forced to act.

rationale:
Israel is likely to expand deeper into southern Syria to prevent a potential return of Iran-backed militias, such as Hezbollah, and respond to escalating sectarian violence, particularly near Druze communities, under the pretext of security and humanitarian intervention. This expansion, driven by the transitional Government’s inability to maintain control and provide protection, could result in further displacement and local clashes.
Immediately after the fall of Al Assad’s rule in December 2024, Israel expanded its presence in southern Syria, seizing the demilitarised buffer zone (around 400km²) beyond the Golan Heights and occupying strategic areas in Quneitra, including Tel Al Hara and several border villages. The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) launched intensive air strikes targeting Syrian and Iranian military infrastructure, significantly weakening local resistance, which included remnants of Syrian army units and Iran-backed militias still active in the area at the time. These moves prompted clashes and displacement, notably from villages such as Al Hameidiyyeh, Rasem Al Rawadi, and Um Batna in Quneitra, with at least 100 Syrian families forcibly displaced by December. Many displaced civilians fled to Damascus or safer towns outside Israeli-held territory.
Israel sees the potential return of Iran-backed militias, especially Hezbollah, as a driver for further expansion in southern Syria, regardless of how likely that return may be. Although many of these forces withdrew after Al Assad’s fall, Israeli officials remain concerned they will regroup in areas near the Golan Heights, such as Quneitra and parts of western Dar’a governorate. The IDF are already positioned just over 20km from Damascus and have declared the presence of any Iranian or Iranian-backed groups a red line, indicating it would trigger immediate air strikes or other military responses to prevent their advancement near Israeli-controlled areas. The transitional Government has condemned the Israeli presence but avoided direct confrontation, focusing instead on internal stability. If Hezbollah attempts to re-establish rocket sites or weapon routes, Israel will likely push deeper into Quneitra or even Dar’a to enforce its buffer zone.
If sectarian attacks escalate near Israeli-held areas, especially against Druze communities, Israel is also likely to expand its presence in Syria under the pretext of protecting the minorities. For example, in April 2025, the IDF conducted air strikes near Damascus, targeting Sunni armed groups accused of attacking Druze civilians in Sahnaya district in the governorate, and subsequently evacuated three wounded Druze individuals to Israeli hospitals. Israel has publicly committed to protecting Syrian Druze. With Sunni and other armed groups subjecting Druze-majority towns to attacks, any assault may prompt a group of Druze leaders to seek Israeli help, especially the ones following Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, who is trying to establish stronger relations with Israel. A wider Israeli incursion into Al Sweida may be framed as a humanitarian intervention to protect Druze civilians from sectarian violence or Government-affiliated militias, though most Druze still reject annexation and prefer local autonomy within Syria under the transitional Government.
Another factor triggering Israel’s expansion into southern Syria is the transitional Government’s continued struggle with lack of security. Some non-state armed groups remain active in Quneitra and Dar’a. With some of Al Assad’s Syrian army units fleeing the country and others switching allegiance to the new Government, Israel has stepped in, issuing ultimatums for groups in the Yarmouk Basin to surrender all weapons, submit to home searches, and evacuate their villages or face military action. This has forced many families to evacuate their homes. Israeli officials claim the move is necessary to prevent armed groups from building up near their border. If the transitional Government fails to gain control, Israel is likely to deepen its presence, expanding the buffer zone under the pretext of counterterrorism. So far, the transitional Government has not taken any steps to oppose Israel’s expansion in southern Syria.
The IDF could move far beyond the initial 15km buffer zone towards the Damascus–Al Sweida highway, aiming to secure most of Quneitra and Dar’a and parts of Al Sweida. Syrian factions, including armed groups affiliated with the transitional Government, might try to stop the advance, though their capacity to pose a sustained military threat remains limited owing to fragmentation, resource constraints, and a lack of advanced weaponry. There is also a low to medium likelihood of Iran and Hezbollah reopening fronts in Lebanon or southern Syria to slow Israeli gains. The probability of large-scale retaliation remains moderate to low, and isolated attacks or proxy activity are more likely.
The continued absence of the transitional Government in these areas, its inability to counter Israeli expansion, and failure to protect civilians are likely to fuel further tensions and protests similar to the ones that erupted in Al Sweida in April 2025 against Israel and the Government’s failure to protect civilians. Between 8 December 2024 and 12 June 2025, Israeli attacks killed at least 22 civilians in Al Sweida, Dar’a, Quneitra, and Rural Damascus. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs
triggersPreview:
Trigger ID: R1002 - T0513
Title: Increased crackdown on smuggling routes
Description: 
The Syria–Lebanon border remains a major smuggling corridor for fuel, weapons, and drugs—particularly Captagon—facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. Efforts by Syria’s transitional Government to crack down on these routes have triggered violent resistance from local armed clans, risking further cross-border clashes in areas where smuggling underpins local power and livelihoods.
Sources: 
https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysi

triggerList.title: Increased crackdown on smuggling routes
triggerList.description: The Syria–Lebanon border remains a major smuggling corridor for fuel, weapons, and drugs—particularly Captagon—facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. Efforts by Syria’s transitional Government to crack down on these routes have triggered violent resistance from local armed clans, risking further cross-border clashes in areas where smuggling underpins local power and livelihoods.

triggerList.title: Hezbollah presence near the Lebanon - Syria border
triggerList.description: Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeastern border, supported by allied Shia clans and control over key smuggling routes, is viewed by Syria’s transitional Government as a security threat. Although direct clashes have been avoided, rising tensions and recent incidents—including the shelling of Shia villages and weapons seizures—have strained relations between Hezbollah, Syria, and the Lebanese Government.

rationale:
The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. After Al Assad’s fall, Syria’s transitional Government’s forces launched an anti-smuggling campaign in early 2025, targeting routes used by Hezbollah-linked clans near Al Qasr village on the Lebanese side of the border. Armed networks, such as the Jaafar clan (of Lebanon), resisted violently, ambushing Syrian patrols and firing anti-tank rockets. These confrontations escalated into clashes in March near Al Qasr.
Without clear coordination between Lebanese and Syrian authorities, both aiming to stop smuggling, efforts to dismantle these networks will likely trigger more cross-border skirmishes, especially in areas where smuggling remains a main source of income and power for local armed groups.
On 16 March 2025, clashes broke out along the Syria–Lebanon border after transitional Government soldiers crossed into Lebanon and were shot by local Lebanese clans. Syria’s transitional Government accused Hezbollah of abducting and executing three of its soldiers, which Hezbollah denied. In response, Syrian troops shelled Lebanese border villages, killing civilians and triggering counterfire from local clans and the Lebanese Army. The two days of fighting killed at least ten people, including a 15-year-old boy, and wounded over 50 in Al Qasr. The two Governments reached a ceasefire on 17 March, ending the clashes.
Areas including Al Qasr have served as hubs for Iranian weapon transfers, protected by clan networks aligned with Hezbollah. Another factor driving tensions between Syria and Lebanon is, in fact, Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeast border and its ties to local Shia clans and longstanding smuggling routes from Syria. Syria’s new transitional Government sees these ties as a security threat and has targeted Shia-populated border zones, shelling villages and expelling Lebanese Shia families. Hezbollah has avoided direct clashes with Syria’s transitional Government so far, but tensions have been rising between the two parties and within Lebanon, between Hezbollah and the Lebanese Government. When Lebanese forces seized Hezbollah weapons in April, local supporters of the party and armed groups accused the Lebanese army of betraying them for cooperating with Syria.
If crackdowns on smuggling continue and Hezbollah and drug-smuggling criminal groups see their supply routes further threatened, localised armed confrontations along the border also have the potential to turn into broader fighting. Syrian forces already advanced up to 5–7km into Lebanese territory around Al Qasr in March to dismantle smuggling routes, and further incursions to similarly shallow depths — meaning within the 5–7km border zone — remain possible, though recent diplomatic talks between the Governments of Lebanon and Syria in April and the creation of a joint border committee may reduce the likelihood of a sustained escalation. The committee, established as part of a bilateral border agreement, is a ministerial-level body tasked with coordinating border management, preventing unauthorised crossings, and overseeing dispute resolution in sensitive areas.
Although Syrian forces have imposed military control over the border with Lebanon, challenges such as difficult terrain, Hezbollah’s presence, and some southern clans’ reliance on smuggling continue to threaten lasting border security. These factors may enable smuggling networks to regroup, casting doubt on Syria’s capacity for sustained and effective border monitoring. Hezbollah could respond militarily to any advance of Syrian troops, not only to defend strategic smuggling routes that sustain its operations but also to assert its role as a protector of Lebanese sovereignty and maintain influence in border areas with high Shia presence. That said, considering the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel between October 2023 and November 2024, which significantly weakened Hezbollah’s military capacity, the likelihood of its direct engagement remains between medium to low.
Given its limited capacity and history of constrained responses, including during recent Israeli operations, the Lebanese Army is unlikely to play a decisive role but may be drawn into localised clashes. On the other hand, Syrian Sunni armed groups could exploit the instability to target Lebanese and Syrian Shia communities in border areas, driven by sectarian tensions and perceptions of Hezbollah’s alignment with Al Assad’s rule, further escalating the violence. Although the likelihood of escalating tensions and an advance by the new Syrian army remains moderate, the consequences could include a prolonged border conflict, mass displacement, and rising casualties on both sides. [(ACAPS 22/07/2025)](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

title: Severe shortage of services triggers unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps
triggersPreview:
Trigger ID: R1003 - T0515
Title: US funding freeze
Description: 
The US funding freeze, ordered in January 2025, halted nearly all humanitarian aid to northeastern Syria, including critical support for Al Hol and Al Roj camps. This led to the suspension of essential services like water, sanitation, food distribution, and security, creating severe gaps in camp management and raising the risk of unrest, disease outbreaks, and mass escape attempts.
Sources: 
https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/the-foreign-aid-freeze-poses-risks-to-us-interests-in-syria 
https://www.atlanticcouncil.or

triggerList.title: US funding freeze
triggerList.description: The US funding freeze, ordered in January 2025, halted nearly all humanitarian aid to northeastern Syria, including critical support for Al Hol and Al Roj camps. This led to the suspension of essential services like water, sanitation, food distribution, and security, creating severe gaps in camp management and raising the risk of unrest, disease outbreaks, and mass escape attempts.

triggerList.title: Severe lack of services
triggerList.description: Overcrowding and poor sanitation in Al Hol and Al Roj camps have led to disease outbreaks, including cholera in late 2024. The deterioration of WASH infrastructure, worsened by the US funding freeze, is likely to trigger mass rioting and escape attempts, particularly as weekly escapes, mostly by women and children, continue.

rationale:
If security in Al Hol and Al Roj camps collapses due to mass rioting or breakouts, ISIS-affiliated IDPs are likely to escape, regroup, and rejoin IS cells, potentially sparking renewed insurgencies in both Syria and Iraq. Unlike typical displacement sites, Al Hol and Al Roj function as detention facilities housing individuals with suspected IS ties, including non-Syrians and their families, making the risk of escape a security concern rather than a humanitarian one. As of April 2024, Al Hol hosts 42,000 people, and as of December 2024 Al Roj hosts over 2,600 people. As of early April, around 1,500 international troops remain in Syria, some of whom are tasked with preventing an IS resurgence; large-scale escapes could prompt renewed military operations in Syria. Iraqi officials have repeatedly warned that instability in Al Hol poses a direct threat to their internal security, as escaped IS members may attempt to cross into Iraq. Compounding this risk, a recent US funding freeze has weakened camp management, including WASH services, and could create further security vacuums that IS may exploit.
In January 2025, President Trump’s administration ordered a temporary freeze on nearly all US foreign aid, including humanitarian assistance. This affected funding to support humanitarian programmes and aid delivery in northeastern Syria. Aid and service delivery in Al Hol camp and Al Roj camp, hosting people displaced from areas previously under the control of the IS in Syria, had relied heavily on USAID support. In 2024, the United States spent over 1.2 billion US dollars on humanitarian aid in Syria and the Middle East, far more than any other donor. The US contributed with 24% of the total funding for Syria in 2024 within the coordinated response plan, followed by Germany which contributed with almost 14%. The United States contributions to Al Hol operations were ten times larger than those of the next largest funder.
Even with a short-term waiver for life-saving aid, the funding pause has already disrupted some humanitarian services. Humanitarian workers report that once USAID contracts were frozen, agencies delivering fuel, food and water became unsure how to proceed. The US-funded contractor Blumont, responsible for camp management at Al Hol and Al Roj, halted its activities on 24 January and pulled out all personnel, including security staff. This led to immediate gaps in essential operations of water trucking, sanitation, food distributions, and education. As the temporary measures used to manage the funding cuts crisis, such as using emergency funds and relying on other NGOs, are almost depleting, conditions in the camps are expected to worsen further. If US funding remains frozen, Al Hol and Al Roj will face acute shortages of food, fuel, and medicine, and the threat of disease which is likely to result in civil unrest and increase insecurity.
Overcrowding and poor sanitation have already fuelled disease. For example, a cholera outbreak impacted Al Hol camp in late 2024. The already poor WASH infrastructure in the camps, aggravated by the disruption of services due to the US funding freeze, is likely to trigger mass rioting and breakout attempts. Escapes are already common, especially from Al Hol camp, where escapes are reported every week. Most of those who escape are females and children of foreign nationalities.
On 26 May, the transitional Government and Kurdish authorities reached an agreement on a mechanism to safely evacuate Syrian families from Al Hol camp to Damascus. This measure is likely to ease pressure on camp services and reduce the likelihood of mass riots or breakout attempts by the camp’s IDPs. However, as of 12 June, it remains unclear how many people will be evacuated or whether the process has already begun. As of 27 May, approximately 200 Syrian IDPs were being prepared for return from Al Hol to Aleppo governorate. Additionally, 800 Iraqi IDPs were transferred from Al Hol to Al Jada’a camp in Mosul governorate, northern Iraq on 31 May. It is likely that those returns are not part of the new agreement between the transitional Government and the Kurdish authorities.([ECHO 19/06/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-historic-drought-impacting-food-security-dg-echo-un-ocha-fao-wfp-echo-daily-flash-19-june-2025), [FAO accessed12/09/2025](https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/bf52f354-c8f3-4f3f-9367-4d5347016c7b), [UNICEF accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.unicef.org/syria/situation-children-syria), [CSIC accessed 12/09/2025](https://features.csis.org/the-future-of-the-Euphrates-River/), [Ul 03/05/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com))

title: Water scarcity, especially in northeast and northwest Syria result in livelihoods and services’ disruptions, reduced food production and protests
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
triggersPreview:
Trigger ID: R1004 - T0517
Title: Dry winter and spring in 2024/2025
Description: 
Syria experienced an unusually dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. This contributed to declining water levels, including a major drop at the Euphrates Dam, worsening the country’s ongoing drought and water scarcity.
Sources: 
https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/giews-country-brief-syrian-arab-republic-04-april-2025
https://www.aljazeera.net/climate/longform/2025/4/22/%D8%A8%D9%85%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AC%D9%87%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%81

triggerList.title: Dry winter and spring in 2024/2025
triggerList.description: Syria experienced an unusually dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. This contributed to declining water levels, including a major drop at the Euphrates Dam, worsening the country’s ongoing drought and water scarcity.

triggerList.title: The weaponisation or politicisation of water
triggerList.description: Water scarcity in Syria is worsened by its politicisation and weaponisation. Türkiye has restricted Euphrates River flow below treaty levels and targeted infrastructure like the Alouk station, while Israel’s control over the Yarmouk basin and Unity Dam has cut off southern water sources, leaving over a million people affected.

triggerList.title: Upcoming lean season
triggerList.description: The lean season in Syria, typically from June to September, is expected to be one of the driest since 1989 due to poor rainfall and low reservoir levels. Water scarcity is likely to intensify during this period, further straining resources and increasing humanitarian needs.

rationale:
As of February 2025, about 13.6 million Syrians lack access to safe water and sanitation. Conflict since 2011 has damaged water infrastructure, resulting in a 40% reduction in the drinking water supply as of 2021. Almost half of the water systems no longer function reliably, forcing many to rely on tankers or unsafe wells. Ongoing electricity and fuel shortages have crippled water pumps and treatment plants, exacerbating water rationing and existing sanitation problems and driving disease outbreaks. 
Syria and the region experienced an exceptionally dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. In April 2025, water levels in Lake Euphrates Dam dropped to about six meters, which is five meters below the normal level.
Upstream water retention and weaponisation of water are also drivers of water scarcity in Syria. Türkiye has sharply reduced the Euphrates’ waters flow into Syria by restricting releases from upstream dams, such as the Atatürk Dam, often to around 200 cubic meters per second, well below the 500 cubic meters per second agreed in bilateral treaties. It has also used dam releases as political leverage and targeted key water infrastructure like the Alouk station in Al Hasakah in August 2024 and October 2023, disrupting access to water for more than a million people. Similarly, Israel’s occupation of the Golan Heights since 1981 and control over the Yarmouk basin and Unity (Al Wahda) dam in December 2024 have cut Syria off from its southern water sources. Communities, especially agricultural, living in southern Syria are likely to experience the impact of the loss of these water sources throughout 2025.
The lean season in Syria typically runs from June to September. In 2025, it will likely be one of the driest since 1989. April forecasts showed poor soil moisture and low reservoir levels heading into summer. As rainfall was far below average during the October–April season, water scarcity will likely intensify through June to September. Water levels are likely to continue to decrease in 2025, as projections indicate that by 2050, Syria’s water supply will decrease by 20%.
Water-related tensions have driven protests and localised disputes before, and are likely to drive further protests and disputes in 2025. In June 2024, water shortages and electricity cuts led to localised protests in Al Hasakeh. In February 2024, residents in Deir ez-Zor protested over lack of drinking water and accused local officials of corruption. In July 2022, displaced people in several camps in north Idlib protested water shortages, while water service providers went on a strike to protest an international organisation's decision to reduce water supplies.
Northeast and Northwest Syria, particularly Al Hasakeh, Al Raqqa, Idlib, and rural Aleppo, are likely hotspots for water-related tensions during the 2025 lean season. People’s livelihoods in these areas are already the most impacted by water scarcity, and they have limited alternative sources. If shortages persist, it is likely that people will protest at wells or water trucks, attempt to blockade water pipelines, or engage in local skirmishes over water resources. For example, communities might block a contested pump station or forcibly redirect tanker convoys. ([ECHO 19/06/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-historic-drought-impacting-food-security-dg-echo-un-ocha-fao-wfp-echo-daily-flash-19-june-2025), [FAO accessed12/09/2025](https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/bf52f354-c8f3-4f3f-9367-4d5347016c7b), [UNICEF accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.unicef.org/syria/situation-children-syria), [CSIC accessed 12/09/2025](https://features.csis.org/the-future-of-the-Euphrates-River/), [Ul 03/05/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com))

triggerList.description: A further expansion of Israeli positions, checkpoints or closed military zones beyond the current areas of control in Quneitra and western Dar'a could indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. If Israeli forces begin holding additional territory or restricting civilian access on a sustained basis, this could increase local resistance and create conditions for a broader Israeli-controlled zone extending towards areas linked to As-Sweida.

triggerList.title: Renewed large-scale violence in As-Sweida
triggerList.description: An escalation of violence between Druze groups, Syrian Government forces or other armed actors in As-Sweida could prompt Israel to reframe military intervention as necessary to protect the Druze population. This could revive calls for a Golan–As-Sweida humanitarian corridor and provide a justification for expanding or formalising Israeli military access in southern Syria.

triggerList.title: Establishment of a settler outpost
triggerList.description: Pioneers of Bashan or other Israeli settler groups successfully establishing a sustained civilian outpost inside southern Syria, rather than being detained and removed, could create pressure for Israeli forces to protect the settlement. This could accelerate the conversion of the existing military presence into a more permanent security or territorial arrangement.

rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions. ([Ynet 20/08/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bktp9qfyxx), [Ynet 16/09/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/hyhslcujxx), [Jewish Policy Center 01/10/2025](https://www.jewishpolicycenter.org/2025/10/01/focus-on-the-druze/), [AA 31/07/2025](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-finance-minister-calls-for-humanitarian-corridor-to-syria-s-suwayda-for-druze-community/3646880), [Reuters 26/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-syria-talks-hit-snag-over-humanitarian-corridor-sources-say-2025-09-26/), [AP 29/07/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-syria-netanyahu-jewish-settlers-bashan-461c4c4f686d5cf74f0617a7e70ffa29), [TOI 29/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/fringe-settler-group-sneaking-into-syria-in-bid-to-claim-land-for-jewish-outpost/), [TOI 11/08/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/three-settlement-activists-illegally-enter-syria-overnight-are-detained-by-idf/), [L'Orient Today 14/07/2026](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1541299/who-are-the-bashan-pioneers-the-israeli-settlers-eyeing-southern-syria.html), [Arab News 06/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649854/amp), [SOHR 27/06/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/en/383771/), [Enab Baladi 25/08/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/08/jordan-talks-fail-to-halt-israeli-incursions-in-southern-syria/), [EUAA accessed 28/07/2026](https://dip-aws.euaa.europa.eu/syria-security-situation/2142-territorial-control-and-main-armed-actors), [ACLED accessed 30/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [FP 24/07/2025](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/07/24/risks-israel-druze-policy-syria/))

title: Spreading of the violent insurgency of Cabo Delgado into the Tanzanian territory.
rationale:
There has been no violent attacks taking place in Tanzania since the entry of this risk in November. On 14 October, some 300 insurgents from Mozambique attacked Kitaya, a riverside border village in the Mtwara region. The Tanzanian authorities acknowledged for the first time an attack in Tanzania carried out by insurgents coming from the neighbouring country.
In November 2020, Tanzania and Mozambique have signed a memorandum of understanding aimed to join forces against ISIL-linked fighters in Cabo Delgado. Recently raids have been carried out in Tanzanian villages near the border and many fighters are believed to come from Tanzania.
The population of Mtwara region (which borders with Cabo Delgado) is over 1,270,000 people.

Update (Sep 2021): Rwandan and Tanzanian police forces held a bilateral meeting to discuss their approach to counter the possible threat of insurgents from Cabo Delgado. Terrorists fleeing from their hideouts in Mozambique may infiltrate the borders and establish cells in Rwanda, Tanzania or other neighboring countries.

triggerList.description: Regions with steep slopes are more susceptible to landslides when combined with heavy rainfall.

rationale:
Since 2010, the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in Tanzania have increased, including heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides. These events pose a significant threat to people’s lives, basic infrastructure, food security, and public health. According to Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts for February–April 2025, several regions will experience above-average rainfall, which could heighten existing vulnerabilities, such as weak infrastructure, poor waste management, and unsustainable land use.
Past floods in Kilimanjaro, Kilombero, Manyara, Mbeya, Morogoro, and Rufiji regions have had significant humanitarian and socioeconomic impacts, including loss of life, property destruction, displacement, and economic decline. Crop damage poses a serious threat to livelihoods, and stagnant floodwaters increase the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera and malaria. The lack of effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms further aggravate the crisis, leaving affected populations with limited coping capacity.

triggerList.title: Restrictions imposed by the Indian government on its rice exports, affecting the imports of rice by Timor-Leste
triggerList.description: The Indian government introduced measures aimed at stabilising domestic food prices which included a ban on exports of non-basmati white rice, 20% export duty on non-basmati parboiled rice, and the imposition of a minimum export price. These measures are aggravating the already worsened rice availability and subsequently consumption situation in Timor-Leste.

rationale:
RATIONALE AND IMPACT
Timor-Leste has around 262,000 people facing high acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) as per IPC projections for May - September 2023. The food insecurity situation will be worsened due to certain environmental and economic factors. Drought conditions due to the El Nino, high rice prices in the international market, and restrictions imposed by India on their rice exports worsen food insecurity outcomes

The entire country of Timor-Leste is showing signs of drought due to the ongoing El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) conditions and is forecasted to strengthen and persist until early 2024. Prolonged dry spells will negatively impact agriculture output in the country. The agriculture sector accounts for around 27% (around 63,000) of total employment. Outside of the labour force, around 162,000 people are subsistence foodstuff producers. 

The international rice prices surged between July and September 2023, which raised the costs of rice within Timor-Leste and the retail prices of imported rice in the country. The surge in rice prices have made it unaffordable for impoverished families in Timor-Leste. People in the country depend heavily on imports of rice, especially imported Indian rice which comprise around 90% of rice imports by Timor-Leste. The Indian government introduced measures aimed at stabilising domestic food prices which included a ban on exports of non-basmati white rice, 20% export duty on non-basmati parboiled rice, and the imposition of a minimum export price. These measures are aggravating the already worsened rice availability and subsequently consumption situation in Timor-Leste. 

Current stock of rice may only cover just over one month of national rice consumption needs. If the country is unable to secure enough rice and nutritious food as soon as possible, there will be further deterioration of the nutritional and food security status among the poorest and most vulnerable Timorese families. 

AGGRAVATING FACTORS
Oil and gas are the main export products in the fuel and mining products category. In 2022, fuel and mining products contributed to more than 80% of total exports. It also contributes to around 70% of total government revenues. Timor-Leste’s real GDP is estimated to fall by around 17% in 2023, primarily due to reduced oil and gas production.  The real GDP is expected to decline by 6% in 2024. The current and short-term economic situation will reduce livelihood opportunities, aggravating the food insecurity situation in the country.

Disappointing economic and labour reforms from new cabinet.

rationale:
Tunisians in the south of the country – especially in Tataouine province, where the unemployment rate is 30% – have been protesting since the Government failed to follow through on a 2017 agreement to create more jobs and development in the south. Tunisia is facing a worsening socioeconomic crisis compounded by the impact of COVID-19. In July, Tunisia asked to delay debt repayments to four countries, underscoring the dire condition of Tunisia's public finances. In July, in a meeting between Italian Minister of the Interior Luciana Lamorgese and Tunisian President Kais Saied, Lamorgese raised concerns over the recent spike in the number of Tunisian migrants crossing the Mediterranean Sea to Italy. Tunisian migrants are the biggest single national group reaching Italy by sea. Since the beginning of 2020, nearly 11,200 migrants have landed on Italy’s shores, more than 5,200 having set out from Tunisia and nearly 4,000 of them Tunisian citizens.

In case of unsatisfactory performance from the newly appointed cabinet, especially in terms of economic and employment reforms, the number of Tunisians and third-country nationals leaving from the coasts of Tunisia towards Italy in search of better livelihood conditions might increase, particularly during the summer months when sea and weather conditions are generally more stable. An increase in departures along the Central Mediterranean route exposes migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers to the dangers of death and injury, especially in case of lengthy response times from rescue teams, raising serious protection concerns.

triggerList.title: 2021 Elections

rationale: The streets of Uganda have been increasingly restive as the presidential elections inch closer. Opposition presidential candidate, Bobi Wine, has been subject to several arrests by national armed forces without justification. His supporters have taken to the streets to protest his arrests, and in the latest wave of protests, 38 people (to date, 24 November 2020) were killed and at least 36 injured. Police fired live rounds on the crowds, claiming that they had defied the COVID-19 pandemic restriction of a maximum of 200 people in a public space. Political protests: 3 people have died and 38 have been injured by live rounds fired at protesters who gathered in the streets after opposition party leader, presidential candidate, and rap/reggae artist Bobi Wine (aka Robert Kyagulanyi) was arrested and detained once more by government forces. This follows an arrest of Bobi Wine on Tuesday 3rd November, during which he was temporarily blinded when police smashed the car in which he was travelling and sprayed pepper spray into his eyes. Authorities countered civilians at the protest on the premise that large gatherings of more than 200 people are currently not allowed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and accusations that Bobi Wine was inciting unrest that put the citizens at a public health risk. There is currently no actual date for the forthcoming elections; they are due to take place sometime in 2021. The first arrest of Bobi Wine was after registering his candidacy for President in the upcoming Ugandan presidential elections threatens a potential turn to violence during, and in their aftermath.

triggerList.title: Implementation of information blackouts and internet shutdowns
triggerList.description: The government has recently issued directives imposing a blanket ban on live broadcasting of "unlawful processions" and has previously used internet shutdowns to manage national security. This move will remove the digital witness disrupting the ability to document security force conduct in real-time. Hence creating a window of impunity that encourages more aggressive state crackdowns, as security units like the Joint Anti-Terrorism Task Force (JATT) are more likely to use lethal force or carry out arbitrary arrests when they believe their actions are not being monitored by the international community or local media.

rationale: The risk of violence following Uganda’s January 2026 general elections is driven by a documented pattern of militarised state response to political opposition and the erosion of civic space. Historical precedents from the 2021 cycle, combined with current reports of over 160 enforced disappearances and the detention of more than 550 opposition members in the lead-up to the current polls, indicate a high likelihood of a violent post-election crackdown. Security forces, including the military and specialised units, have consistently used disproportionate force such as live ammunition, chemical irritants, and drone van abductions to suppress dissent and manage civil unrest. This volatility is further intensified by deep-rooted public frustration over governance, a significant urban-youth divide, and internal ruling party succession dynamics. With the Government already threatening internet shutdowns and enforcing bans on live broadcasting of unlawful processions, the lack of transparency creates a high-risk environment for severe human rights violations, arbitrary killings, and movement restrictions for civilians and humanitarian responders. ([DW 07/01/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/uganda-2026-election-system-explained-presidential-candidates-key-issues/a-75369002), [AP 06/01/2026](https://apnews.com/article/uganda-election-military-violence-bobi-wine-b3bec5ee8b68125c49ba9e91e9b992ac))

triggerList.description: Russia aims to decrease any support to Ukraine in the EU as it is a major donor.

rationale:
Prior to 2022, 90% of all exports from Ukraine were via its Black Sea ports, with the remaining 10% via land. Additionally, all seaports in Crimea have been under Russian occupation since 2014. In February 2022, Russia started a full-scale invasion against Ukraine and a sea blockade. 

In May 2022, the European Commission established alternative 'Solidarity Lanes', which are alternative export routes through the EU to support Ukraine. The Solidarity Lanes have enabled the export of around 60% of Ukraine's grain since 2022. The Grain deal reached in July 2022 also supported Ukraine's sea exports until Russia withdrew from it in July 2023. Although Ukraine managed to resume sea exports by targeting the Russian navy, it still depends on EU Solidarity Lanes. 

Farmers across EU are protesting against rising costs and taxes, environmental rules and competition from lower cost food imports. In Poland, protestors have been blocking Ukrainian agricultural products from transiting. 

The additional strain on Ukraine's economy that is already affected by war could increase as more EU farmers join the blockade of Ukraine's border with the EU. As sociopolitical tensions increase, the blockade could start affecting the movement of civilians and other goods, as well as humanitarian and defense related movements of goods and personnel. 

UPDATE 28 February 2024

According to media reports as at 28 February 2024, Poland is planning a temporary closure of the border with Ukraine, including the exchange of goods. The stated aim by Poland is to protect its market, despite Poland's ban on grain from Ukraine. This developing situation will likely lead to trade between Poland and Ukraine being affected. On 20 March, media reported a blockade at Medyka-Shehyni cross point for transportation buses for civilians traveling to and from Ukraine. On the same day, mass protests took place across Poland, with police estimating blockades in 570 locations, including against access into major cities and the capital Warsaw.

In reaction, Ukraine started planning to increase the use of the Danube River export route to avoid the potential Polish border blockade despite the ongoing risk of Russian attacks on Ukraine's ports and export infrastructure.

On 25 February 2024, there was a sabotage attack that resulted in spilling of 160 tons of grain from Ukraine transiting by railway through Poland to other countries. Prior to this incident, there were several small-scale incidents in which grain was deliberately spilled by protestors in Poland, with no suspects detained. The sabotage of grain and the usage of anti-Ukrainian slogans by some protestors in Poland increased tensions between Ukraine and Poland. 

UPDATE 30/03/2024

On 7 March, according to protest organisers 150,000 people took to the streets, while official figures stated there were 30,000 people.

On 20 March 2024, there were also country wide protests with 70,000 protestors, and 570 or 580 blockades in major cities including the capital Warsaw, as well as on the border with Ukraine where Polish protesters restricted the passage of buses transferring travellers at the Medyka-Shehyni crossing according to Ukraine's Border Guard Service, in addition to the movement of trucks with goods.

UPDATE 29/04/2024
Polish farmers suspended the blockades and protests on the border with Ukraine in late April 2024 after the Polish government decided to pay subsidies to the farmers, however there is yet some uncertainty whether the suspension would last.

The US will likely avoid acknowledging Russian violations in order to push a full ceasefire, the negotiations of which are ongoing, and which Russia will likely continue to delay, and the Russian forces use the end of the partial ceasefire in late April to wage a country-wide combined missile and drone attack against the energy infrastructure.
