rationale:
On 25 March 2025, the new US administration – under President Donald Trump – reached an agreement with Ukraine and Russia on a temporary 30-day pause in attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine agreed with the US on a list of energy facilities that Russia should stop attacking, although Russia took some oil and gas production facilities off the list and has continued attacking them.
It is unclear whether this partial ceasefire applies to the use of long-range missiles and drones or artillery. The full details of the partial ceasefire have not been made public. Energy infrastructure located near the front line remains vulnerable to damage.
Given the history of Russian forces violating ceasefire agreements since 2014, they are likely to also violate this agreement and resort to disinformation and false flag attacks to conceal the violations, possibly blaming Ukraine for disrupting the ceasefire agreement. In this context, US officials may downplay these violations to claim the success of the US-led ceasefire.
Russian forces, having stockpiled missiles and drones for use against the energy sector, may step up their attacks on civilian infrastructure, such as residential areas, as a sustained political tactic especially following the US-led negotiations for a full ceasefire. A recent such attack was on 4 April, which targeted a residential area in Kryvyi Rih city, Dnipropetrovska, killing 19 people (including 9 children). Alternatively, Russian forces could accumulate the missiles and drones that they planned to use in 2024 then launch a major countrywide combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure immediately after the partial ceasefire ends in late April while also stalling negotiations. ([ACAPS 13/09/2024](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20240913_ACAPS_Ukraine_Analysis_hub_Attacks_on_the_energy_infrastructure_in_Ukraine.pdf), [ACAPS 12/02/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250219_ACAPS_Ukraine_-_Energy_infrastructure_attacks-_Updated_outlook_and_impact_during_the_2024-2025_cold_season_.pdf), [Dixigroup 31/03/2025](https://dixigroup.org/en/analytic/russian-war-against-ukraine-energy-dimension-dixi-group-alert-weekly-review-93/), [Kyiv Independent 03/04/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-informs-us-about-russias-energy-ceasefire-violations/))

triggerList.title: Significant Military Defections
triggerList.description: Significant military defections in Venezuela would represent a major turning point capable of precipitating regime instability. Facing a growing U.S. military buildup in the Caribbean and increasing internal pressure, parts of the Venezuelan armed forces may begin to abandon loyalty to President Maduro.

triggerList.title: Economic Collapse Acceleration
triggerList.description: Recent data indicate that Venezuela’s economy continues to contract in 2025, primarily due to falling oil production exacerbated by U.S. sanctions. Inflation remains hyperinflationary, eroding real wages and purchasing power, especially for low-income populations. The depreciation of the national currency, combined with widening gaps between official and parallel exchange rates, further destabilises the economy. As economic conditions worsen, food and medicine shortages intensify, businesses close, unemployment rises, and poverty deepens.

rationale:
The current US military presence in the Caribbean marks the largest deployment in the region in decades, involving multiple strikes against vessels suspected of drug smuggling. This build-up has significantly heightened tensions with Venezuela, which perceives the presence as a direct threat and a prelude to regime change, prompting increased military mobilisation. Opposition groups are likely to interpret these developments as signals of external support or possible military intervention, potentially emboldening them to escalate activities such as strikes, protests, and sabotage. Such actions risk weakening state control and destabilising the Government.
Should opposition momentum grow and fractures emerge within the Nicolás Maduro regime’s internal cohesion, Venezuela could rapidly destabilise without a coordinated transition plan or sustained international engagement. This instability might create power vacuums, especially in regions with limited government presence. Non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and criminal networks could exploit this uncertainty to expand territorial control, particularly in economically strategic zones such as Bolívar state, known for its gold reserves, and the Orinoco Oil Belt, the centre of oil extraction. Civilians in these areas would face severe consequences, including increased violence, targeted attacks, forced displacement, and restricted movement.
At the same time, US antitrafficking campaigns disrupting Caribbean routes for gold, oil, and narcotics will aggravate the crisis by further destabilising the local economy. The intensification of political and economic instability may trigger new waves of displacement, pushing thousands to seek refuge in neighbouring countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador. These countries, already hosting millions of Venezuelan refugees, will face increased pressure on their humanitarian and basic service systems. ([The Conversation 02/10/2025](https://theconversation.com/venezuela-and-us-edge-toward-war-footing-but-domestic-concerns-international-risks-may-hold-washington-back-266509), [WLRN 22/09/2025](https://www.wlrn.org/americas/2025-09-22/u-s-military-buildup-in-caribbean-signals-broader-campaign-against-venezuela), [Newsweek 03/10/2025](https://www.newsweek.com/five-signs-possible-us-war-venezuela-10821751), [Diario Libre 07/20/2025](https://www.diariolibre.com/usa/actualidad/2025/10/07/posible-ataque-a-venezuela-operaciones-militares-de-ee-uu/3270080), [NYT 07/10/2025](https://www.nytimes.com/es/2025/10/07/espanol/america-latina/trump-maduro-venezuela-guerra.html), [The Guardian 07/10/2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/07/venezuela-on-edge-trump-regime-change-whispers), [AJ 04/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/9/4/venezuela-has-the-worlds-most-oil-why-doesnt-it-earn-more-from-exports))

title: The Southern Transitional Council push for an independence of the south results in local fighting, leading to displacements and increased needs for the affected
rationale: since the beginning of 2023, Political conflict in southern Yemen have deepened and may escalate into open fighting, especially in Aden as the interim capital and main port for the Southern Yemen, with the potential to spread into other governorates such as Lahj, Abyan, Ad Dali’, and Hadramawt,  .  The STC has been openly advocating for an independent Southern state, using the deterioration of the economy, depreciation of local currency and worsening of public services (especially electricity and healthcare), and the overall frustration of the population, to maintain support for its goal of independence. Their position contradicts that of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of Yemen’s Internationally Recognized Government (IRG), which operates outside of DFA-controlled areas (De-Facto Authority known also as Houthis/Ansar Allah movement). On 8 May 2023, the head the STC has restructured the council leadership by appointing three of the PLC members as vice presidents. This was done in an attempt to make clear that the STC represented all the southern governorates, including Hadramawt, the key southern governorate rich in oil and gas fields. In response, Saudi Arabia and the IRG retaliated by forming the Hadramawt National Council and establishing the National Shield Forces, reporting directly to the Head of PLC. These forces may eventually find themselves in conflict with STC’s forces (AGSIW 18/07/2023; sanaacenter 09/03/2023;  south24.net 13/02/2023; Yemen Future 22/09/2023;  sanaacenter 10.03/2023). The creation of the Hadramawt National Council was intended to create an alternative entity to the STC and its secessionist aspirations (Middle East Institute 24/07/2023; south24.net 13/02/2023; Yemen Future 21/09/2023). The demand for a southern secession escalated recently when the head of the STC, threatened to use force to protect the STC’s objectives for the secession of southern Yemen's provinces during meeting with STC’s military and security forces (debriefer 10/07/2023). Furthermore, the STC threatened to expel all IRG’s forces from Hadramawt and other southern governorates during a public rally in the city of Al Mukalla (Debriefer. 08/07/2023). Also, while attending the United Nations General Assembly's annual meeting, the head of STC stated that he will prioritize establishing a independence country in the south In any In negotiations with Houthi (yahoo.news 22/09/2023). In response to the STC declarations, on 24 June 2023, the head of the PLC visited Hadramawt for the first time, timing the visit to highlight the growing disagreement between STC and IRG  ( Al Bawaba 26/06/2023). On 23 June, in the same week of the head of the PLC visit to Hadramawt, the STC leader stated that peace in Yemen can only be accomplished when “southerners’ calls” for independence are addressed, and that the IRG corruption is driving the country to the brink of economic failure. Head of STC also stated that Yemen cannot move forward in any peace process unless the issue of southern independence is addressed ( Middle East Eye 23/6/2023)AGSIW 18/7/2023; ).

triggerList.title: US or Israeli military strikes on Iran
triggerList.description: The Houthis have explicitly pledged to respond to any US or Israeli military strike on Iran, most likely by escalating attacks on Israel, Red Sea maritime traffic, and US military assets in the region. Any such Houthi response would likely invite a renewed US or Israeli air campaign targeting Houthi military and economic infrastructure, including Hodeidah port and other critical installations in northwest Yemen. A January 2026 speech by the Houthi leader signalled the group's combat readiness and assigned equal blame to Saudi Arabia for recent US and Israeli attacks, indicating the potential for a broader regional escalation.
triggerList.objective: No

rationale:
The de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) have pledged to respond to any US attack against Iran in early 2026, most likely by escalating Red Sea maritime attacks and launching direct strikes against Israel and US military bases in the region. By 19 February 2026, this risk had become imminent following a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US Administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement, placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March. Any Houthi retaliatory attack would likely invite a renewed, intensified US or Israeli air campaign against Houthi military and economic infrastructure, with ports and other critical civilian infrastructure among the most likely targets.
Previous rounds of strikes have demonstrated the severe humanitarian consequences of this pattern. Israeli strikes on Sana’a between August–September 2025 killed at least 45 people and wounded over 230 others across multiple incidents, with residential areas, a fuel station supplying hospitals, and media offices among the sites struck. Al Hodeidah port – through which approximately 70% of Yemen's commercial imports and 80% of its humanitarian assistance pass – has been repeatedly targeted, with its operational capacity severely degraded. This infrastructure damage is compounded by access constraints stemming from the DFA's targeting of humanitarian organisations. The DFA has increasingly accused humanitarian responders of criminality, raided UN compounds, detained staff, and levelled accusations of espionage against aid workers. These raids and detentions have a cooling effect on NGOs working in DFA-controlled areas, with organisations reducing staffing to 'essential levels' and lowering operational risk thresholds, leading to reduced programming or withdrawal.
The WFP’s January 2026 decision to shut down operations and lay off all 365 staff in northern Yemen exemplifies this compounding effect, leaving 18 million people without humanitarian aid. This, alongside restrictions and the targeting of UN bodies and INGOs by the DFA, means the transfer of risks to grassroots organisations, which often serve as the first and sometimes only responders in remote areas.
A resumption of this pattern in the context of a wider US–Iran escalation would simultaneously degrade infrastructure and intensify humanitarian space contraction through the targeting of aid workers and facilities. With port damage reducing supply throughput and DFA harassment driving the withdrawal of major institutional responders, escalated strikes would compound humanitarian access constraints at a moment when Yemeni organisations – already bearing increased operational burden – face heightened political targeting. With 23.1 million people projected to be in need in 2026, this would deepen a severe humanitarian crisis.

triggerList.description: Enforcement of the Houthi-declared maritime blockade or attacks on commercial shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait triggers broader international military involvement, including through the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition (announced 30 July 2026).

triggerList.title: Large-Scale Intra-Yemeni Fighting
triggerList.description: Intensified military mobilisation and sustained clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed IRG.

rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure. ([OCHA 29/03/2026](https://yemen.un.org/en/312711-ocha-yemen-yemen-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-march-2026), [JP 25/07/2026](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-903606), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemen-teeters-towards-renewed-war-shadow-iran-conflict-2026-07-24/), [ICG 17/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/qna/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-iran-saudi-arabia/yemens-de-facto-truce-risk-how-prevent-return-war), [AJ 05/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/5/at-least-15-yemeni-government-troops-killed-in-hodeidah-fighting), [The Guardian 23/07/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/23/houthis-claim-attack-ship-tanker-saudi-arabia-red-sea), [Reuters 23/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-say-they-attacked-saudi-tankers-red-sea-threatening-new-chokepoint-iran-2026-07-23/), [Arab News 25/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2652234/middle-east), [SPA 25/07/2026](https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2640956))

title: Deterioration of food security due to poor agricultural seasons, COVID-19, and economic crisis
riskType: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale:
Zimbabwe imposed new Covid-19 restrictions, following an increase in cases at the beginning of June. Restrictions, include private and public offices being limited to a 50-percent capacity, and retail businesses, markets, and shops may operate from 08:00-18:00. Such restrictions might impact economy and ultimately affect food insecurity. 
Over 600 cases confirmed during the first week of June, while in May, only 132 new cases were recorded in the first week.
Consecutive poor agricultural seasons, current economic issues, and the impacts of COVID-19 measures are contributing to increased acute food insecurity across the country, particularly rural areas. 5-6 million people are estimated to experience Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and above levels of food insecurity in rural areas between October and December 2020, compared to 4.3 million people between February and June 2020.

Update: IPC projection for the period between Jan and March 2021 is 35% of the population analysed to be in Crisis (IPC-3) or above, compared to 27% in October-December 2020.
“The food insecurity is primarily due to shocks and hazards experienced in the country such as drought, reduced livelihood opportunities due to restrictions linked to COVID-19, pests and diseases, and high food prices.”

triggerList.title: Climate and Weather Phenomena
triggerList.description:
The World Meteorological Organization's declaration of El Niño's onset, coupled with a 90% likelihood of its persistence into late 2023, acts as a primary catalyst for the anticipated dry spell. This meteorological phenomenon is poised to usher in arid conditions, particularly impacting Zimbabwe's agricultural season.
Compounding this looming threat are the lingering effects of past extreme weather events such as Cyclone Freddy and other significant floods. These prior disasters have already eroded the resilience of Zimbabwe's populace and its infrastructure, rendering them more susceptible to the adverse impacts of subsequent climatic shocks, including the predicted El Niño-induced drought.

triggerList.title: Pre-existing Vulnerabilities and Crises
triggerList.description:
Zimbabwe's protracted economic crisis is a major underlying issue, significantly hindering people's ability to cope with unexpected events and limiting their access to vital resources. This ongoing instability makes the population far more susceptible to various vulnerabilities.
Furthermore, the presence of ongoing or recurrent disease outbreaks, such as cholera and typhoid, highlights critical weaknesses within the country's public health systems and its water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure. This fragile state leaves the population highly vulnerable to even more widespread disease outbreaks, especially those that could be triggered by water scarcity.

rationale:
The World Meteorological Organization has announced the beginning of El Niño, which has a 90% probability of continuing through the second half of 2023. During the November 2023 to March 2024 period, El Niño is expected to drive drier conditions than average in Zimbabwe. This period coincides with the agricultural season, which might significantly affect crop planting, growth, and harvest.

In 2023, an estimated three million people, including two million children, will need humanitarian assistance as a result of the effects of drought, Cyclone Freddy, floods, disease outbreaks, and the protracted economic crisis in the country. Priority needs include nutrition, health, protection, education, and WASH services.

The effects of El Niño could heighten the needs of the people in Zimbabwe who have not fully recovered from the impact of currently below-average rainfall, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and economic instability. The reduction in yield and scarcity of water resulting from El Niño would respectively lead to increased food insecurity and heighten WASH needs. Water scarcity is likely to lead to the spread of endemic diseases, such as cholera and typhoid, which can result from poor sanitation and water contamination.
